  • Alt-Enter queues. The message waits for the run to finish, then starts a new run of its own with the selection current when it was queued. Queued messages run one at a time, oldest first.

On an idle session both keys simply start a run. The daemon decides between starting, steering, and queueing atomically, so a run that another client starts or that ends while you type only changes which of those happens.

The Pending strip shows both lanes: ⏳ rows are steered messages and ⏭ rows are queued ones. It shows up to three rows and folds additional entries into +N more. Several clients can share one daemon (see Architecture); a message another client sent is labelled with that client, such as · tui-0192f3. Click one of your own rows to take that message back into the composer for editing, or press Up in an empty composer to take back your newest one. Only the client that sent a message can take it back.

Queued messages run only after the current run completes normally. If the run fails or is cancelled, or the daemon restarts mid-run, the queue is cleared, and each client gets its own unsent messages, steered or queued, back in its composer, as it does with steered messages a run never reached. This happens only for a run that ends while the TUI is connected; replayed history never restores text, so opening or reattaching to an old session leaves the composer alone.

docs.title: Selection and clipboard
docs.text:
Drag in the conversation or composer to select text. Ctrl-C copies the selected text and clears the selection; Ctrl-X cuts only a composer selection. With no selection, Ctrl-C cancels the active run; when there is nothing to interrupt, pressing it twice within two seconds quits. Esc clears a selection before it can count toward the double-Esc run-cancel gesture.

Conversation copy removes role gutters, borders, and code-fence chrome, so code is copied as raw source. Clipboard writes use OSC 52 and work over SSH when the terminal emulator supports OSC 52.

docs.title: Session picker
docs.text:
/sessions lists the root sessions of the directory the TUI started in, newest first under day headings; type to filter them by title, and press Enter or click a row to open one.

  • Ctrl+A, or the All directories button, lists every directory's sessions instead, each row naming its directory; press it again (the button now reads This directory) to go back. In the search field, Home still moves to the start of the text.
  • Ctrl+D, Delete while the list has focus, or the Delete button asks to delete the highlighted session. The confirmation names the session and says how many subagent sessions go with it; y or Enter (or Confirm) deletes it, and n or Esc (or Cancel) keeps it. While it is open, the rows behind it do not respond to clicks.

Deleting removes the whole tree from disk: the session, its subagents, and their messages, tool output, and attachments. It cannot be undone. The daemon refuses while the session or one of its subagents is running, while another cookie process owns it, and when it changed since the picker showed it; the status line then says why. A daemon older than client protocol 1.5 cannot delete sessions, and the TUI says so instead of asking. When the session you are viewing is deleted, from this TUI or another client, the TUI leaves it for a new session, as it does when it starts without one. See Delete.

docs.title: User-message menu
docs.text:
Click a past You message to open its action menu. Use Up/Down and Enter, Esc to close, or the c, r, and f accelerators.

  • Copy writes the original message text to the clipboard.
  • Revert asks for confirmation, removes that message and everything after it from the session (including subagents it started), and restores the message text to the composer. If the session gained events since this view last showed it, for example a turn another client started, the revert is refused so nothing unseen is deleted; review the new turns and revert again.
  • Fork creates and selects an independent session whose copied prefix includes that message.

Assistant and tool rows keep their normal expand/collapse behavior and do not open the message menu.

docs.title: Transcript details
docs.text:
System prompts, AGENTS.md context, loaded skills, context compaction checkpoints, plugin-injected messages, and committed media parts appear collapsed by default. An AGENTS.md row appears at a run whose loaded context differs from the previous run's: the first load, a change, or loading again after a run without AGENTS.md. A run that reloads identical files adds no row. Expanded, it shows each file's source and content. A skill row shows the skill's source path, arguments, and rendered body. An AGENTS.md file skipped for size appears as a warning row. A session's system-prompt row remains hidden until its first run starts, then identifies the agent from the latest run snapshot. If the next-run draft uses another agent, the row also shows next: <agent>. Click one of these rows to show or hide its text or metadata. Expansion state is kept separately for each session. Expanded system prompts, skill bodies, and each AGENTS.md file are display-bounded to 256 lines or 32 KiB of sanitized text; compaction, plugin-message, and media bodies are bounded to 64 lines or 8 KiB. Oversized content ends with a truncated-lines indicator while the complete data remains in session state.

Expanding a tool row opens its title block: the header, followed by the rest of the call's title and primary argument when the collapsed header had to shorten them. The whole title block is one click target. A row's icon comes from the tool's hint (shell, file read, file edit, fetch, search, delegation, and so on; any other tool gets the hammer), never from its name, so a plugin or MCP tool shows the same way a built-in one does when it describes itself the same way. The header shows the call's title, and its primary argument after it unless the title already names it. While a call runs, its latest progress message follows the title.

Expanded tools use ordinary text colours and end with a blank row: a grey title block over a lighter grey panel. The panel shows the call's argument blocks (a command, a URL) under a muted arguments label, leaving out what the header already says: a block whose text is the header's primary argument or the text its title quotes, and a key/value row that only repeats the primary argument. A block that says more, such as a long command the header shortened, stays. Then comes what the call shows, drawn by the kind of each block rather than by which tool sent it:

  • Diffs name how the file changed (created, modified, deleted, or renamed), its path, and the lines added and removed, then each hunk with real file line numbers and +/- markers in a gutter, added and removed rows on the theme's diff tints, highlighted by language. A diff too large to carry its lines shows the counts alone.
  • Terminal output draws the program's SGR colours (fitted to the terminal's colour depth, and none under NO_COLOR), stderr in the warning tone unless the program coloured it, and the exit code below, red when it is not zero. It grows while the command runs.
  • File excerpts and code show file line numbers and are highlighted by language; JSON is pretty-printed; markdown renders like the assistant's text; tables and key/value lists align their columns.
  • Media shows a chip, 📎 name · type · size; a link its label and address; a session reference a row you can click to open that session.

A call without argument blocks shows its raw arguments instead, and only when the diagnostic filter is info or debug (see /events). Output beyond the row budget ends with … N more lines (click to expand). A block the tool had to cut says how much is missing, and when it names its complete content (a long command's stdout, a large diff), click to load the full output reads up to 1 MiB of it from the daemon and shows it in place of the cut rows; click the row under it to put it away again.

OpenAI Responses turns can retain opaque continuation witnesses for provider metadata such as message phase, annotations, and logprobs. Keep these parts alongside native replay data when preserving or restoring history. Internal agents validate the transport parts while using the text for summaries, approval decisions, and titles. Older saved turns may lack witnesses that were not captured at the time; historical events are not rewritten to invent them.

docs.title: Error details
docs.text:
When the daemon refuses a request, the TUI's status line and the CLI show its message, a sentence a person can act on, and then its hint, what to do next. Every refusal also has a stable code (see Errors). Technical detail, such as the upstream cause or a path, is shown on request: the TUI adds an error row to the session you are viewing whose first line is the error and whose collapsed rest, behind ▸, is the detail; the CLI prints it with --error-details, an option of every command.

Run failures show a concise headline followed by available model/provider identity, HTTP status, provider code, request ID, and response body. The same diagnostics are retained in session events and shown on replay. Model fallback and internal agent failures also include the available response diagnostics. Warning and error rows lead with 🚨 or ❌ instead of a badge row. A multiline diagnostic row shows only its first line, behind a ▸; click it to show the rest, such as a response body. A warning or error identical to the row before it counts on that row (repeated 6×) instead of adding a copy, so a retry loop hitting the same provider error stays one row; this includes subagent rows shown in an ancestor's transcript. For a failed tool, expand the tool row for its display output. Failed tools show their failure reason before their bounded inline output, even when they supplied separate display text. Tools with usable output do not add a separate TUI error row; output-less failures still do. A bash command's non-zero exit code is normal result data, not a tool failure. Genuine execution failures such as timeouts remain failures. Bounded diagnostics prioritize exit status, source context, and diagnostic streams such as stderr. Each stream gets space for its beginning and end so loud stdout cannot hide a later failure cause. MCP connection failures appear in /mcp; plugin initialization and RPC failures preserve operation context and selected cause fields. Configuration errors identify invalid settings and, for file/parse failures, available paths and locations without printing configuration source lines. Transport failures retain send/receive context for pending calls and appear as connection diagnostics in the TUI. Rejected WebSocket handshakes show a bounded, response body with its content preserved when supplied, without printing response headers.

Response bodies are capped at 4,096 UTF-8 bytes with a truncation marker. JSON is formatted for reading; plaintext and HTML gateway errors remain plain text. Terminal controls and Unicode format controls are stripped or replaced with spaces; newlines and tabs are preserved. The application does not redact credential-like text, sensitive field names, header records within a response body, or echoed secret values. It does not add request headers or credential-store dumps to diagnostics. MCP OAuth failures likewise preserve bounded response bodies and authorization error descriptions. Retained diagnostics have the same access and persistence rules as other session events.

The pinned model SDK preserves sanitized HTTP error-body text for OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Google, Google Vertex, Bedrock, Azure, and Cohere. SDK body retention is bounded to 64 KiB; the application further sanitizes and bounds displayed and persisted body diagnostics to 4 KiB. The pinned SDK still redacts some provider response fields before the application receives them; the application preserves the text it receives and cannot recover replaced values. A body is available only when the provider returned one: validation, connection, or cancellation errors may have no HTTP response body. Missing detail is not reconstructed or fetched with another API request.

cookie run reports failures on its own streams; see Failure diagnostics.

Internal tracing logs are off by default. Setting RUST_LOG (for example RUST_LOG=debug, using tracing-subscriber filter syntax) writes them to stderr, never stdout, so they cannot mix into cookie run output or the daemon ready line. The TUI draws on the same terminal, so redirect stderr to a file when logging a TUI session: RUST_LOG=debug cookie 2>cookie.log.

docs.title: Live tool output
docs.text: Expanded command rows show sanitized stdout and stderr while the command runs, with the call's latest progress message above them. The live display is capped at 64 KiB. On completion, failure, cancellation, or interruption, the same row swaps to the call's result display; a call that ended without one keeps what it showed while running. Reopening a session renders only that committed content. Assistant text follows the same rule: streamed partials are replaced by the committed turn.

docs.title: Background calls
docs.text:
A running call of a tool that supports the background (such as bash or delegate_subagent) shows a [background] button at the right end of its title row. Clicking it moves the call to the background once the tool can be detached: the call's row ends with the result the model got (User manually moved this call to the background …) and · background, and the run goes on while the call keeps running. The model can also start a call in the background itself.

While the selected session has background calls, a bar above the composer lists them; clicking it, or /background, opens a panel with one row per call (job, tool, its argument, how long it has run, and who moved it). Up/Down select a row, s or a row's [stop] stops that call, and Esc closes the panel. A stopped call still reports to the model, as stopped by you. A subagent working on its own, outside a call that waits for it, is listed under its handle; stopping it cancels the turn it is running, and the subagent reports that turn as cancelled. Cancelling the session's run (Esc) never stops its subagents. See Background calls for what the model sees.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
An approval docks above the status bar in place of the composer, leaving the conversation visible above it. It shows the call it gates the way you need to judge it: its icon and title, its argument blocks (such as a command), and its preview (such as an edit's or write's diff as of preparing the call), drawn as the transcript draws them; a call that describes neither shows the request's resources. Below that, why says what asked (your permission rule and its source, or the model's own reason), and a second row says what the focused decision does. A countdown appears in the top border when the request expires, and d (or clicking details) expands the full prepared-operation identity: ids, fingerprints, and the policy trace.

The decisions follow the request's constraints: allow once, allow for the session tree, reject, or cancel. Left/Right or Tab move focus between them and Enter answers with the focused one; each button also names its own key: y allows once, a allows for the session tree, n rejects, and Esc cancels when the request is cancellable. Letter keys are case-insensitive and do nothing for a decision the request does not offer. Clicking a button answers with it.

e opens a note for a rejection: type why, or what the agent should do instead, and press Enter to reject with it; the agent receives the note with the refusal. Esc closes the note without answering, and an empty note sends a plain rejection. Long panels scroll with arrows, Page Up/Page Down, Home, and End, or the mouse wheel.

While an approval is on top it owns the keyboard: other typing and pastes are dropped rather than landing in the hidden composer (a paste goes into an open note), and Ctrl-C still cancels the run. Enter, the letter keys, and e ignore presses for 400 ms after a request appears, so keystrokes already on their way to the composer cannot answer it; the panel says so beside its buttons, and a second press once it has settled goes through.

The permission mode appears in the bottom bar. Click it to cycle auto-approve -> auto-n -> auto-y -> ask -> yolo; the mode applies to subsequent approvals throughout the selected session tree, including delegated descendants. While a new-session draft is open, the mode shown and cycled is the draft's own, applied when its first prompt creates the session. Hard policy denies and doom-loop rejection still win in every mode. See Permissions.

When pricing is available, the bottom bar also shows the selected session's estimated cost between the permission mode and context usage. Click the cost to open the /usage dashboard. Unpriced sessions omit the segment.

The left of the bottom bar shows the runtimes the selected session, or a new session before its first prompt, attaches besides global. With one, it shows the runtime and its workspace, for example labpc · ~/api; with several, their attachment names, for example local_web, labpc_api. It shows global when that is all the session attaches, and no runtimes for a session with none.

docs.title: Runtimes panel
docs.text:
/runtime (titled Attached runtimes) lists the selected session's runtime attachments: each attachment's name, runtime and capability (labpc/coding), workspace, and instance status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, stopped, or not running). The details pane shows the selected attachment's kind, what its capability offers (the runtime's description of it), platform, and, for a failed instance, the reason. The panel refreshes on every runtime change and while it is open.

Press a to attach: the panel lists every capability of every runtime (labpc/coding, devbox/computer_use), with its description and whether the runtime is connected; the details below the list repeat the selected capability's description. Type to filter by runtime, capability, kind, or description, choose with the arrow keys, and press Enter. A capability that takes no workspace attaches at once; one that takes a workspace asks for its path next (Enter attaches, Esc returns to the list). A runtime that has not connected yet is one entry: attaching it connects it and takes its only capability, its workspace is optional, and the details show why its last connection failed. The path is passed to the runtime as typed and resolved on its machine (see Runtimes). Press d to detach the selected attachment, and r to retry its instance now, for example after fixing why it failed (runtimes.reconnect). The daemon refuses both while the session has an active run, and refuses attaching an instance the session already has; the refusal appears in the status line. Attaching starts the instance first and records nothing when it fails to start.

Before a new session's first prompt (at startup, or after /new), the panel edits the runtimes that session will attach, starting from the defaults: global, and the coding capability at the TUI's directory (local's, or this machine's when the daemon is remote). Each instance opens as soon as it joins the list, so its status and any failure show before the session exists, and an instance the list already holds is refused. a, d, and r edit the list and contact no session; the first prompt creates the session with exactly the listed runtimes, and fails without a session when one of them cannot start.

When an MCP server or runtime instance a session uses fails to connect, or drops and does not reconnect, the TUI adds an error row to each affected session naming the server or runtime and the reason (see MCP connection lifecycle).

docs.title: Usage dashboard
docs.text:
/usage opens a read-only view with the selected session first and its complete delegation tree second. The tree count includes the selected session. Each section shows request count, input, output, and reasoning tokens, cache reads and writes, cache hit percentage, estimated cost when configured, and a per-model breakdown. Models are sorted by descending estimated cost, with unpriced models last; ties use input tokens and then model name. Token counts use thousands separators, hit rates use one decimal place, and costs use the same formatting as the bottom bar. unpriced means the active configuration does not provide all rates needed for the observed token categories, while n/a means a hit rate cannot be computed.

Use Up/Down, Page Up/Page Down, or the mouse wheel to scroll when needed, and Esc to close. Clicking the selected session cost in the bottom bar still opens this panel.

See Usage and cost for recording and pricing semantics.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: cookie daemon serves a web client on the same port as its client endpoint. Open it in a browser on the daemon's machine, or on a laptop or phone that reaches that port (see Remote access). It does what the TUI does with the daemon's sessions and the daemon itself: chat, approvals, subagents, history edits, goals, attachments, skills, permissions, runtimes and machines, MCP servers, providers, the configuration, memory, and plugins. Two things stay in the TUI and the CLI; see What the page does not do.

docs.title: Opening the page
docs.text:
The daemon takes the page's connection from any origin, and the token is the guard (see Web clients). Print the page's address with the token:

cookie web          # prints http://127.0.0.1:7419/#token=<token>
cookie web --open   # also opens it in the system browser

cookie web finds the daemon like cookie attach:

  • --url and --token (or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN) first;
  • then [server] url and [server] token in this machine's config.toml.

The page is the client URL with ws turned into http (wss into https) and the final /ws dropped. The daemon also prints the page's address, without the token, after its ready line.

The token travels in the address's fragment (#token=), which a browser never sends to a server. The page keeps the token in the browser's localStorage under the daemon's URL and removes the fragment from the address bar.

docs.title: The connect screen
docs.text:
• Daemon URL. The page fills it in from its own address:
  • http becomes ws, and https becomes wss;
  • the host and port stay the same;
  • ws is added to the page's directory.

You can edit it; the page remembers the last URL it connected to. - Token. It comes from a cookie web link, or you paste it from the daemon's ready line. - Connecting. With both a URL and a token, the page connects without a click. - Forget this daemon deletes the stored token. Once connected, the same button is in the connection panel (below), behind a confirmation. - A refused connection. A browser shows a page no reason when the daemon refuses or closes its connection before the handshake, or nothing answers. The page says so and asks you to check the daemon URL and that the daemon is running. - Once connected, the foot of the rail (see Layout) shows the connection's state: connected, connecting, reconnecting, or offline. Hover over it for the daemon's address and version, or click it for a panel with them and Forget this daemon. Settings › This browser has Forget this daemon too. - Dropped connection. The page redials with the TUI's backoff, 500 ms rising to 10 s, under the same client identity. - Background tab. When it becomes visible again, the page checks the connection. - Separate clients. Each browser tab is its own client. - Theme. The theme button at the foot of the rail (in the header of the connect screen) cycles through system (a half circle), light (a sun), and dark (a moon). The choice stays in the browser.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• The rail. An icon strip on the far left switches between five views; each icon names itself in a tooltip, and the view shown is marked by a bar at the rail's edge:
  • Chat (the default): the sessions sidebar and the transcript;
  • Agents: the agent documents and their presets;
  • Settings: config.toml, providers, MCP servers, plugins, and this browser's preferences;
  • Machines & runtimes: the daemon's machines and its runtime registry;
  • Memory.

The connection and the theme button are at its foot. - Chat. The title bar has the sidebar button, the session's title, and the ⋮ menu of the session's commands. Below the transcript are the composer and the bottom bar. While a subagent's session is open, the title is a path from its root, such as Fix the greeting › reviewer: check tests: click a parent to go up to it. The ⋮ menu acts on the session shown. - Widths. - 1024 px and wider: the sessions sidebar is pinned beside the transcript. The sidebar button hides and shows it, and the browser remembers the choice. - 640 to 1023 px: the rail stays; the sidebar button slides the sessions over the transcript. - Narrower, a phone: see Phones. - Sheets. The session's panels open as a sheet on the right (from the bottom on a phone): approvals, the agent, model, permission mode, and preset pickers, usage, the diagnostics filter, compacting, the goal, background calls, skills, permission rules, a message's actions, the session's runtimes, and the ⋮ menu. - Long lines in code, diffs, and terminal output scroll inside their block.

docs.title: Sessions and chat
docs.text:
• Sessions. The page has no directory of its own, so the list shows every directory's sessions, with a filter by directory.
  • Rows. Each session shows its title, an icon for its status (running, completed, failed, cancelled, interrupted, or idle), the name of its directory, and how long ago it was last active. Hover over a row for the directory's full path.
  • New session starts a draft in a directory you name; leave it empty for the daemon's own. The first message creates the session with the agent, model, and permission mode the bottom bar shows.
  • Owned elsewhere. A session another cookie process owns opens as a read-only snapshot.
  • Deleting. Hover over a session's row for its trash button (on a touch screen, press the row for about half a second; the press never opens the session, and scrolling cancels it). A confirmation in the row names the session; Delete removes it and its subagents from the daemon's disk, for good. The daemon refuses while the session tree runs, while another cookie process holds it, or when it changed since the list showed it; the row then shows the daemon's reason. A deleted session leaves every client's list, and a page showing it starts a new session. A daemon older than client protocol 1.5 cannot delete, and the page offers no trash.
  • Subagents. Only the open session's row has its subagents nested under it, each with its status (a turning circle while it runs, a check, failed, or cancelled), its agent, its short handle, and its task. Click one to open it. Subagents have no trash: they go with their root. The tree has two states; click the open session's own row to switch between them (clicking another session still opens it), and the browser remembers the choice for each session:
  • Collapsed (the default): only the subagents that run, at any depth, and the one you have open. A running subagent whose parent has finished shows under its parent, dimmed, so it sits in its place. When nothing runs, nothing shows under the session.
  • Expanded: the whole hierarchy, finished subagents included; the chevron beside a subagent folds its own.
  • Transcript. Markdown is rendered with any HTML in it shown as text. Links open in a new tab, but only http, https, and mailto links; images show as links.
  • Tool calls are one line each until you open them, as in the TUI: an icon for the kind of tool (from its presentation hint, never its name), the title, the primary argument unless the title names it, and the status: a turning circle while running, a check when done, and a word with its icon when it failed, was cancelled, or was interrupted. While a call runs, its latest progress follows the title. A call waiting for your approval says approve? on its line, which opens the approvals. A running call that can move to the background offers background.
  • An open call. Click a call's line (or press Enter on it) to open it, and again to close it. It shows its arguments under a muted arguments label, leaving out what the line already says (a block or key/value row that only repeats the primary argument or the text the title quotes), then its output. Output past 64 lines ends with "… N more lines (click to expand)", which shows up to 1024. The page remembers which calls you opened in each session until you reload it.
  • A delegate call names the subagent it started with its handle and an open link; while the subagent runs, the row says whether it is thinking, running a tool, or waiting for an approval.
  • Output blocks each have their own view: code highlighted by the bundled highlight.js, diffs with the file's line numbers, terminal output with its colours, tables, JSON, links, session links, and media shown inline.
  • Cut output offers its complete content.
  • Your messages show the files they attached. Their ⋯ shows while the mouse is over the message's row (or the keyboard is in it); on a touch screen a long press on the message (about half a second; moving or scrolling cancels it) opens the same menu. The menu copies the message, reverts to before it (it and every later turn are removed, and its text comes back into the composer), or forks a new session with the conversation up to it. A revert is refused when another client added to the session since the menu opened.
  • Composer. One line to start; it grows with what you write up to five lines, then scrolls, and shrinks back when you send. The paperclip (and on a phone the camera) is inside it at the bottom left, and round buttons at the bottom right:
The session The box The buttons idle empty Send, disabled idle has text or files Send starts a run running or compacting empty Stop cancels it, as Escape does running has text or files Queue and Steer

Text that starts with / is sent like any other message: the page has no slash commands (the ⋮ menu has them). Each button's tooltip names its key. The keys work like the TUI's: - Enter sends, steering a running run. - Alt+Enter queues the message behind the run. - Shift+Enter or Ctrl+J inserts a newline. - Escape cancels the run, or a compaction in progress. - Up in an empty composer takes back your newest pending or queued message.

The strip above the composer lists pending and queued messages; tap one of yours to take it back. - Commands. The ⋮ menu in the title bar has the session's commands, each by name with an icon and a line saying what it does, and each opens a sheet with labelled fields and a main button: Compact context, Goal, Skills, Background calls, Runtimes, Permission rules, Usage, Diagnostics, and Agent preset. The others have their place in the page: the bottom bar picks the agent, model, and permission mode and answers approvals; the composer attaches, sends, and stops; the sidebar starts and opens sessions; and the rail has the daemon's views. - Approvals. When a tool call needs an answer, the bottom bar says so. Open it to approve once, approve for the session tree, or reject. - Compacting. Compact context opens a sheet with an optional Focus (what the summary should keep) and Compact. While it compacts, the sheet offers Cancel compaction, as the composer's Stop and Escape do, and then says how it went. - Goal. Goal shows the root session's goal, its checklist, and the controls its state allows (Pause, Resume, Cancel), and sets a New objective with the agent and model shown. The goal bar above the composer shows the objective with the same controls. Goals belong to root sessions; a child session or a read-only snapshot offers none. - Background calls. While the session has calls running in the background, a bar above the composer lists them. Click it, or use Background calls, to see how long each has run and stop one; a stopped call still reports to the model. - Files. Attach files with the paperclip (the file picker), by dropping them on the page, or by pasting them; on a phone, the camera button takes a photo. They upload at once and wait on the draft as chips; the × on a chip removes it. - Only the kinds of file the selected model takes are offered: the picker lists their types, and a model that takes none offers no attaching. - The page reads each file's type from its content, as the daemon does, and says why it cannot attach one the model does not take. - An image too large for the model or the daemon is offered as Downscale and attach: the page redraws it smaller and attaches that. Video is never downscaled. - Skills. Skills lists the skills you can run, searched as you type. Pick one, give its arguments, and run it. - Permissions. Permission rules shows the session's rules by action, and where each comes from: the agent, the default, or a session override. Click an effect to override it, add a rule for a pattern, or the × on an override to remove it. While a new session is composed, the same table edits the rules it will be created with, previewed against its agent. - Bottom bar. Below the composer; each part has an icon and says more on hover: - the agent, the model, and the permission mode, as three chips of one shape, each opening its picker. The mode chip has a shield of its own for each mode; its picker lists every mode with its shield and what it does, checks the current one, and sets the one you click: - auto-approve (the default): the approval agent decides; what it won't approve comes to you; - auto-approve-n: the approval agent decides; what it would pass to you is rejected; - auto-approve-y: the approval agent decides; what it would pass to you is approved once; - ask: every ask comes to you; - yolo: every ask is approved at once.

Deny rules and the loop guard hold in every mode;
  • the approvals waiting, when there are any (click to answer them);
  • working… while the session runs;
  • the last status message;
  • the context size, in tokens, of the last request (also in Usage);
  • the session's cost (click for Usage).
  • Diagnostics. Diagnostics picks which diagnostic rows the transcript shows; the choice stays in the browser.
  • Messages from producers (goal control and reminders, background-call reports, delegation reports, plugins) show as one folded line with their summary; click one to read it whole.

docs.title: Managing the daemon
docs.text:
• Runtimes. Runtimes (in the ⋮ menu) lists the session's attached runtimes with their status: Attach a runtime searches every runtime's capabilities and asks for a workspace when one is needed, Detach removes one (the daemon refuses while the session runs), and Retry restarts a failed instance.
  • While a new session is composed, the list is the runtimes it will attach: global and local's coding at its directory to start with. Each starts at once, so a runtime that cannot start says why before the session exists.
  • The open panel reads the runtimes again every second, and links to the Machines & runtimes view.
  • Machines. The Machines & runtimes view lists each machine with its runtimes. Rename or forget a machine, merge it into another (its memories move too), move a runtime to a machine, or unpin it. Under the machines, the runtime registry lists every runtime: whether it is connected, its machine and platform, its capabilities, and why it last failed to connect.
  • MCP servers. Settings › MCP servers lists every runtime's servers with their state, tools, and last error. The global runtime's servers can be added, edited, enabled or disabled, removed, and kept in your config.toml; a coding runtime's come from its template. Reconnect works for any server.
  • A server that needs authorization says so. The page cannot sign in to it: run cookie mcp auth <server> on a machine with a browser, or authorize it from the TUI.
  • Providers. Settings › Providers lists the catalog's providers. Pick one to connect it, or to update or disconnect its stored connection. Credentials are typed into password fields, read once when you connect, and never kept by the page; closing the form clears them.
  • Configuration. Settings › Configuration has config.toml, and the Agents view the agent documents, by preset. Open one to edit it in the page and Apply it. A change the daemon refuses stays open with the reason, to be fixed and applied again; a document that changed meanwhile is reloaded instead. The Agents view creates an agent document or deletes one; both reload from disk after editing files by hand.
  • Memory. The Memory view lists the memories by layer, grouped by machine and project, with the files that are not valid memories. Open one to edit it, create one at a URL (clicking a layer or group fills in its prefix), or delete one. A memory that changed since you opened it is never overwritten silently: you choose to reload it, overwrite it, or drop your edit.
  • Plugins. Settings › Plugins lists each plugin with its state, tools, hooks, and why it last failed, and restarts one. A plugin's events show in the bottom bar.
  • This browser. Settings › This browser picks the diagnostics the transcript shows (as Diagnostics does) and forgets the daemon.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
• Size. The page works from 360 px wide, in portrait and landscape. Buttons are at least 44 px, and long lines in code, diffs, and terminal output scroll inside their block rather than the page.
  • Chat.
  • Title bar: the sidebar button, the session's title on one line, and ⋮, which opens the session's commands as a sheet from the bottom. A subagent's session has ‹ before its title, which goes to its parent.
  • Bottom bar: one row. The model chip takes the room left and shortens its name first; the agent chip shows only its icon below about 380 px; the permission mode chip shows only its shield; the cost shows to the cent ("$0.02") and opens Usage, which also has the context size. Every picker, and every sheet of the ⋮ menu, opens from the bottom.
  • Status line: a thin line above the composer, only while the session runs, while approvals wait (tap the badge to answer), or for a few seconds after a status message.
  • The drawer. The sidebar button opens a drawer from the left over the dimmed page: the rail as an icon strip, with the theme button at its foot, beside the sessions, with the open session's subagents nested under its row. A tap outside, browser Back, or choosing a session or a view closes it; a tap on the open session's row switches its tree and leaves the drawer open. It opens only from the button: a swipe from the edge is the browser's Back. A long press on a session's row reveals its Delete, then the confirmation.
  • Other views fill the screen under the same title bar. Lists open their details one level at a time, such as a Settings section, then a document: the back arrow in the title bar, or browser Back, goes up one level. An editor fills the screen with Apply or Save and Cancel at its foot. Only Chat has the composer and the bottom bar.
  • On its side (about 844×390), a phone gets the 640 px layout: the rail stays, the sessions slide over, and the bottom bar sits beside the composer.
  • The on-screen keyboard. The page sizes itself to what the keyboard leaves visible, so the composer and an open sheet stay above it. While the composer has focus, the bottom bar steps aside, so only the composer (and the status line, when it shows) sits above the keyboard.
  • Home screen. The page installs as an app; see Installing as an app.
  • Background tabs. A phone suspends a tab it does not show. When the tab shows again, the page checks its connection, reconnects if the daemon stopped answering, and catches up on what happened meanwhile.
  • Reaching the daemon from a phone takes one of the ways in Forwarding and tunnels. Without TLS the token crosses the network in the clear.

docs.title: Installing as an app
docs.text:
The page installs to a phone's home screen, or as a desktop app, and then opens in its own window without the browser's address bar, with the cookie icon. It still works only while it reaches the daemon: it stores nothing for offline use, so it always matches the daemon's own build.

It needs HTTPS. A browser installs only a page from a secure origin: HTTPS, or localhost and 127.0.0.1 on the daemon's own machine. A page opened over plain HTTP on a LAN or Tailscale address cannot be installed, and Settings › This browser says so. The easy way to HTTPS is Tailscale Serve on the daemon's machine, with the daemon on its default loopback address:

tailscale serve --bg 7419   # https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ → 127.0.0.1:7419

Open the page on the phone with cookie web --url wss://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ws's link.

Tailscale Serve needs HTTPS certificates turned on for the tailnet (MagicDNS and HTTPS in its admin console).

Where the browser can install the page, the page offers it:

  • Android (Chrome and other Chromium browsers) and desktop Chrome or Edge. Install app opens the browser's install prompt. It is in Settings › This browser and under the connect screen, and on a phone a banner over the page offers it once (× dismisses it for good). Chrome offers the prompt once the page has been used for a moment; before that, or in a browser without one (Firefox), Settings › This browser points to the browser's own menu (Install app, Add to Home screen).
  • iPhone and iPad. iOS has no install prompt, so the same places say how: tap Share in the browser's toolbar, then Add to Home Screen and Add. The app iOS adds keeps its own storage, apart from the browser's, so the first time it opens it asks for the token: paste the link cookie web prints into its Token field (the page takes the token out of it).
  • Already installed. Running as an app, the page offers nothing, and Settings › This browser says it runs as an installed app.

The app opens at the page's own address without a token and connects with the token the browser stored when a cookie web link was opened. Its title bar follows the page's theme, the user's choice included.

The page has a service worker, sw.js, which installing needs on some browsers. It caches nothing and passes every request to the daemon, so a daemon that is not running shows the browser's own error, and a restarted daemon of a new build serves its own page at once. It never touches the /ws and /runtime WebSockets.

docs.title: What the page does not do
docs.text:
• Sign in to an MCP server. Authorizing a remote MCP server needs a callback on the machine's loopback address, which a page in a browser cannot offer. Settings › MCP servers marks such a server as needing authorization: run cookie mcp auth <server> on a machine with a browser, or authorize it from the TUI.
  • Offer this machine as a runtime. A browser has no workspace to share. The TUI's machine can attach as a runtime that dials in; the page uses the runtimes the daemon already has.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: The page's icons are Font Awesome Free by Fonticons, Inc., under the CC BY 4.0 licence. The connect screen and the connection panel credit them. They are inline SVG in the page's code (from the icondata crate, shown through leptos_icons), not a web font.

docs.title: Hosting the page elsewhere
docs.text: Every release attaches the page as cookie-agent-web.tar.gz. Its files use relative paths, so any static host can serve them from any path. The page then fills in a URL on that host, which you edit to name the daemon.

docs.title: Building the page
docs.text:
A cookie built from a fresh checkout serves a placeholder page. scripts/build-web.sh builds the real one:

  • it needs trunk 0.21.14 and the wasm32-unknown-unknown target;
  • it writes the page to crates/web_assets/bundle/, which the next build of cookie embeds;
  • it fails when the page, gzipped, is over its budget of 10 MB, a backstop against runaway growth.

The daemon sends the page gzip-compressed to browsers that accept it, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows only the page's own scripts and WebSocket connections to daemons.

docs.title: Agents and presets
docs.text:
An agent is a role a model plays: a system prompt, the models it runs on with their fallbacks, the permissions its tools get, and whether it runs as a root, as a subagent, or both. Agents are Markdown documents with YAML frontmatter in ~/.cookie-agent/agents/, <id>.md:

---
description: Reviews a change for correctness
mode: subagent
enabled: true
models: [{ model: "openai/gpt-5" }]
permissions:
  read: allow
  bash: ask
---
You review diffs. Report bugs with file and line.

Replace the model with one your providers offer. See Agent document structure for every key.

docs.title: Roots, subagents, and internal agents
docs.text:
An agent's mode says where it may run: primary as a root that you talk to, subagent only when another agent delegates to it, all for both, or internal for the daemon's own helpers. A root agent's permissions say which subagents it may delegate to, so a set of agents forms a team: a primary that plans and delegates, and specialists for exploring, testing, or review.

The daemon also runs three internal agents of its own: approval, the classifier that answers permission asks in the auto-approve mode; compaction, which summarizes context; and title, which names sessions. Each can be replaced by an authored internal document. See Internal agents.

When no authored agent can run as a root, the daemon supplies a built-in default coding agent on the first available model, so a fresh install works without any documents. See Layering and replacement.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: A preset is a named team. Documents directly in agents/ are shared; a directory one level down, such as agents/python/, is a preset whose documents replace shared ones of the same ID and add their own. Choosing a preset (/preset, or cookie run --preset) switches the whole team for new runs at once; no preset is selected by default. See Agent presets.

docs.title: Choosing what runs
docs.text: A session's selection, its agent, model, variant, and preset, is shared by every client and changes with /agent, /model, /preset, or the CLI's --agent, --model, and --preset. When a model fails, the run falls back along the agent's model chain, and later runs keep starting from the model that worked. See Selecting an agent and Providers for models and variants.

docs.title: Context an agent gets
docs.text:
Besides its own prompt, a run's context carries the repository's AGENTS.md files, the skills it may load, sections the tools contribute, and a memory snapshot; all of it is fixed when the run starts and visible in the transcript. See System prompt, Skills, and Memory.

Agents are changed live: edit them with /config or cookie config, and the next run uses the new documents. See config.toml.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
A client shows the daemon's sessions and acts on them. cookie ships three:

  • the terminal UI, cookie or cookie attach;
  • the web page the daemon serves on its own port, opened with cookie web;
  • the command line: cookie config, memory, machine, mcp, connect, and the other commands that call a running daemon. cookie run is the exception: it runs its own engine.

docs.title: One protocol
docs.text: All of them speak the same client protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 over a WebSocket, versioned with semver and frozen at its major (see Compatibility). A connection starts with a handshake naming the protocol version and the client: a free-form kind such as tui, cli, or web, and an instance_id the client keeps across reconnects. The daemon never treats one kind differently from another, so a client of your own is a peer of the shipped ones; see Write a client.

docs.title: Many clients at once
docs.text:
Any number of clients can attach to one daemon. Each sees every session live, can work in any of them, and is told about changes another client makes:

  • Selections are shared. A session has one agent, model, variant, and permission mode. When one client picks them, every client's draft follows, and the latest pick wins.
  • Steer or queue. While a run is active, a message either steers, joining the running conversation at the next tool or completion boundary, or queues, starting a run of its own when this one completes. The daemon decides atomically, so a run that another client starts or that ends while you type only changes which happens. See Steering and queueing.
  • Only the sender takes a message back. A pending message shows which client sent it; only that client can recall it into its composer.
  • Edits check what you saw. Reverting a session is refused when it gained events the client has not shown yet, so nothing unseen is deleted.

docs.title: Browsers
docs.text: A browser page connects like any client, with the token in its handshake. The daemon takes it from any origin; the token is the guard. See Web clients.

docs.title: A client's machine
docs.text: A TUI attached to a daemon on another machine offers its own machine to it as a runtime that dials in, client_<host name>, so its sessions still work in the directory it was started in. See Runtimes.

docs.title: The daemon
docs.text: The daemon is the gateway at the center of cookie. It owns everything that outlives one terminal: the provider connections and the model catalog, the sessions and their history, the agents and presets, the permission rules and approvals, and memory. It runs the models, and it reaches the tools a session uses through runtimes. Clients only show and steer what the daemon holds.

docs.title: In process or on its own
docs.text:
The same daemon runs in two ways:

  • Inside a client's process. Plain cookie with no daemon around starts one inside the TUI's process; the bottom bar then says standalone. cookie --standalone always does this, and cookie run always runs an engine of its own for its one prompt. When the process ends, so does the daemon.
  • On its own. cookie daemon serves the client protocol on a WebSocket, by default ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws, until it is stopped. Every client that reaches it shares its sessions, and it can run as a service. See Persistent daemon.

Either way it is one engine with one store: sessions, artifacts, memory, and the machines registry live under ~/.cookie-agent.

docs.title: Finding a running daemon
docs.text:
Plain cookie looks for a daemon on this machine before starting its own, but only when config.toml has [server] token, which cookie daemon writes at its first start. It dials ws://<host>:<port>/ws from the [server] table, never [server] url:

  • nothing listening within half a second: it starts its own engine, silently;
  • a daemon that accepts the handshake within two seconds: the TUI opens on it;
  • something that answers but cannot be used, such as a refused token or another protocol major: it starts its own engine and says why.

Reaching a daemon on another machine takes cookie attach --url, and listening for other machines takes cookie daemon --listen; see A daemon already running and Remote access.

docs.title: The token
docs.text: Every connection presents the daemon's bearer token, [server] token. Clients and runtimes on the daemon's machine read it from the same config.toml; elsewhere it is passed with --token or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN. Anyone holding the token is a fully trusted client. See Security.

docs.title: One store, one owner
docs.text: A session tree is written by one process at a time, which holds its owner.lock. An engine started beside a running daemon still lists the daemon's sessions, but opens them as read-only snapshots. See Sessions.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Persistent daemon and Remote access for running it.
  • Server [server] for its keys.
  • Architecture for how the engine, the server, and the clients are built.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: A machine is the daemon's name for a computer its runtimes run on. Several runtimes can share one: the daemon's local runtime, a cookie runtime serve started over ssh, and a TUI's client_<host> runtime on the same laptop. The daemon groups them so that you, and the agents' memory, can talk about the computer rather than each connection to it.

docs.title: How a runtime finds its machine
docs.text:
A runtime reports a machine ID when it connects. cookie's own runtimes report a hash of the operating system's machine ID (/etc/machine-id or /var/lib/dbus/machine-id), or of a random ID kept in ~/.cookie-agent/machine-id where there is none, together with the host name. The daemon then places the runtime, first match first:

  1. on the machine the runtime ID is pinned to;
  2. on the machine that already lists the reported machine ID;
  3. on a new machine named after the host name;
  4. without a reported ID, on a new machine named after the runtime ID, which pins it there.

A runtime's machine is worked out each time; only the machines themselves are stored, in ~/.cookie-agent/machines.json, which only the daemon writes.

docs.title: Regrouping
docs.text:
Two IDs can be one computer (a container and its host), or one ID can be the wrong place for a runtime. cookie machine and the Machines tab of /runtime (TUI and web) change the registry:

  • rename a machine, which moves its memory folder;
  • assign a runtime ID to a machine, pinning it, or unassign it so it follows the ID it reports;
  • merge one machine into another, moving its IDs, pins, and memories;
  • forget a machine that has no connected runtime and no memories.

See cookie machine and Machines.

docs.title: Memory per machine
docs.text: The machine memory layer keeps notes per machine: machine://<machine>/<name>, such as where a toolchain lives or which ports are free on it. Renaming or merging a machine carries its memories along. See Memory.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Memory is what agents keep between sessions: notes about you, about each agent's work, about each machine, and about each project. The daemon stores memories as Markdown files with a short frontmatter, and agents read and write them with tools, so what one session learns the next can use.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer URL For user user://<category> you: preferences, conventions, how you like to work agent agent://<agent> one agent's own notes about doing its job machine machine://<machine>/<name> one machine: toolchains, paths, services project project://<project>/<name> one project, wherever its checkouts live

Every agent has its agent:// memory from the start: the daemon makes one file per agent, names the agent in its description and keywords, and keeps those in line with the agent's document; the agent writes the body. An empty one is not shown to the model. See Agent memory.

A project memory names what identifies the project across machines, such as repository names, remote URLs, and <machine>:<path> places, so an agent can search for it from any checkout. See Layers and files.

docs.title: How agents use it
docs.text:
Memory comes with the global runtime, which new sessions attach. A run starts with a snapshot of it after the AGENTS.md context: every user memory, the run's agent's own, and an index of the memories of the machines the session works on; project memories the agent searches for. The memory tools, memory_search, memory_read, memory_write, memory_edit, and memory_delete, read and change memories by URL. Writes name the revision they read, so a memory that changed meanwhile is never overwritten. See What the model sees and Tools.

The memory and memory_write permission actions govern the tools, with the memory URL as the resource. Without rules of its own, a primary agent may read and write every memory, while a subagent may read every memory but write only its own agent:// memory. See Memory defaults.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text: Memories are files under ~/.cookie-agent/memory/ on the daemon's machine, one folder per layer, so you can read, edit, or version them like any other files. /memory in the TUI and the web page, and cookie memory, list, edit, create, and delete them through the daemon, and show files that are not valid memories with the reason. See Managing memory and the [memory] settings.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Every tool call a model makes passes a permission check before it runs. The check asks one question: may this action touch this resource? The answer comes from rules, and an ask answer comes from you, or from a classifier on your behalf, depending on the session's mode.

docs.title: Actions and resources
docs.text:
Each tool declares a permission action and names the resource of each call:

  • read and write (write also covers edit): the file path;
  • bash: the whole command string;
  • webfetch: the URL;
  • delegate: the subagent's agent ID; message: the recipient's relation, parent, child, or sibling;
  • mcp: the MCP tool's name; skill: the skill name;
  • memory and memory_write: the memory URL.

Actions are free-form labels, a lowercase letter then up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores, so a runtime's or a plugin's tools can declare actions of their own. A few tools declare none and are always allowed, such as read_artifact, which reads only the tree's own retained output. See Resource labels.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
An agent document maps each action to an effect, allow, ask, or deny, either outright or per resource pattern:

permissions:
  read: allow
  bash:
    "git status": allow
    "*": ask
  write:
    ".env*": deny
    "*": ask

The most specific pattern wins, and a resource no rule matches is denied. A tool whose action has no allow or ask rule is not even offered to the model. See Permissions.

Rules can also be added to one session tree without touching the agent, in /permissions or with cookie run --allowed-tools; these overlay rules are checked before the agent's. See Session permission overlays.

docs.title: Rules for one runtime
docs.text: A rule keyed action@runtime_id applies only to that runtime's tools, whatever workspace they work in, so bash: ask with bash@labpc: {"git *": allow} lets git run freely on labpc and asks for everything else. Actions of the daemon's own tools, delegate, message, and skill, take no selector. See Runtime selectors.

docs.title: Modes and approvals
docs.text:
A rule that says ask is resolved by the session tree's permission mode, shown in the TUI's bottom bar and shared by every client:

Mode An ask is auto-approve (the default) decided by the approval classifier agent, which passes to you what it will not approve auto-approve-n decided by the classifier; what it would pass to you is rejected auto-approve-y decided by the classifier; what it would pass to you is approved once ask always yours yolo approved at once

A deny rule and the doom-loop guard hold in every mode. An approval shows the call as it will run, such as the command or the diff of an edit, and you allow it once, allow it for the whole session tree, reject it, or reject it with a note for the agent. See Live permission modes and Approvals.

docs.title: What permissions do not do
docs.text: Rules decide which calls run; they are not a sandbox. An allowed bash command runs with your user's rights, and cat .env is a bash call, not a read. See Security.

docs.title: Runtimes and capabilities
docs.text: A runtime is where a session's tools run. It offers one or more capabilities, each a named set of tools with a self-declared kind, and says whether the capability works in a workspace directory. A session attaches the capabilities it uses; each attachment brings its tools into the session.

docs.title: The runtimes there are
docs.text:
Runtime Where it runs Capability Offers global inside the daemon, always global, no workspace top-level MCP servers, plugins, the memory tools, a fallback webfetch local inside the daemon coding, any directory on the daemon's machine read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, project skills, AGENTS.md [runtimes.<id>] a process the daemon starts from a template, typically ssh host cookie runtime serve --stdio whatever it declares; cookie runtime serve offers coding the same as local, on that machine dial-in a process that connects to the daemon's /runtime route, such as cookie runtime serve --daemon the same the same

A new session attaches global and local's coding at the client's directory. The runtimes panel (/runtime) attaches and detaches others, before the first prompt or between runs. See Runtimes for templates, dial-in, and lifecycles.

Every runtime other than the built-in ones speaks the runtime protocol, so a runtime of your own can offer any tools; see Write a runtime.

docs.title: Attachments and tool names
docs.text:
Each attachment has a session-unique name: global for the global runtime, and for a workspace the runtime ID and the directory's name, such as local_web or labpc_api (with _2, _3, … when taken). The model sees a tool by its bare name while one attachment offers it. When several do, each copy is published as <attachment>_<tool>, such as local_web_bash and labpc_api_bash, and the bare name disappears. A tool can instead declare that it overrides others of its name, or that it is only a fallback, like the global runtime's webfetch, which hides whenever local offers one. A runtime tool never takes the name of a built-in tool such as delegate_subagent. See Example: a repository on another machine.

Permission rules can target one runtime's tools with action@runtime; see Permissions.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text: Attaching a capability at a workspace opens an instance of it. One runtime process serves every instance of every session that uses it, and an instance reports its status: starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, or stopped. A dropped runtime is reconnected; a session whose instance stays down shows an error row. See Lifecycle and failures.

docs.title: A client's machine
docs.text: When a TUI attaches to a daemon that runs on another machine, its sessions still need tools in the TUI's directory. Plain cookie and cookie attach pick, in order: the daemon's own local runtime when the daemon is on this machine; else a connected runtime on this machine that takes a workspace; else the TUI dials in as client_<host name>, serving only its directory, for as long as it runs. See Persistent daemon.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: Each runtime reports the machine it runs on, and the daemon groups runtimes by machine; see Machines.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is one conversation: its messages, the runs that answered them, every tool call with its result, and the settings it ran with. The daemon keeps each session as an append-only event log, and every client renders the session from those events.

docs.title: Trees and delegation
docs.text:
A session you start is a root. When its agent delegates a task with delegate_subagent, the daemon creates a child session for the subagent, under the root; the subagent may delegate in turn, up to the configured depth. Together they form a session tree. Each subagent has a short handle, such as explore_1a2b3c4d, by which the agents address it: to read its result, send it a message, or stop its turn. A subagent reports every turn it finishes to its parent, and runs on whether or not the parent waits. See Delegation, Agent messaging, and the delegation tools.

Usage, permission modes, and approvals granted "for the session tree" all apply to the whole tree; /usage shows the selected session and its tree.

docs.title: Where sessions live
docs.text: Sessions are stored per directory under ~/.cookie-agent/sessions/, each tree in its own folder with its subagents below it and the artifacts its tools retained. A session exists on disk from its first message. Its directory decides where it is listed: the TUI shows the sessions of the directory it was started in, and Ctrl+A in its session picker switches to every directory's; the web page lists every directory's. See Lifecycle and persistence.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: One process writes a tree at a time. The daemon that opens a tree takes its owner.lock; another cookie process, such as a standalone TUI beside a running daemon, can read the tree but shows it as a read-only snapshot until the owner exits. Clients of one daemon share its ownership, so they all write. See Tree-scoped session ownership lock.

docs.title: History that lasts
docs.text: The log is a compatibility surface. Each session records the history format it was written in (currently 1); a later build reads it tolerantly, skipping what it does not know, and a build that changes the format converts older logs when it opens them, keeping the originals as events.jsonl.v<N>.bak. cookie sessions upgrade converts a directory's sessions at once. See History formats and Compatibility.

docs.title: Changing history
docs.text:
• Revert removes a message and everything after it, subagents it started included, and puts the message back into the composer. It needs an idle session and is refused when the session gained events the client has not shown. See Revert.
  • Fork copies a session up to a message into a new, independent session. See Fork.
  • Compaction replaces older context with a summary when the context fills, or on /compact. See Compaction.
  • Delete removes a whole tree from disk: the root, its subagents, their events, and their artifacts. Only a root is deleted, after you confirm; it is refused while a session of the tree runs, while another process owns the tree, and when the root gained events since you looked. It cannot be undone. See Delete.

docs.title: What a session is bound to
docs.text: A session has one selection (agent, model, variant, preset) shared by every client, one permission mode for its tree, and the runtimes it attaches. A run freezes its model binding and system prompt when it starts, so changes to the configuration apply from the next run. See Agents and presets and Runtimes.

docs.title: Persistent daemon
docs.text: This page covers running the daemon as a process of its own: starting it and attaching clients to it, how plain cookie finds a daemon already running on the machine, and running the daemon and its runtimes as services. Its clients are the terminal UI, the web client, and the command line; Remote access covers reaching it from other machines, Runtimes the runtimes it uses, and Security its trust boundaries.

docs.title: Separate server and client
docs.text:
The daemon binds to 127.0.0.1:7419 by default:

cookie daemon

Its first stdout line is the machine-readable ready frame; everything the daemon prints afterward is human logging. A supervisor writes the daemon's stdout to a pipe, reads exactly that one line, and ignores the rest:

daemon-ready {"url":"ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws","token":"<43-char base64url>"}

The token is [server] token in config.toml; the daemon writes a fresh one there at its first start when there is none, and keeps it across restarts. Treat it, and the ready line, as a secret: anyone who reads either can connect to the daemon. Pass --port 0 to let the OS pick an ephemeral port; the ready line then carries the real port, and clients must use that URL rather than guessing 7419.

Plain cookie in another terminal on the same machine finds it (see A daemon already running). cookie attach requires it:

cookie attach

attach, web, connect, disconnect, mcp, config, machine, and memory find the daemon in this machine's config.toml: [server] url, else the local daemon the same table describes (ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/ws), and [server] token. Flags override either: --url (any host, ws:// or wss:// with the exact /ws path) and --token (or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN), so a local cookie attach can still reach a daemon elsewhere:

cookie attach --url wss://laptop.example:7419/ws --token '<43-char base64url>'

A daemon on another machine listens with --listen; see Remote access. The daemon also serves a web client on its port; cookie web prints its address with the token (see Web). Unlike plain cookie, cookie attach never falls back to an engine of its own: a daemon it cannot reach or use is an error.

docs.title: A daemon already running
docs.text:
Plain cookie looks for a daemon on this machine before it starts an engine of its own, so every client of a running daemon, cookie daemon as a service included, sees the same sessions:

  • It looks only when config.toml has [server] token, which cookie daemon writes at its first start. Without one it starts its own engine and touches no network.
  • It looks at ws://<[server] host>:<[server] port>/ws and never at [server] url, which may name another machine: reaching another machine takes cookie attach. A daemon started with --port or --listen on another address, or serving only TLS, is not found.
  • Nothing listening (the connection is refused, or it is not open within half a second) starts its own engine, silently.
  • A daemon that answers within two seconds and accepts the handshake gets the TUI, exactly as cookie attach would: a dropped connection is retried, and quitting the TUI leaves the daemon running.
  • Something that answers but cannot be used, such as a daemon refusing the token, a daemon of another protocol major, a TLS listener, or another program, starts its own engine with a notice that names the address and the reason.

When the daemon runs another version of cookie than this binary, the TUI says so once; restart the daemon to upgrade it. cookie --standalone always starts its own engine and never looks; it takes no subcommand. cookie run never looks either: it always runs its own engine. An engine of its own beside a running daemon opens the daemon's sessions as read-only snapshots. A daemon running as another OS user is not told apart: it reports the same machine, so its local runtime serves the directory with that user's file permissions. Use --standalone or a runtime that dials in with such a daemon.

The daemon, cookie runtime serve, and the TUI stop cleanly on a stop signal: SIGINT, SIGTERM (kill, systemd), or SIGHUP (a closed terminal); on Windows Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break, a closed console, logoff, or shutdown. The daemon stops listening and shuts down its engine and the runtimes it started; a runtime cancels its calls and stops its MCP servers; the TUI restores the terminal. A second signal during that shutdown exits the daemon or runtime at once.

docs.title: Running as a service
docs.text:
Both the daemon and a runtime that dials in run until stopped, so each can be a systemd user service. On the daemon's machine, ~/.config/systemd/user/cookie-daemon.service:

[Unit]
Description=Cookie Agent daemon

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.cargo/bin/cookie daemon --listen 0.0.0.0:7419
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

On a machine whose config.toml names the daemon ([server] url and token; see Runtimes that dial in), ~/.config/systemd/user/cookie-runtime.service:

[Unit]
Description=Cookie Agent runtime

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.cargo/bin/cookie runtime serve --daemon
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

Enable each with systemctl --user enable --now <name>, and run loginctl enable-linger so they run without a login session. Either may start first: the runtime retries until the daemon answers. The journal keeps the daemon's ready line, token included, readable by whoever can read your user journal. A daemon running as a service has no SSH_AUTH_SOCK from your shell, so an ssh [runtimes.<id>] template needs a key file in its arguments (-i) or an agent socket set with the unit's Environment=.

One daemon serves sessions of any directory. The TUI, whether attached or running the daemon itself, creates its sessions for the directory it was started in: they work there with local's coding capability, and its session list shows that directory's sessions. Sessions stay in the store of the directory the daemon started in.

Plain cookie on a found daemon and cookie attach choose the runtime for the directory the same way, first match first:

  1. The daemon runs on this machine (its handshake reports this machine's ID, or either side reports none): its local runtime.
  2. A connected runtime of the daemon runs on this machine (the daemon places it on a machine whose IDs include this one's; see Machines) and offers a capability that takes a workspace: new sessions attach that capability at the directory. With several, the lowest runtime ID wins. An example is a daemon in a container with cookie runtime serve --daemon running beside it on the host.
  3. Otherwise the TUI offers this machine to the daemon: it dials in a runtime named client_<host name> that serves the TUI's directory only, and the TUI's new sessions use its coding capability there. The runtime lives as long as the TUI; sessions keep its attachment and find it again when the TUI attaches again from this machine. Another TUI's client_<host name> is never chosen in step 2.

The bottom bar shows the chosen runtime and the directory. Configured plugins and eager MCP servers, which come only from the user config.toml, start during engine initialization, before a model tool call is approved. Repository AGENTS.md files and project skills still enter model context, so open unfamiliar workspaces with care. Allowed shell commands run without a filesystem sandbox; see the security contract.

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text: This page covers reaching a daemon from other machines: listening on another address with TLS, web clients, and forwarding the daemon's port through SSH, a private network, or a tunnel. Persistent daemon covers starting the daemon and attaching clients to it, Runtimes the runtimes that dial in from elsewhere, and Security what the token and the listener protect. The [server] keys are in Server.

docs.title: Listening on other addresses
docs.text:
For clients and runtimes on other machines, cookie daemon takes:

Option Meaning --listen <addr:port> Bind this address instead, such as 0.0.0.0:7419. Without TLS the token crosses the network in the clear, so a plaintext listener belongs on a private network such as a VPN. Conflicts with --port. --tls-cert <path>, --tls-key <path> Serve wss with this PEM certificate chain and private key; the ready line then shows a wss:// URL. Both or neither.

The daemon serves clients on /ws and dial-in runtimes on /runtime?id=<runtime ID>. Both present the same bearer token: a runtime in the Authorization header, a client there or in its handshake. A request to /runtime carrying a browser Origin header is refused; /ws ignores the header.

docs.title: Web clients
docs.text: A page in a browser connects with the token in its handshake. The daemon takes it from any origin: the daemon's own page, a page served elsewhere, or the daemon's page behind a proxy, which a browser reports under the proxy's origin. The token is the guard, so keep it secret. A page served over HTTPS can only connect with wss://, so it needs the daemon's TLS options or a proxy that provides them.

docs.title: Forwarding and tunnels
docs.text:
The web page and /ws share one port, so forwarding that port forwards both. The page then finds the daemon at its own address.

  • An SSH tunnel: ssh -L 7419:127.0.0.1:7419 host. Open http://127.0.0.1:7419/.
  • Tailscale Serve gives the loopback daemon an HTTPS address on the tailnet without listening anywhere else: tailscale serve --bg 7419 serves https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/. An HTTPS page can be installed as an app on a phone.
  • Tailscale or a LAN. Run cookie daemon --listen 0.0.0.0:7419 and open its address, such as http://100.101.102.103:7419/. Without TLS the token crosses the network in the clear, so keep this to a private network.
  • A tunnel such as cloudflared gives an HTTPS address, such as https://cookie.example.com. Point it at the daemon's port.
  • A page served over HTTPS connects with wss://. The tunnel provides that.
  • A proxy may serve the daemon under a subpath, such as https://example.com/cookie/. The page then connects to wss://example.com/cookie/ws.

docs.title: Runtimes [runtimes]
docs.text: A runtime is where a session's tools run. It offers one or more capabilities, and a session attaches each one it uses separately. The daemon's built-in local runtime offers coding (read, write, edit, bash, webfetch) for any directory on the daemon's machine, and the global runtime offers global: top-level MCP servers and plugins. A [runtimes.<id>] table configures another runtime, typically on another machine over ssh, so a session on your laptop can read, edit, and run commands in a repository on that machine. The runtimes specification and the runtime capabilities specification describe the model; this page covers configuration and use.

docs.title: Example: a repository on another machine over ssh
docs.text:
Install the same Cookie Agent version on the remote machine (the runtime protocol versions must be compatible: their majors must match) and make sure ssh labpc cookie --version works without a password prompt. Then add a template to ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml on the machine that runs the daemon:

[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]
startup_timeout_ms = 20000

Start cookie, open /runtime, press a, type labpc and press Enter, then type a path on the remote machine such as ~/cookie-agent and press Enter. Before the first prompt this chooses the runtimes the new session starts with; in an existing session it attaches labpc to it. The daemon runs the command once, the remote cookie runtime serve resolves the path on its own machine and opens its coding capability there, and the session gains an attachment named after the runtime ID and the workspace's directory name, here labpc_cookie_agent. Tools that two attachments offer are prefixed with the attachment name, so the model sees local_web_bash and labpc_cookie_agent_bash; detach local (d on its row) to keep the bare names for the remote runtime only.

Attaching another workspace on labpc opens it over the same connection: one cookie runtime serve process serves every workspace and every session that uses labpc.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
A runtime reports its capabilities when it connects. Each has a name, a self-declared kind, and whether it takes a workspace. runtimes.list and the /runtime panel show them once the runtime has connected. When a runtime offers one capability, attaching it needs no capability name; when it offers several, choose one (/runtime lists each capability of each runtime as its own entry). Each attached capability is its own attachment, with its own name and tools.

Runtime Capability Workspace Offers global global none top-level MCP servers, plugins, the memory tools, the fallback webfetch local coding any directory on the daemon's machine; the daemon's own directory when none is named read, write, edit, bash, webfetch, project skills, AGENTS.md cookie runtime serve coding any directory on its machine, or under its --root directories the same

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
runtimes maps a runtime ID to a template; it is empty by default.
