Key Type Default Meaning command array of strings required The program and its arguments. env table of strings {} Variables added to the daemon's environment for the process. startup_timeout_ms positive integer 10000 Bound on starting the process and its answer to runtime/initialize, and on each capability opening, which follows its MCP servers' first connection attempts. shutdown_grace_ms positive integer 3000 How long a stopping runtime gets before its process group is killed. mcp.servers.<name> MCP server table none MCP servers each coding instance hosts on the runtime's machine; see below.
  • Runtime IDs match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31} because they become tool name prefixes. global is reserved. [runtimes.local] configures the built-in local runtime and accepts only an mcp table.
  • command must be nonempty and its first element must name a program. One process serves every workspace, so the command names none. An element containing {workspace}, which older templates used, is rejected.
  • No shell is involved. cookie starts the program directly. ssh itself, however, joins its arguments into one string that the remote login shell interprets, so arguments with spaces or shell metacharacters need quoting that survives that shell. A workspace path travels in the runtime protocol, not on the command line, and cookie runtime serve expands a leading ~ in it.
  • Environment. The process inherits the daemon's environment, which ssh needs for SSH_AUTH_SOCK and similar variables, plus env. Names must be nonempty without = or NUL. ssh finds its configuration, keys, and known_hosts through that environment's HOME, so a daemon run with another HOME (a scratch or service home) needs env = { HOME = "/home/me" } in the template, or the files named on its command line as absolute paths, since no shell expands ~ there: -F /home/me/.ssh/config, -i /home/me/.ssh/id_ed25519, and -o UserKnownHostsFile=/home/me/.ssh/known_hosts.
  • MCP servers are parsed with the MCP server schema, and a server that enables OAuth (oauth = true or an oauth table) is rejected: OAuth credentials live on the daemon and are available to top-level [mcp] servers only. Static-header HTTP servers are allowed. See template MCP servers.
  • Templates declare no capabilities and accept no plugins table: the runtime reports its capabilities when it connects, and plugins run only in the global runtime.

Unknown keys and invalid values fail the configuration load, as everywhere in config.toml. Changes take effect when the daemon next starts.

docs.title: Template MCP servers
docs.text:
Every coding instance hosts the template's mcp.servers itself: the runtime process (cookie runtime serve on the remote machine, or the daemon's process for [runtimes.local]) starts each server for each workspace it opens, so commands, working directories, and URLs are resolved where the repository is.

[runtimes.labpc]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "labpc", "cookie", "runtime", "serve", "--stdio"]
startup_timeout_ms = 30000

[runtimes.labpc.mcp.servers.rust_analyzer]
command = "rust-analyzer-mcp"

[runtimes.local.mcp.servers.docs]
command = "docs-mcp"
  • Connecting. An instance connects every enabled server before it answers the daemon, so its tools are listed when a session first uses the instance. startup_timeout_ms covers these first attempts; raise it for servers that start slowly. A server that fails publishes no tools, and clients viewing a session attached to the instance get an error naming it.
  • Tools. The servers' tools are the instance's tools, named <server>_<tool> like any MCP tool and gated by the mcp permission. When another attachment offers the same name, they are prefixed with the attachment name like the built-in tools.
  • Drops and retries. The runtime restarts a dropped server (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) with its tools still published, and drops them when every attempt fails. A failed server is retried when a session that uses the instance is created or opened, when the instance is attached or retried (r in /runtime), and with r on the server in /mcp.
  • Status. /mcp lists the servers of every instance as <runtime> at <workspace>. They cannot be edited there; change the template and restart the daemon.

docs.title: Instances and workspaces
docs.text: A capability instance is one capability of a runtime opened for one workspace (or none), shared by every session attached to it. The daemon passes the workspace path exactly as it was typed and never resolves it on its own machine; the runtime reports the canonical path on its machine, and that path identifies the instance. Two requests that resolve to the same directory, such as ~/cookie-agent and /home/me/cookie-agent, share one instance. A session records the reported path, and reopening the session asks for that path.

docs.title: Lifecycle and failures
docs.text:
• Start. A runtime's process starts when a session first needs one of its capabilities, and stays up until the daemon exits; its instances open as sessions attach them. A start that fails or exceeds startup_timeout_ms publishes no tools; the attach is rejected, and clients viewing an affected session get an error naming the runtime and the reason. runtimes.list shows why the runtime last failed to connect.
  • Refused workspaces. A runtime that is up can still refuse to open a capability, for example for a workspace outside its --root directories. The error then reads runtime `labpc` could not open `coding` for workspace `/tmp`: workspace /tmp is outside the directories this runtime serves rather than saying the runtime failed to start. Attaching, creating a session, and retrying (runtimes.reconnect) record nothing when the instance never opened: no attachment, and no failed instance in runtimes.list.
  • Diagnostics. The process's standard error is captured into a bounded buffer (its last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB). Failure reasons end with that tail, so an ssh or cookie runtime error shows up in the TUI. The daemon does not copy the process's standard error to its own as it arrives, but when a session is created, opened, or starts a run while one of its attachments is unavailable, the daemon writes cookie-agent: session <id>: runtime `<attachment>` is unavailable: <reason> to its standard error, and that reason ends with the tail.
  • Drop. When the process exits or its pipe closes, calls in flight fail with runtime_unavailable (a backgrounded call reports the failure as its background result), and the daemon starts the process again up to 3 times after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s, reopening every instance over the new connection. Meanwhile the instances show as reconnecting, their tools stay published, and new calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable. A successful restart re-lists their tools under a new instance generation (a call the model planned before the restart fails as operation_changed). When every attempt fails, their tools are dropped, they become failed, and clients get an error.
  • Retry. A failed instance is retried when a session that uses it is created or opened, and on demand with r in /runtime (or runtimes.reconnect).
  • Shutdown. When the daemon exits it sends runtime/shutdown, waits up to shutdown_grace_ms, and then kills the process group (a job object on Windows).

docs.title: cookie runtime serve
docs.text:
cookie runtime serve --stdio [--root <dir>]...
cookie runtime serve --daemon [<url>] [--id <runtime ID>] [--token <token>] [--root <dir>]...

With --daemon it dials in instead (see Runtimes that dial in); the rest of this section describes --stdio.

Serves this machine's runtime over standard input and output with the runtime protocol: the coding capability for every workspace the daemon opens. --root (repeatable) limits coding to workspaces under those directories; a root that does not exist fails at start. It needs no provider configuration and reads no config.toml; a leading ~ in a workspace or root is expanded, and paths are resolved on the machine it runs on. Standard output carries only protocol messages and diagnostics go to standard error. It exits on runtime/shutdown, when standard input closes, or on a stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP). A template normally runs it; running it by hand is only useful for debugging.

docs.title: Runtimes that dial in
docs.text:
A runtime can also run on its own and connect to the daemon, instead of the daemon starting it. It needs no template: it names itself, and sessions attach it like any other runtime while it is connected.

# On the daemon's machine: a listener the runtime reaches.
cookie daemon --listen 0.0.0.0:7419

# On labpc, ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml: the daemon to dial in to.
[server]
url = "ws://laptop:7419/ws"
token = "<the daemon's token>"

# On labpc: dial in, named after the host, and stay connected.
cookie runtime serve --daemon
  • Daemon. --daemon takes the daemon's client URL, or, without one, [server] url of this machine's config.toml, else the local daemon that table describes. The token is --token, COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN, or [server] token; flags override the configuration. The daemon keeps its own token in its config.toml, so it survives restarts.
  • Identity. --id is the runtime ID, [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}; without it, the host name, sanitized (host_ in front when it does not start with a letter). It must not be global, local, or a configured [runtimes.<id>], and only one runtime may be connected under an ID at a time.
  • Refusals. The daemon says why it refuses a runtime, and the runtime prints it. A refusal that retrying cannot fix, a configured or reserved ID or a wrong token, ends cookie runtime serve --daemon with an error:
cookie: cannot dial in to ws://laptop:7419/ws as `labpc`: the daemon refused the runtime (HTTP 403): runtime `labpc` is configured on the daemon ([runtimes.labpc]) and cannot dial in

Any other, such as an ID a runtime is still connected under (the daemon may not have noticed yet that an earlier connection dropped), is printed and retried with the same backoff as a drop:

cookie runtime: cannot dial in to ws://laptop:7419/ws as `labpc`: the daemon refused the runtime (HTTP 409): runtime `labpc` is already connected; retrying in 1 s

A dropped connection prints the reason too, such as disconnected from ws://laptop:7419/ws: the daemon closed the connection with code 1011: runtime `labpc` failed to start: … for a runtime of an incompatible version. See Dial-in refusals. - Reconnecting. The runtime reconnects after every drop, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, and so on up to 30 s. While it is away, its instances go reconnecting and then failed, and their tools leave the sessions' tool lists; when it dials in again, the daemon reopens them over the new connection. runtimes.list shows it with lifetime dial_in, and, while it is away, why it disconnected. It stops on a stop signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP), so it runs as a service; see Running as a service. - Stopping. A stopping runtime closes its WebSocket with a close handshake (normal closure). The daemon records that as runtime `labpc` disconnected: the other end closed the connection, in runtimes.list and in its instances' reasons as they go reconnecting and then failed; a runtime that vanished without one, such as one that was killed or lost its network, shows the transport's error instead, for example Connection reset without closing handshake. - MCP servers. It hosts its own machine's MCP servers: those of [runtimes.local.mcp] in that machine's config.toml. - Roots. --root limits its workspaces, as for --stdio. - Clients on its machine. Plain cookie and cookie attach on the runtime's machine use it for their directory when the daemon runs elsewhere, such as in a container; see A daemon already running.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Every runtime belongs to a machine, the computer it runs on. The model is told which machine each attachment's runtime runs on, so it knows which tools share files (see the system prompt). The daemon groups runtimes into machines on its own: runtimes that report the same machine ID, such as global, local, and a cookie runtime serve on the daemon's own computer, share a machine, and a computer it has not seen gets a machine named after its host name. A runtime that reports no machine ID gets a machine of its own, named after its runtime ID. Machines are kept in ~/.cookie-agent/machines.json, which only the daemon writes; there is no configuration for them.

Regroup them by hand when the automatic grouping is wrong, for example when a container reports its own machine ID. In the TUI, the Machines view of the /runtime panel (press m, or click its tab) lists each machine with its runtimes; select a machine to rename (n), merge (g), or forget (f) it, or a runtime to move it to another machine (v) or unpin it (u). From a terminal, cookie machine does the same and works against a remote daemon like cookie config:

cookie machine list                  # machines, their runtimes, and memories
cookie machine rename labpc lab      # a machine's memory folder moves with it
cookie machine assign box labpc      # pin runtime `box` to machine `labpc`
cookie machine unassign box          # follow the machine ID it reports again
cookie machine merge box labpc       # move `box`'s IDs, pins, and memories
cookie machine forget old-laptop     # only with no connected runtimes or memories

A change applies to connected runtimes at once; sessions see the new machine names from their next run.

Each machine has its own memories, machine://<machine>/<name>, in the folder ~/.cookie-agent/memory/machines/<machine> (see Memory): renaming a machine moves its folder, merging moves its memories into the other machine's and fails when both have a memory of one name, and a machine can be forgotten only once its folder is empty. A session's model sees an index of the memories of the machines its attachments run on.

docs.title: Security guarantees
docs.text: Cookie Agent combines permission policy with platform-specific filesystem and process controls. Permission rules decide whether a prepared tool call may run; they are not an operating-system security boundary. Rules deny by default: an unmatched action or resource is refused, and a tool whose action has no allow or ask rule is not advertised to the model at all. In particular, a permitted bash command is not parsed into filesystem operations and runs without syscall filtering.

docs.title: Filesystem capabilities
docs.text:
The read, write, and edit tools resolve their filesystem target when the call is prepared, before policy evaluation, and operate on that resolved location when it executes. Relative paths are rooted at the workspace. Absolute paths remain absolute and must be controlled with explicit permission patterns; the filesystem capability layer does not confine them to the workspace.

These tools follow supported filesystem links. write and edit preserve a link and modify its destination rather than replacing the link itself. If a final link is dangling, write prepares the missing destination and creates it, while read and edit fail because their destination must already exist. Link resolution is bounded, so cycles and routes exceeding the bound fail closed.

Only the route is bound, not the content. A file that changes while an approval is pending is read, edited, or replaced as it is at execution, and a write prepared for an absent path replaces a file created there in the meantime.

Permission matching is deliberately separate: it uses only the normalized lexical path requested by the caller, even when that alias leads outside the workspace. The resolved destination does not receive a second permission check. See Permissions.

docs.title: Unix
docs.text:
Filesystem traversal is descriptor-anchored. Each path component is opened relative to its parent descriptor with no-follow semantics, and links are expanded in place: a relative link target is traversed from the directory that holds the link, an absolute one restarts from the filesystem root. Preparation keeps the target's parent directory open, and execution opens, creates, or renames the target relative to that descriptor with no-follow semantics. A link swapped into the route after preparation therefore cannot redirect the operation, and a link planted at the target itself is never followed: reads fail with operation_changed and writes replace the link. Directories missing at preparation are created at execution without following links.

Writes stage the complete content in a temporary file beside the target, sync it, rename it over the target, and sync the directory.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows filesystem capabilities remain path-based. For symbolic links and junctions that the backend supports, Cookie Agent follows the route to the destination while preserving the alias for writes. Other reparse-point forms fail closed. The backend:

  • normalizes the requested native path and rejects unsafe components;
  • resolves supported links and canonicalizes the existing portion of the path, then checks component-wise, case-insensitive containment in the prepared sandbox root;
  • resolves the route again immediately before use and fails with operation_changed if it now leads to a different path; and
  • stages complete file content beside the target and publishes it by renaming the staged file over the target with the superseding POSIX rename (SetFileInformationByHandle, FileRenameInfoEx), which re-points the name in one metadata transaction so a concurrent reader opening the path by name never finds it absent; where that rename is unavailable the publish falls back to MoveFileExW with write-through and replace-existing flags.

Containment is a capability constraint, not another permission decision. In particular, a relative request remains constrained to its prepared sandbox root even though permission policy would authorize an external destination through the lexical alias. Absolute requests retain their existing native-root checks. Support is limited to link and junction forms that this path-based backend can resolve; unsupported reparse tags are rejected.

Windows does not provide the descriptor-anchored openat traversal used by the Unix backend. A path or supported link can therefore change after the final route check and before the path-based read or mutation; the check narrows this window but does not eliminate it.

docs.title: Private state
docs.text:
On Unix, Cookie Agent creates new private-state directories with mode 0700 and new files with mode 0600. Store updates use flock-locked journals and atomic publication. Existing paths are not checked for owner, mode, type, link count, or symlinks; they are opened and used as-is.

On Windows, new state directories and files are created with a protected DACL whose single access-control entry grants the current user full control. Secure-store lock files use an exclusive whole-file LockFileEx lock, and durable state replacement stages and flushes a private file before publishing it with a superseding POSIX rename (SetFileInformationByHandle, FileRenameInfoEx with replace-if-exists and POSIX semantics) followed by a flush of the target's parent directory. That rename keeps the published name resolvable for the whole replacement, so a concurrent reader always sees the old file or the new one. Kernels and filesystems that reject the information class fall back to MoveFileExW with replace-existing and write-through flags, which is not atomic for concurrent opens by name. Existing paths are not checked for owner, DACL shape, reparse points, object type, or hard links; they are opened and used as-is.

Creation-time modes and DACLs protect newly created state from other ordinary users. They do not protect state that already exists or is later replaced. A local actor able to pre-create or replace a state path can redirect reads and writes through a symlink or provide loose/foreign-owned storage; Cookie Agent will use that path. Treat the parent storage location as trusted and remove unexpected state before starting the daemon. Neither platform protects secrets from privileged code such as root, SYSTEM, or an elevated administrator.

docs.title: Daemon authentication token
docs.text:
The daemon authenticates every connection, from clients and from dial-in runtimes alike, with a constant-time compare of a bearer token. A runtime presents it in the Authorization header of its WebSocket upgrade; a client presents it there or in its handshake request, which is how a web page authenticates, since browsers cannot set WebSocket headers. A client connection that has not authenticated may send only handshake, is closed after a wrong token, and is closed after 10 seconds without one. It binds IPv4 loopback unless --listen names another address; off loopback, serve TLS (--tls-cert, --tls-key) or keep the listener on a private network, since a plaintext ws:// connection carries the token in the clear. Anyone holding the token is a fully trusted client and may also offer a runtime.

Web pages. /ws does not check a browser's Origin header (see Web clients): any page in any browser on a machine that can reach the daemon can open a connection, and the token is the only protection. Gating on origins protects nothing once a reverse proxy serves the page, since the browser then reports the proxy's origin. A page served over HTTPS can only connect to a wss:// daemon. Runtimes never connect from a web page: a request to /runtime with an Origin header is always refused.

The token is durable: it is [server] token in the user config.toml. When the configuration has none, the daemon draws a fresh 32-byte token from the operating system at its first start and writes it there, rewriting the file owner-only (0600 on Unix), so it stays the same across restarts and a runtime that dials in can reconnect after one. The WebSocket subcommands (attach, connect, disconnect, mcp) and cookie runtime serve --daemon read it from the same file unless given --token / COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN. Any process that can read your config.toml can therefore connect to the daemon; keep the file private, and replace the token (delete the line and restart the daemon) if it leaks. Plain cookie sends the token to whatever listens at [server] host and port when it looks for a running daemon (see A daemon already running), as cookie attach with default settings does; it looks only when the token is set. The daemon also prints the token in its first stdout line:

daemon-ready {"url":"ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/ws","token":"<43-char base64url>"}

A supervisor that logs daemon stdout verbatim persists the token in its logs, and a token pasted on a shell command line is visible in shell history. Treat the ready line as secret and do not archive it.

docs.title: AGENTS.md context files
docs.text: For root runs, repository-controlled AGENTS.md files are read automatically and their text enters model context. They are instructions, not trusted policy, and cannot grant permissions or bypass tool preparation. A malicious repository can still influence model behavior within permissions. Review or disable AGENTS.md context before running unfamiliar workspaces, avoid placing secrets in these files, and use restrictive tool permissions. See AGENTS.md context.

docs.title: Retained tool output
docs.text: Tool-output truncation is a presentation bound, not redaction. The preview shown to a model or user can omit bytes that remain in the content-addressed artifact store, and those retained bytes may contain secrets. A session reads them with read_artifact(artifact="<digest>", stream=…), which needs no permission rule and is always allowed: it resolves only artifacts stored in the session's own tree, without visibility or revert checks. Digests are content-derived, not random access tokens. Display clipping does not redact stored content. See the tool artifact lifecycle.

docs.title: Media attachments
docs.text:
Media files read through read or returned by MCP servers are sniffed by content and structurally validated before bytes are retained or sent to a provider: images must parse as a complete PNG, JPEG, static WebP, or GIF container whose header dimensions, pixel count, and frame count stay within bounds; PDFs need a version header, an %%EOF marker near the end, a startxref offset that lands on a cross-reference table or stream, and no encryption dictionary; audio and video get frame-sync and container magic-byte checks. Pixel data and PDF content streams are never decoded, so a file with a valid container but corrupt compressed data is accepted and left to the provider. A provider that rejects such a file fails the request, and because history replays the attachment, later requests fail too until the session is reverted or forked to before it.

Validation rejects malformed input, but it is not content screening: an image or PDF can embed adversarial text intended for the model (visible prompt injection). Media attachments are in the same trust class as file text the model already reads; apply the same judgement about which files an agent is pointed at.

docs.title: Process boundary
docs.text:
On Unix, Bash commands run in a new session so cancellation and timeout can kill the process group. On Windows, Bash commands are assigned to a Job Object before their initial thread resumes, and cancellation or drop kills the job so child processes cannot escape during startup.

The process-group and Job Object controls bound process lifetime; they do not restrict what an approved command can access. Windows commands do not run in an AppContainer or restricted token and have no seccomp-like syscall filter. Treat bash permission as authority to run the complete command with the Cookie Agent process's user privileges.

docs.title: Web fetching
docs.text: webfetch requests run with the Cookie Agent process's network access and inherited proxy environment. Permission policy checks only the exact initial URL, including its query string; redirect destinations are not re-checked, and there is no SSRF protection, host or IP blocklist, or DNS pinning. A broad pattern therefore authorizes requests to any reachable host, including local network services — scope webfetch rules accordingly. See the tool reference.

docs.title: Toolchain and source checkout
docs.text:
Development requires Git and Rust 1.88 or newer. Clone the repository and enter the workspace:

git clone https://github.com/cookie-agent/cookie-agent.git
cd cookie-agent

Cargo fetches the locked, git-pinned Oven SDK dependencies automatically. Build the debug binary with:

cargo build --locked -p cookie_agent

The binary is target/debug/cookie. To install the workspace version into $CARGO_HOME/bin, run:

cargo install --locked --path crates/cookie_agent

The workspace contains twelve crates: coding_runtime, config, cookie_agent, engine, identity, mcp, models, plugin_sdk, protocol, runtime_api, server, and tui. Their public interfaces are available in the Rust API documentation.

docs.title: Required gates
docs.text:
Use locked dependency resolution for workspace builds and tests:

cargo build --locked --workspace --all-targets
cargo test --locked --workspace

Run formatting and Clippy with warnings denied under stable and the Rust 1.88 minimum supported toolchain:

cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo +stable clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo +1.88.0 clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings

Check the protocol compatibility baselines, documentation, and dependency policy:

crates/protocol/scripts/check-schema-additive.sh
./scripts/build-docs.sh
cargo deny --locked check advisories licenses sources

The compatibility check and documentation require Python 3. Before the protocols freeze, any change to a wire type, method, or protocol version needs regenerated baselines: run crates/protocol/scripts/update-compat-baseline.sh and commit crates/protocol/compat/. For the documentation, install requirements-docs.txt before running ./scripts/build-docs.sh. That script builds workspace rustdoc and runs MkDocs in strict mode.

docs.title: Windows targets
docs.text: CI builds and tests both x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-pc-windows-msvc on native Windows runners. Use the matching MSVC Rust target when validating Windows-specific changes.

docs.title: Write a client
docs.text: A client is any program that speaks the client protocol to a daemon: the TUI, the web page, and the cookie subcommands are three. The daemon treats every client alike, so a client of your own, an editor integration, a dashboard, a bot, sees and does what the shipped ones do. This page is the path through the protocol; the protocol reference and the event reference hold the details it links to.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Open a WebSocket to the daemon's client URL, by default ws://127.0.0.1:7419/ws (wss:// when it serves TLS). The URL and the token come from the same places the CLI takes them; see Reaching a daemon. Each WebSocket text frame carries one JSON-RPC 2.0 message, up to 128 MiB.

Present the token one of two ways:

  • A header, Authorization: Bearer <token>, on the upgrade request. A wrong token is refused with HTTP 401 before the WebSocket opens. Native clients should use this.
  • The handshake, for clients that cannot set headers, such as a browser page. The daemon ignores the Origin header a browser sends; see Web clients.

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
The first request must be handshake:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"handshake","params":{
  "protocol_version":"1.6.0",
  "client":{"kind":"mytool","instance_id":"0192f3c4-8d1e-7a2b-9c3d-4e5f60718293"},
  "features":[]}}
  • protocol_version is the version your client was written against. The daemon accepts any version of its major and both sides use the lower minor; another major is refused with -32002 unsupported_protocol. Send only the methods and members of the version you name.
  • client.kind is a label of your choosing, a lowercase letter and up to 15 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. client.instance_id is a UUID you keep across reconnects, so your client recognizes what it sent.
  • token goes here when you did not send the header.

The reply names the daemon's protocol and engine versions, your origin, the label your submissions carry, and the daemon's machine_id. Until the handshake succeeds the daemon answers no other request, and it closes a connection that has not authenticated within 10 seconds. See Handshake and authentication and Compatibility.

docs.title: Call methods
docs.text:
After the handshake, send requests with any id; replies can arrive out of order, and the daemon runs up to 64 of one connection's requests at once. methods.json lists every method with its params and result schema, and Methods describes them by area: sessions, runs, approvals, runtimes, machines, memory, configuration, providers, MCP servers, and plugins.

A typical flow: session.list to show sessions, session.create for a new one, session.submit_input to send a message (it starts, steers, or queues a run; see Submitting from several clients), approval.list and approval.respond when a tool call waits for an answer, and run.cancel to stop.

docs.title: Follow a session
docs.text:
events.subscribe with a session_id and a cursor, the last seq you hold, returns the events after it and starts events.subscription notifications for that session. Each notification is one of:

  • event: a stored event, with its seq; advance your cursor.
  • transient: live-only output, such as streamed text or tool output, placed after the stored event after_seq; it never advances the cursor, and the committed event that follows replaces it.
  • gap: you fell behind and the daemon dropped your tail; subscribe again from your cursor.
  • rewound: a revert cut the log; drop what you hold past through_seq.

Large histories page with limit and has_more, and cursor_timestamp lets you detect that a revert reused your cursor's sequence number. Read events openly: an event type or a member you do not know is skipped, not an error. See Subscriptions, Records, and Decoding.

Changes outside one session arrive as their own notifications, such as sessions.changed, runtimes.changed, or memory.changed, after which you refetch the matching list; see Daemon-wide changes.

docs.title: Show tool calls
docs.text: Tool calls describe themselves to clients as typed display blocks: text, markdown, code, file_excerpt, diff, terminal, key_value, table, json, media, link, and session_ref. Draw each kind you support. The daemon fits blocks to your protocol version: a kind newer than your minor reaches you as text, and every block has a text rendering to fall back on. See Tool display.

docs.title: Handle errors
docs.text: An error reply carries a JSON-RPC code and, for the daemon's own errors, data.code, a stable snake_case name, with a message for people, an optional hint saying what to do, and an optional detail. Branch on data.code, show message and hint, and show detail on request. The error reference lists every code and its fields.

docs.title: Send files
docs.text: Attachments upload in chunks before the message that uses them: artifact.upload.begin with the session and size, artifact.upload.chunk with base64 data of at most 1 MiB, each after the previous one is answered, and artifact.upload.finish with the SHA-256, which returns the artifact to put in the message content. artifact.read reads media back. See Media.

docs.title: Any language
docs.text: The protocol's schemas are published with these pages: methods.json, one JSON Schema per params and result root under schemas/client/schemas/, and the version they describe. They are committed in crates/protocol/compat/client/, and a checker keeps every change additive within a major, so code generated from them keeps working with later daemons. See Published schemas.

docs.title: Rust
docs.text:
The cookie_agent_protocol crate has the client the TUI and the web page use. With its websocket feature, Client::connect_websocket_with_token connects natively, and on wasm32 Client::connect_browser_websocket uses the browser's WebSocket (send the token with handshake_with_token). The client pairs replies with requests, reads events openly, and delivers events, replays, and notifications in order on one stream. A sketch:

use cookie_agent_protocol::{Client, ClientIdentity, ClientKind, SessionListParams};

let client = Client::connect_websocket_with_token(url, &token).await?;
client
    .handshake_as(ClientIdentity::generate(ClientKind::new("mytool")?))
    .await?;
let mut deliveries = client.subscribe_deliveries().expect("taken once");
let sessions = client.list_sessions(SessionListParams::default()).await?;
client.subscribe_events(session_id, None).await?;
while let Some(delivery) = deliveries.recv().await {
    // ClientDelivery::Live, ReplayEvent, SessionsChanged, Disconnected, …
}

cookie_agent_client_state folds those deliveries into per-session state, rows ready to draw, pending approvals, runtimes, and the rest, with the panel rules the TUI and the web page share; it builds for wasm32 too. See the Rust API and Session mechanics.

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text:
A plugin is a local program the daemon starts and talks to over its standard input and output: newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line. A plugin can:

  • declare tools, which it prepares and runs with the runtime protocol's tool messages;
  • intercept engine hooks, such as a tool call or a model request;
  • stream session events and a bus other plugins publish to;
  • produce messages to any session.

This page covers the Rust SDK and the plugin protocol. To install or configure a plugin, see the user guide. The protocol's design and history are in the plugins spec.

docs.title: Rust SDK
docs.text:
The cookie_agent_plugin_sdk crate (Apache-2.0) handles the handshake, framing, tool preparation, hooks, and producer requests. Until it is published, add it as a path dependency:

[dependencies]
cookie_agent_plugin_sdk = { path = "../cookie-agent/crates/plugin_sdk" }
serde_json = "1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] }

A plugin with one tool:

use cookie_agent_plugin_sdk::{
    DisplayBlock, PermissionAction, PluginServer, Presentation, ToolDecl, ToolFailure, ToolOutput,
};
use serde_json::json;

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() -> Result<(), cookie_agent_plugin_sdk::PluginError> {
    let mut echo: ToolDecl = serde_json::from_value(json!({
        "name": "echo",
        "description": "Echo text back to the model",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"text": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["text"]
        }
    }))?;
    echo.permission = Some(PermissionAction::new("echo").expect("valid action"));
    PluginServer::builder("echo", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
        .tool(echo, |_call, arguments| async move {
            let text = arguments["text"]
                .as_str()
                .ok_or_else(|| ToolFailure::new("text is required"))?;
            Ok(ToolOutput::success(text).display(DisplayBlock::text(text)))
        })
        .prepare_presentation("echo", |call| {
            Presentation::new("Echo")
                .primary_argument(call.arguments["text"].as_str().unwrap_or_default())
        })
        .run_stdio()
        .await
}

The name given to builder must be the plugin's configured name. The SDK derives the plugin's capabilities from what is registered and validates each tool's name and parameter schema when the server is built.

  • Tools. tool(declaration, handler) registers a tool whose calls are approved under its declared permission with no resource; tool_with_resource(declaration, resource, handler) also derives each call's permission resource, such as a path or an issue number, from its arguments. The daemon builds each call's approval identity from them. A handler gets a ToolContext (the session, run, and call IDs, whether the model asked for the background, cancellation, progress, progress_display, and detachable) and the call's arguments, and returns a ToolOutput or a ToolFailure.
  • Results. ToolOutput is a builder: ToolOutput::success(text) or ToolOutput::error(text) (a result the model should see as a failure), then title, display (one display block; displays for several), metadata, attachment(mime_type, filename, bytes), and failed. The model reads the text and the metadata; clients show the display blocks, or the text when there are none. The SDK sends an attachment's bytes with the result.
  • Presentation. prepare_presentation(tool, |call| …) returns a Presentation for each prepared call of tool: a title, a hint for icons (such as shell or fetch), a primary_argument, and display blocks of its arguments and a preview of what it will do. Without it a call is titled with the tool's name and shows its permission resource.
  • Progress. progress(message, output) reports a status line and output text; progress_display(message, delta) changes the call's live display with a DisplayDelta (Append { index, text, stream } or Replace { blocks }).
  • Hooks. One builder method per hook, named after it, such as tool_before_call; helpers like allow(), block(reason), modify, replace, append_system_prompt, inject_message, and cancel_compaction build results, and transform_input, rewrite_input_text, replace_messages, rewrite_history_text, replace_message_content, and rewrite_message_text build the replacements of user_before_input, model_before_request, and message_end (the rewrite_* ones change text parts and keep every other part as sent). on_hook_error(hook, ExtensionHookOnError::Block) makes a failure of that hook block its operation (see Hooks).
  • Events. on_event and on_bus_event receive streamed notifications; event_patterns(["run_*", ...]) narrows the event types on_event gets. A handler may publish one bus event with context.emit_bus(...) after enable_bus_publishing(). on_unknown receives notifications the SDK does not know or cannot read (see Compatibility).
  • Producers. enable_producers() and, optionally, on_recovery(...). See Producers.

The examples echo_plugin.rs and producer_plugin.rs in crates/plugin_sdk/examples build with cargo check -p cookie_agent_plugin_sdk --examples. The SDK exposes the protocol version it speaks as PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_VERSION; its crate version's major follows the protocol's major.

docs.title: Reference plugin
docs.text:
examples/plugins/python/ holds a plugin in plain Python with no dependencies, written against the protocol rather than the SDK:

  • cookie_plugin.py is a small helper for any Python plugin: framing, the handshake and its version check, tool preparation and execution, hooks, events, and producer requests, single-threaded, keeping what the daemon sends while a handler waits for an answer.
  • reference_plugin.py uses it: a tool, word_count, with a presentation, a live display, and a result of display blocks and metadata; a tool_before_call hook with on_error = "block"; an event subscription by pattern (run_*, tool_call_*); and a producer that queues a message once a call has finished.
  • check_reference_plugin.py plays the daemon through a scripted conversation and validates every message both sides send against the published schemas, with a standard-library validator for the subset of JSON Schema they use. CI runs it, and an engine test runs the plugin against the daemon.

To try it, add it to config.toml:

[plugins.reference]
command = ["python3", "/path/to/cookie-agent/examples/plugins/python/reference_plugin.py"]
producer_messaging = true

and allow its permission action in an agent (text_read: allow).

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
The daemon starts the plugin's command in its own process group (a job object on Windows), with the daemon's environment plus the plugin's env, and sends plugin/initialize within startup_timeout_ms:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"plugin/initialize","params":{
  "protocol_version":"1.2.0","engine_version":"0.3.0",
  "features":["producer_messaging"],"interception_timeout_ms":2000}}

features lists what the plugin's configuration enables: today only producer_messaging, sent when producer_messaging = true. A version never implies a feature. interception_timeout_ms is the plugin's interception_timeout_ms: how long the daemon waits for a hook's answer. The plugin answers with its own protocol version, its configured name, its own version, its features, its capabilities, and its tools:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{
  "protocol_version":"1.2.0","name":"issues","version":"1.2.0","features":[],
  "capabilities":{"producer_messaging":false,"subscribe_events":["run_*","tool_call_*"],
    "subscribe_bus":false,"publish_bus":false,
    "intercept":[{"hook":"tool_before_call","on_error":"block"}]},
  "tools":{"tools":[],"prompt_sections":[]}}}

The protocol version is a semver string, currently 1.2.0 (PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_VERSION, which the SDK re-exports). Each end reads the other's protocol_version from the raw JSON before anything else, and refuses an incompatible one with unsupported_protocol naming both versions: the majors must be equal, so no 0.x build from before the freeze connects. A minor only adds, so the two ends use what the lower minor includes and the patch never matters (see Compatibility). A different name also fails the start. No plugin feature is defined yet; the daemon ignores one it does not know and shows it in the plugin's status. Capabilities are fixed for the connection; tools is the runtime protocol's RuntimeTools. The SDK exposes what the handshake said about the daemon to handlers as PluginContext::daemon(): its protocol version, engine_version, features, and interception timeout. Before plugin/initialize the SDK refuses every request with not_initialized.

Request IDs may be integers or strings (the daemon sends integers). Every frame is at most 48 MiB, and a frame that is not a JSON-RPC request, notification, or reply ends the connection. See Compatibility for what each end does with what it does not know. Standard output carries only protocol messages; standard error is kept as a bounded tail (the last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB) that clients see in plugin status.

At shutdown the daemon sends the plugin/shutdown notification, waits shutdown_grace_ms, and kills the process group.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
The plugin protocol follows the runtime protocol's rules:

  • Information is read tolerantly. Everything the daemon sends a plugin (initialize params, hook params, events, bus events, plugin/emit_result, and the tool/* requests), and what a plugin answers or declares (initialize and hook results, tool declarations, runtime/tools_changed), ignores members its reader does not know.
  • Commands are strict. plugin/emit, tool/progress, tool/detachable, and the producer/* requests are refused when they carry a member or an enum value the daemon does not know: a request with -32602, unknown_field or unknown_variant, and the member's JSON path in data.field; a notification with a note in the plugin's status. Gate new fields on the daemon's version (PluginContext::daemon()).
  • Not from a plugin. The daemon ignores the runtime-only capability/tools_changed and mcp/changed from a plugin, with a note in its status.
  • Open enums. Besides the runtime protocol's: an entry of capabilities.intercept naming a hook the daemon does not know, one it cannot read, and one repeating a hook are skipped, each with a note in the plugin's status, and the plugin still starts; an on_error it does not know reads as block; a feature it does not know is ignored the same way; an unknown bus status of plugin/emit_result reads as dropped; a hook's tool origin of an unknown kind, and an event of an unknown type, read as Open::Unknown; an unknown model_before_select source reads as Unknown. A hook result's action and a message role are closed: an unknown one makes the answer malformed, which is a failure of the hook (see Hooks).
  • Errors follow the runtime protocol's scheme: a standard code, or -32000 with data.code, and a message a user can understand. When a plugin fails to start or a call to it fails, the daemon shows the plugin's message and names the plugin.

The SDK does its part: a hook whose params carry members it does not know still runs; an event of a type it does not know reaches on_event as Open::Unknown; a notification it does not know, or an event or bus event it cannot read, goes to on_unknown when the plugin registers it, and is otherwise ignored (one it cannot read with a line on standard error, which the daemon shows as the plugin's stderr). emit_bus waits for its plugin/emit_result at most the daemon's interception_timeout_ms and then resolves as dropped. A ToolFailure with a blank message is sent as one saying the tool failed without saying why.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
A plugin is starting, connected, reconnecting, failed, disabled, or stopped. When it exits or its connection drops, the daemon starts it again after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s, and marks it failed when every attempt fails. A failed plugin stays failed until a client restarts it (plugins.restart); a restart of a connected plugin stops and starts it. Each start is a new connection: the plugin answers plugin/initialize again, and a producing plugin recovers again.

Clients read status with plugins.list and are told of changes with plugins.changed (client protocol). A status carries the plugin's state, why it last failed, its tools and hooks, its dropped-notification count, and its standard error tail.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A plugin's tools are a runtime's tools. It declares them in the initialize result and later with runtime/tools_changed, and the daemon runs them with the same client it uses for a runtime:

Message Direction Purpose tool/prepare daemon → plugin Prepare one turn's calls: the plugin reports each call's normalized arguments, permission and resource, and presentation. The daemon builds the call's approval identity from them. tool/revalidate daemon → plugin Check a prepared call is still valid before it runs. tool/execute daemon → plugin Run a prepared call; the result is its output, optional title, display blocks, metadata, and attachments, and whether it failed. The daemon builds the stored result from it. tool/release daemon → plugin Forget a prepared call that will not run. tool/cancel daemon → plugin Cancel an executing call. tool/progress plugin → daemon Report a running call's status and output, and optionally a display delta (append or replace) of its live display. tool/detachable plugin → daemon The call may now move to the background. runtime/tools_changed plugin → daemon Replace the plugin's tool list.

Their params and results are in the runtime protocol reference; the types are in the protocol crate's runtime_protocol module. A declaration has a name, description, and JSON Schema parameters, and optionally a free-form permission action (a tool may need none), collision, concurrency, result_truncation, an output of one or up to 8 named streams, and background support. The SDK fills in tool/prepare. A plugin written without it reports no approval identity: the daemon builds it from the call's permission, resource, and normalized arguments and from the plugin's name and the tool's, as it does for a runtime's call (see Approval identity).

Names. Plugin tools join the global runtime, but each plugin composes as its own source, prefixed with the plugin's name. A tool keeps its name unless another tool has it. Then the declared collision decides: with prefix (the default), every tool of that name is published under its source's prefix (<plugin>_<tool>, <attachment>_<tool>); with override, the tool keeps the bare name and the others are prefixed (or hidden, if they are fallback). Two overrides of one name are both prefixed, with a diagnostic. Base-layer names, such as skill, are never taken. While a plugin is not connected its tools are not published.

Permissions. A call is approved under the action its declaration names and the resource its preparation reports, like a runtime tool; the agent policy names the action (issue_read: allow). A tool that declares no permission runs without approval.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
A plugin lists the hooks it handles in capabilities.intercept, each as { "hook": "<name>", "on_error": "allow" | "block" } (allow when on_error is absent); it is never sent another. Each hook is a request plugin/intercept/<hook>:

Hook Runs May tool_before_call after a call passes policy and approval allow, block, or modify the arguments tool_after_result after a call finishes, before it is committed replace the model-facing content agent_before_start at a run's start append to or replace the system prompt, inject a message session_before_compact before compaction add or replace its instructions, or cancel it user_before_input before root user input or steering is committed allow, transform it, or handle it without a run model_before_request before each user-facing model attempt replace the messages, adjust inference parameters message_end after an assistant message is assembled replace its content model_before_select before a run's model selection changes, or a fallback block it session_before_fork before a fork block it session_before_revert before a revert block it, or override its instructions

Hooks run in the order the configuration lists the plugins, each within its interception_timeout_ms. A modification is validated before the next plugin sees it, and an invalid one is skipped with a diagnostic. A block stops later hooks.

A hook call fails when it times out, when its plugin is not connected or exits, or when the plugin answers with an error or with a result that does not decode (an unknown action included). The session records a diagnostic of source plugin:<name> and kind interception_timeout, interception_crash, or interception_rejected, and the entry's on_error decides what happens next:

  • allow (the default): the hook fails open. The operation goes on as if the plugin had not intercepted it, and later plugins still run.
  • block: the operation is blocked as if the plugin had blocked it, and later plugins do not run. Declare it for a hook that enforces a policy, so that the policy holds while the plugin is down.
Hook With block, a failure tool_before_call fails the call before it runs; the model reads "Tool call blocked: plugin <name> could not check this: …" tool_after_result fails the call after it ran, withholding its result; the model reads "Tool result withheld: …" agent_before_start, user_before_input, model_before_select (a run's model) refuses run.start, run.steer, or session.submit_input model_before_select (a fallback) ends the run without falling back model_before_request, message_end abandons the model attempt, without a model error, and fails the run session_before_compact refuses session.compact; an automatic compaction is skipped, as when the plugin cancels it session_before_fork, session_before_revert refuses the fork or revert

A refused request fails with the error plugin_hook_failed, whose data names the plugin and the hook and whose detail says what went wrong. A failed run's error says the same.

docs.title: What hooks see
docs.text:
Hook params never carry the daemon's internal or provider types. Three hooks see views of them:

  • model_before_request gets messages, a list of { "role": "system" | "user" | "assistant" | "tool", "content": [part] }, and model, { provider_id, model_id, adapter }. A part is {"type":"text","text":…}, {"type":"file","artifact":{sha256,byte_length,media_type,filename?}}, {"type":"tool_call","id":…,"name":…,"arguments":{…}}, or {"type":"tool_result","tool_call_id":…,"content":"…","is_error":false}. A tool result's content is its text (JSON values as JSON text), and the files it carries follow it as file parts. The view leaves out reasoning, provider metadata, replay state, and extension parts. With {"action":"replace","messages":[…]}, a message returned exactly as it was sent keeps all of that; any other message is built from its parts alone (an assistant message so built has no reasoning or replay state). A file part must name a file of the request, by its sha256; a replacement cannot add files. A system message holds only text, a user message text and files, and a tool message results and the files after them.
  • message_end gets content, the assistant message's parts: text, reasoning ({"type":"reasoning","text":…}), tool_call, and file (metadata only), the same shapes as above. With {"action":"replace","content":[…]}, a part returned exactly as sent keeps its metadata; others are built from their fields. Parts the view leaves out (sources, provider-run tool results, approvals, extensions) stay after the part they followed, or end the message when that part is gone. A file must be one of the message's own.
  • user_before_input gets content, the input as user content, as the input-lane events store it: a nonempty list of text parts and file parts, whose artifact is metadata only. With {"action":"transform","content":[…]}, a plugin may change, reorder, or remove parts, but every file part must be one of the input's, unchanged, and the result must not be blank.

Parts are open: a part of a type the SDK does not know reads as Open::Unknown, and the daemon refuses a replacement that holds one. A replacement the daemon refuses is skipped with an invalid_modification diagnostic, as before.

agent_before_start gets prompt_context:

Member Meaning input The user content that starts the run, after user_before_input; null when a producer's message starts it. system_prompt The agent's composed system prompt: its own prompt with the runtimes', tools', and skills' sections, and what earlier plugins changed. injected_messages The messages earlier plugins injected ({ role, content }), in order.

Each plugin sees what the plugins before it made of the prompt.

tool_before_call and tool_after_result carry the call's origin: {"kind":"base"} for a daemon base tool, or {"kind":"runtime","attachment":"local","runtime_id":"local"} for a runtime's or plugin's tool. The SDK reads it as Open<ExtensionToolOrigin>, so an origin of a kind it does not know reaches the hook as Unknown. permission_name is null for a tool that needs no permission. A hook cannot change a call's permission or resource, never sees calls policy denied, and never grants permission.

Internal agents (title, approval, compaction) are never intercepted. user_before_input runs for root sessions only; the other agent hooks also run for delegated sessions.

docs.title: Events and the bus
docs.text:
capabilities.subscribe_events lists the event types a plugin receives, as patterns: a type such as run_finished, a prefix ending in * such as tool_call_*, or * alone for every type. An empty list subscribes to nothing; the daemon skips a pattern it cannot read, with a note in the plugin's status. For each event a pattern selects, the plugin receives a plugin/event notification: { session_id, context_id, seq, event, timestamp }, where event is the event's payload under the event contract, which the SDK reads as Open<EventPayload>: an event type it does not know arrives as Unknown. Durable events arrive after they are appended, in sequence order per session. Live-only events (text_delta, reasoning_delta, internal_agent_text_delta, tool_call_progress, native_compaction_started, and native_compaction_finished) are selected by their types like any other, so * includes them and run_* does not; they arrive as they happen, are never stored, and carry the seq of the durable event they follow. There is no replay. The SDK's on_event subscribes to * unless event_patterns([...]) narrows it.

With subscribe_bus, it receives plugin/bus_event notifications that other plugins publish: { session_id, context_id, plugin, name, payload }. A plugin never receives its own bus events.

Each plugin has a queue of 1024 notifications. When it is full, a new notification evicts the oldest of the lowest class it outranks: live output first, then ordinary events, and a tool's termination only when nothing else is queued. Drops are counted in the plugin's status and recorded as diagnostics. A slow plugin never delays the daemon or another plugin.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
A plugin with publish_bus publishes with the plugin/emit notification: { session_id, context_id, name, payload }. The context_id must come from a notification or hook request the daemon sent it for that session; each one may be used once. A notification's context expires five seconds after it is written to the plugin, a hook's when the hook is answered, and every hook call gets its own. The daemon answers with a plugin/emit_result notification: { name, bus, reason }, with bus published, dropped, or rejected. The SDK's emit_bus waits for it at most the plugin's interception_timeout_ms and then resolves as dropped.

A published event goes to the other plugins subscribed to the bus and to clients subscribed to the session (events.plugin); it is not stored and never reaches a model. Payloads are at most 256 KiB, names 128 control-free characters, and a whole event 272 KiB; each plugin may publish 40 events per second and 4 MiB per minute per session.

docs.title: Producers
docs.text:
A plugin sends messages to sessions as a producer, with the runtime protocol's producer methods and types:

Method Direction Params → result producer/register plugin → daemon { session_id, name } → { producer_id } producer/send plugin → daemon { session_id, producer_id, mode, idempotency_key, description, body } → { message_id } producer/unregister plugin → daemon { session_id, producer_id } → {} producer/discard plugin → daemon { session_id, message_id } → {} producer/recovery/start daemon → plugin notification, {} producer/recovery/complete plugin → daemon { outcome } → {}

Producing needs both the plugin's producer_messaging capability and its configuration's producer_messaging = true. A plugin may produce to any session. The daemon names its source plugin:<name> from the connection, so a plugin cannot speak for another. A plugin may run any number of named producers ([a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}), each with its own idempotency keys; the SDK's register_producer registers default.

Each send chooses steer (the next safe model request) or queue (a later run), and carries a description of at most 1024 bytes for display. The body is at most [producers] max_body_bytes. The answer follows durable acceptance; a retry with the same key and the same body, description, and mode returns the original message ID, and a missing answer is commit-uncertain. Discard works on a waiting message the plugin's source sent in that session, under any producer name, even after unregister or a restart. A producer ID lasts only as long as the connection.

After each successful start the daemon sends producer/recovery/start. The plugin restores its pending work from its own storage, registers producers and sends as needed, and then completes recovery with {"status":"ready"} or {"status":"failed","message":"..."}. There is no deadline; goals wait for a starting source, and a failed or disabled source leaves its work unknown. The SDK runs on_recovery and completes recovery when it returns, or reports ready at once when there is none. The external producers spec has the whole contract: external producers.

docs.title: Write a runtime
docs.text:
A runtime gives sessions tools: a shell on a build server, a browser, a database console, a device. The daemon reaches it over the runtime protocol, and any program that speaks it is a peer of cookie runtime serve: its capabilities appear in the runtimes panel, sessions attach them, and their tools pass the same permission checks and approvals as the built-in ones. This page is the path through the protocol; the runtime protocol reference holds the details it links to. For the model behind it, see Runtimes and capabilities.

A runtime is not a plugin. A plugin runs inside the daemon's global runtime, can also hook the engine's lifecycle, and speaks the plugin protocol, which shares the runtime protocol's framing and tool/* messages but has its own handshake. Write a runtime when the tools belong to another machine or another process boundary, and a plugin when they extend the daemon itself.

docs.title: Choose a transport
docs.text:
Both carry JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per frame, at most 48 MiB, and either side sends requests. See Connections and Framing.

  • Standard input and output. The daemon starts your program from a [runtimes.<id>] template, often through ssh, and exchanges one message per line. Standard output carries protocol messages only: no blank lines, no logging (log to standard error). The template's startup_timeout_ms bounds starting and initializing.
  • Dialing in. Your program opens a WebSocket to the daemon's /runtime?id=<runtime ID> route, the client URL with its path replaced, with Authorization: Bearer <token>; one message per text frame. A runtime ID is a lowercase letter and up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores; global, local, and the IDs of configured templates are taken, as is an ID already connected. The daemon allows 30 seconds for initializing and for each capability opening. Reconnecting after a drop is your job; the daemon reopens the session's instances when you are back. See Runtimes that dial in.

docs.title: Initialize
docs.text:
The daemon sends runtime/initialize first, with its protocol_version, the runtime_id you serve as, and settings: the [tool_output] and [agent_md] limits, and MCP servers to host. Answer with your version, your machine, and your capabilities:

{"protocol_version":"1.2.0","platform":"linux",
 "machine":{"id":"3f9a…","host_name":"buildbox"},
 "capabilities":[{"name":"console","kind":"database","takes_workspace":false,
                  "description":"A SQL console on the reporting replica"}]}
  • Versions must share their major; both sides then use the lower minor. Read protocol_version before anything else and refuse another major. See Version.
  • The machine ID is any stable, printable string of up to 128 bytes that is the same for every runtime on one computer; the daemon groups runtimes into machines by it, and the host_name names a new machine. Leave it out and the runtime gets a machine of its own. See Machines.
  • Capabilities each have a name, a free-form kind label, a description for people choosing one, and whether they take a workspace. Their tools come later, per instance. See runtime/initialize.
  • MCP servers are optional to host. A runtime that hosts none rejects a nonempty settings.mcp_servers with the initialize_rejected error; then nobody configures [runtimes.<id>.mcp] for it.

docs.title: Open capabilities
docs.text:
When a session attaches a capability, the daemon sends capability/open with the capability's name and, when it takes one, the workspace exactly as the user typed it; resolve it on your machine. Answer with an instance handle of your choosing, the attachment_name sessions see it under, the resolved workspace, its tools, and its skills. Opening an instance that is already open returns the same one. When an instance's tools change, send capability/tools_changed with the whole new list. See capability/open and Capabilities and instances.

A tool declaration is its name, description, and JSON Schema parameters, as the model will see them, plus:

  • permission: the permission action it is checked under, any label you choose, such as sql; absent means it needs no permission and is always allowed;
  • collision: what happens when another attachment offers the same name, prefix (the default: both become <attachment>_<name>), override, or fallback;
  • concurrency (exclusive or parallel), output (one output or named streams), result_truncation, and background for calls that may run in the background.

docs.title: Run tool calls
docs.text:
A call takes two steps, so that it can be approved between them:

  1. tool/prepare carries a batch of calls with the session, run, agent, and model. For each, check the arguments and answer prepared with a prepared_id, the normalized arguments, the call's permission and permission_resource (the path, command, or URL a rule matches), and a presentation (at least a title) clients show; or answer failed with an error the model reads. The daemon checks permissions and asks for approval from what you returned. See tool/prepare.
  2. tool/execute runs a prepared call and returns its outcome: output the model reads, an optional title, display blocks clients show, metadata, and media. While it runs, tool/progress streams output and display updates; tool/cancel asks you to stop, and the execute request still gets its answer. See tool/execute and Display blocks.

tool/release discards a prepared call that will not run, and tool/revalidate asks whether one is still valid before it runs.

Besides tools, runtime/context asks for an instance's AGENTS.md files (answer with empty lists when you have none), and runtime/shutdown asks you to stop: answer it, then exit. Producer messaging, for runtimes that send messages into sessions on their own, is negotiated at initialize; see Producer messaging. Answer a request you do not know with -32601, and ignore notifications and members you do not know.

docs.title: A minimal runtime
docs.text:
The sketch below serves one capability with one tool over standard input and output, in the style of the Python plugin helper (examples/plugins/python/cookie_plugin.py). It is a starting point, not a complete implementation: a real runtime handles every call of a batch, cancellation, and requests concurrently.

import json, sys, time

def send(message):
    sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(message, separators=(",", ":")) + "\n")
    sys.stdout.flush()

TOOLS = {"tools": [{
    "name": "clock",
    "description": "Tell the time on the build server.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}, "additionalProperties": False},
}], "prompt_sections": []}
prepared = {}

def handle(method, params):
    if method == "runtime/initialize":
        # A real runtime refuses another major with -32002 (see Version).
        return {"protocol_version": "1.2.0", "capabilities": [{
            "name": "clock", "kind": "clock", "takes_workspace": False,
            "description": "The build server's clock"}]}
    if method == "capability/open":
        return {"instance": "clock", "attachment_name": "clock",
                "tools": TOOLS, "skills": {"skills": [], "discoveries": []}}
    if method == "runtime/context":
        return {"agent_md": [], "skipped": []}
    if method == "tool/prepare":
        results = []
        for call in params["calls"]:
            prepared_id = len(prepared) + 1
            prepared[prepared_id] = call
            results.append({"status": "prepared", "prepared_id": prepared_id,
                            "normalized_arguments": call["arguments"],
                            "presentation": {"title": "Read the clock"}})
        return {"results": results}
    if method == "tool/execute":
        prepared.pop(params["prepared_id"])
        now = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z")
        return {"outcome": {"status": "completed",
                            "output": {"kind": "single", "text": now}},
                "media": []}
    if method == "runtime/shutdown":
        return {}
    return None

for line in sys.stdin:
    if not line.strip():
        continue
    message = json.loads(line)
    if "id" not in message or "method" not in message:
        continue  # a notification such as tool/release, or a reply
    result = handle(message["method"], message.get("params") or {})
    if result is None:
        send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": message["id"],
              "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "unknown method"}})
    else:
        send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": message["id"], "result": result})
    if message["method"] == "runtime/shutdown":
        break

Run it from a template in the daemon's config.toml:

[runtimes.buildbox]
command = ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "buildbox", "python3", "clock_runtime.py"]

Then attach buildbox/clock from /runtime. The tool declares no permission, so every agent may call it; declare one to put it under permission rules. A version that dials in instead connects with a WebSocket library and exchanges the same messages as text frames.

docs.title: Check your messages
docs.text: The runtime protocol's schemas are published with these pages: methods.json and one JSON Schema per params and result root under schemas/runtime/schemas/, as crates/protocol/compat/runtime/ commits them. Validate what you send against them in your tests. See Published schemas. In Rust, cookie_agent_coding_runtime's server is the reference implementation, and cookie_agent_runtime_api has the tool provider types it builds on; see the Rust API.

docs.title: AGENTS.md Context [agent_md]
docs.text:
Complete config.toml to disable automatic repository context:

[agent_md]
enabled = false

An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail. See config.toml.

Repository-authored context is untrusted input. Review it before running in an unfamiliar workspace; admission is independent of tool read permissions. See security boundaries.

Controls root-run AGENTS.md discovery documented in Agents. This is the global default; an agent document may set agent_md: true or agent_md: false to override it for that agent, for example to keep a lean agent's context free of repository instructions:

---
description: Minimal-context agent
mode: primary
enabled: true
models:
  - { model: "openai/gpt-5", variant: null }
agent_md: false
---
Answer using only what the user provides.
Key Type Default Description enabled boolean true Load AGENTS.md context files at each root run start. Delegated and internal agents remain excluded. An agent document's agent_md field, when present, overrides this for that agent's root runs.

Files larger than 2 MiB (2097152 bytes) are skipped entirely and surfaced as an AgentMdSkipped warning event; they are never partially loaded or truncated. Loaded entries are rendered into a single user context turn wrapped in a <system-reminder> block, with each file delimited as <contents from="/abs/path/AGENTS.md">…</contents>.

docs.title: Approval [approval]
docs.text:
Set the expiry for pending user approvals. Complete config.toml:

[approval]
timeout_ms = 30000

This does not select a permission mode or grant tools; those decisions belong to Agent permissions. Expiry leaves an unattended request unapproved. The internal approval evaluator's own model-call budget is independent of this user-response window. An omitted table inherits; an authored table replaces the lower table and uses defaults for omitted fields. Unknown fields fail; see config.toml.

Key Type Default Description timeout_ms integer 30000 How long a user approval stays pending before it expires unattended. Must be greater than zero.

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
The engine reads ~/.cookie-agent/config.toml over built-in defaults. The file is not required; an empty file is valid. This complete example changes one setting:

[model_retry]
standard_retries = 1

docs.title: Locations and inheritance
docs.text:
Configuration is the built-in defaults plus one optional authored layer, the user layer in ~/.cookie-agent/. Within it, config.toml and the agents/ directory are optional. There is no workspace layer: a <cwd>/.cookie-agent/config.toml or <cwd>/.cookie-agent/agents/ directory is never opened, so a leftover file there is ignored without a warning. The working directory still supplies AGENTS.md context and project skills, which are context, not configuration.

An authored settings table replaces the built-in table as a whole. Omitted fields in it use defaults. For example, the snippet above leaves overload_retries and backoff_ceiling_ms at their defaults. An omitted table keeps the defaults unchanged. Global headers are the exception: names merge with the built-in headers and empty values delete them. Model and variant sparse inheritance happens within one provider definition.

Agents are separate Markdown documents; skills have their own discovery rules. The client loads tui.toml independently.

docs.title: Accepted top-level keys
docs.text:
Every key is optional. Unknown keys, including removed top-level pricing, fail.

Key Canonical settings page server Server: where the daemon listens, its token, and the daemon clients on this machine use tool_output Tool Output subagent_output Subagent Output agent_md AGENTS.md Context loop_warning Loop Warning approval Approval model_retry Model Retry context_compaction Context Compaction session_title Session Title delegation Delegation messaging Agent Messaging producers External Producers memory Memory headers Request Header providers Providers mcp MCP plugins Plugins runtimes Runtimes

Every key above is a top-level table: write [messaging], [delegation], and so on, never [runtime.messaging] or another nested spelling. Older docs used the [runtime.messaging] form; a nested table such as that is an unknown top-level field and fails strict validation.

docs.title: Changes while the daemon runs
docs.text:
The daemon reads config.toml and the agent documents when it starts. Clients read them with config.get and change them with config.apply: a set of whole-document puts and deletes and single-key set edits of config.toml, checked against the revision and fingerprints the client read, validated whole, written, and applied together (see the protocol reference). After editing the files by hand, reload them with config.reload. A configuration that fails validation is not applied: the daemon keeps running on the one it has and reports the error. Applying a configuration does this:

Part When it takes effect tool_output, subagent_output, agent_md, loop_warning, approval, model_retry, context_compaction, session_title, delegation, messaging, producers, memory At once, from each setting's next use; a run keeps the result limits, retry policy, and delegation depth it started with Agent documents and presets At once for new runs; a run in progress keeps its agent, and its delegated children resolve against the agents it started with providers, headers At once: models are recompiled mcp At once: changed servers restart, removed ones stop; servers added or changed at runtime (/mcp) stay on top tool_output for runtime instances When an instance next starts or reconnects server, plugins, runtimes Only after the daemon restarts; the reload reports them as needing a restart

Skills are not reloaded.

docs.title: Editing from a client
docs.text:
In the TUI, /config lists config.toml, the shared agents, and each preset with its agents. Enter opens the selected document in $VISUAL (else $EDITOR, else vi); saving and quitting applies it. A document the daemon refuses, because the result does not validate, is not applied: the panel shows why and marks the document not applied, and Enter reopens your text to fix it. n creates an agent document (agents/<id>.md, or agents/<preset>/<id>.md with a preset selected) from a template, d deletes the selected agent after a y, and r reloads hand edits. The status pane shows when the files differ from the applied configuration, why the last reload failed, and what needs a restart. The text travels over the protocol, so this works against a daemon on another machine.

From a terminal, cookie config does the same against the daemon that --url and --token (or [server] in this machine's config.toml) name:

cookie config edit                      # config.toml in $VISUAL or $EDITOR
cookie config edit agents/reviewer.md   # a new document starts from a template
cookie config set loop_warning.enabled false
cookie config set 'providers."custom.x".base_url' https://llm.example/v1
cookie config unset model_retry
cookie config remove agents/reviewer.md
cookie config reload                    # after editing the files by hand
cookie config status

set takes a dotted key with TOML quoting and a TOML value; a value that is not TOML, such as a bare URL, is a string. It edits only that key, keeping the rest of the file and its comments. edit asks to edit again when the daemon refuses the result.

docs.title: Strictness and limits
docs.text:
Every authored file is parsed strictly. Unknown keys, leftover schema or schema_version keys, wrong types, and malformed content are hard errors with an actionable path, key, and line where available. No authored-file migrations or unknown-field ignores exist. Decoded values that hold secrets are zeroized when the load completes.

TOML-level limits (enforced before deserialization):

  • Configuration file at most 1 MiB; agent document at most 256 KiB.
  • Maximum TOML nesting depth 32; at most 4096 entries per table or array.
  • String values at most 256 KiB; TOML datetimes rejected; floats must be finite.

docs.title: Environment interpolation
docs.text:
${env:NAME} is single-pass interpolation. ${env:NAME:-fallback} uses the fallback when the variable is unset; the fallback may be empty and is split on the first :-. $$ emits a literal $. Interpolation is allowed only in these paths:

  • providers.<id>.endpoint
  • providers.<id>.base_url
  • providers.<id>.setup.<field>
  • providers.<id>.api_key
  • providers.<id>.auth_override.values.<field>
  • providers.<id>.auth.values.<field>
  • headers.<name>
  • providers.<id>.headers.<name>
  • providers.<id>.models.<model>.headers.<name>
