That answer is not offered for this approval request. – approval_id: The approval. operation_fingerprint_mismatch -32000 A response whose operation fingerprint does not match the approval. The answer is for a different operation than the one awaiting approval. Review the request again and answer it. approval_id: The approval. operation_changed -32000 The approved operation no longer matches what would run. The operation changed after it was approved. Review it again. approval_id (optional): The approval. unknown_provider -32000 provider.connect named a provider the catalog does not have. There is no provider named {provider_id}. Choose a provider from the list. provider_id: The provider. unsupported_provider -32000 The provider needs a protocol or setup this build does not support. The provider {provider_id} cannot be connected by this build of cookie. – provider_id: The provider. custom_provider_not_store_backed -32000 A connect or disconnect of a provider that config.toml defines. The provider {provider_id} is defined in the configuration file, so it cannot be changed here. Edit its entry in config.toml instead. provider_id: The provider. removed_without_retained_recipe_match -32000 The catalog removed the provider and no retained recipe matches. The provider {provider_id} is no longer offered, and its saved setup cannot be reused. Choose another provider. provider_id: The provider. catalog_revision_conflict -32000 The catalog revision the request expected is no longer current. The provider list changed while connecting {provider_id}. Start the connection again. provider_id: The provider. missing_setup_field -32000 provider.connect without a required setup value. A required setup value for {provider_id} is missing. Fill in every required field. provider_id: The provider. invalid_setup_field -32000 provider.connect with a setup value its recipe rejects. A setup value for {provider_id} is not valid. Check the values you entered. provider_id: The provider. missing_credential -32000 provider.connect without a required credential. A credential for {provider_id} is missing. Enter the provider's API key or sign in. provider_id: The provider. invalid_credential -32000 provider.connect with a credential of the wrong shape. The credential for {provider_id} is not valid. docs.title: Event Reference
docs.text: A session's history is events.jsonl: one JSON record per line, appended in order. Subscriptions deliver the same records. The format follows the compatibility specification: events and fields are added without a version bump, and only a change that cannot be made additively bumps the history format.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
{ "engine_version": "0.5.0", "origin": "user", "session_id": "…",
  "run_id": null, "seq": 1, "timestamp": "…", "skippable": true,
  "payload": { "type": "…" } }
Member Meaning engine_version The writing engine's binary semver: diagnostic metadata, not a compatibility gate origin Who authored this record (below) session_id The session run_id Required and nullable: the run a run-scoped event belongs to, null for a runless one seq A positive physical sequence, strictly increasing down the file timestamp When the record was written skippable Present and true exactly on audit events payload The event, tagged by type

origin is either user or <class>:<slug>, where class is engine, plugin, or client and slug matches [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}. It identifies the author of that individual event, not the component described by its payload. For example, a diagnostic about a plugin can have origin engine:plugin-host. Events caused by a client request carry that connection's handshake origin, client:<kind>-<instance id> (see the handshake); the headless CLI's in-process runs use client:headless. A run cancelled through run.cancel records the caller's origin on its run_finished, and the engine's origin when it cancels on its own. When tool-emitted additional messages are materialized as persisted turns, their origin is engine:tool-result: the engine authors the durable turn from a validated tool result, and the tool name remains payload context.

The first record is always session_created. It carries history_format (currently 1, the HISTORY_FORMAT constant of cookie_agent_protocol), and the optional short_id, the tree-unique model-facing handle.

docs.title: Reading a log
docs.text:
Writers are strict: every appended record passes validation (bounds, required fields, grammar, and the cross-event checks below), including a skippable that agrees with its payload's class. Readers are tolerant, since a newer build may have written the log. Each line is read on its own:

  • A fully readable record loads normally. Members this build does not know are ignored, in the envelope (on the first line too) and at any depth of the payload: they are what a newer build added.
  • A known event with an absent or type-mismatched optional field loads with that field defaulted and an in-memory degradation diagnostic.
  • A record with a broken required field, corrupt JSON, or a failed record check is skipped with a diagnostic.
  • An event type this build does not know is skipped silently when its record says skippable. Without skippable it is a state event from a newer build: the record is skipped with a diagnostic naming its type, and the session is render-only. It opens and can be viewed and subscribed, but nothing appends to it: run.start, run.steer, session.submit_input, revert, fork, compaction (manual or automatic), title generation, and every other change fail with error code session_requires_newer_engine, and adopting it repairs nothing.
  • Sequence numbers must increase strictly. Gaps are retained and reported, one bounded diagnostic per contiguous missing range. A sequence that does not increase ends the readable log at that line: what follows is not read, a diagnostic names the line, and the session is render-only as above, except that changes fail as a broken sequence. Nothing is cut from the file.

Records that decode are then checked against each other: runs, attempts, turns, tool calls, approvals, internal agents, delegations, and admitted input must agree with the records they name. A record that fails such a check is quarantined instead of failing the open: it is left out like a skipped record, with a quarantined: … diagnostic (the first 64, then one that counts the rest), and every record that depends on it is excused the same way a dependent of a skipped record is. Appends stay strict: a new record must pass every check against what the log holds. A delegation whose stored records the delegation store cannot verify becomes unrecoverable on its own, and the tree still loads.

Nothing derived is recomputed on read. Stored approval operation fingerprints and delegation request fingerprints are trusted, and the size caps writers keep to that no schema states (a tool result's output, metadata, and display budget, a model turn's serialized size, native replay payloads, a diagnostic's detail, a delegation's seeded-context total) bound only what is written. Bounds a schema states stay part of the type.

A metadata cache that does not decode is rebuilt from events.jsonl, so the session stays listed; subagents/index.json likewise rebuilds from the tree.

docs.title: What survives a newer build
docs.text: A loaded log keeps the bytes it was read from. Rewriting a log whole — a fork, or a conversion — copies every line it read as it was written: a record this build reads in full keeps the members it does not know, and a skipped event, a quarantined record, or a degraded one survives as well. A fork sets only each copy's session_id to the new session's; records appended since the log was read are written as this build serializes them. The exception is a fork's source's delegation records, which it leaves behind with its subagents (see Delegation): each becomes a record_omitted written by this build, so what a newer build added to one goes with it. Artifact liveness (what a revert may delete, and what a fork links into its own tree) scans the lines as they were read, so a reference inside an unknown event or an unknown member keeps its artifact: both an artifact://sha256/<digest> anywhere in a string and an ArtifactRef object (sha256, byte_length, media_type) count.

docs.title: History formats
docs.text:
The first record decides whether the log opens at all. Without a readable session_created the session cannot open: the engine reports an unsupported-era or corrupt-log error. A session_created without history_format was written before history formats and is not read. A higher history_format than this build's fails with session_requires_newer_engine. A lower one is converted to this build's format by the chain of converters it ships, one per format step, each a function from the old log's JSON lines to the new one's:

  • A read-only open converts in memory and leaves the files alone.
  • Taking a tree for writing converts the whole tree under its lock first: the root's log, every child's, and their metadata caches. Each new file is written beside its original and synced; only once every log converted does each original become events.jsonl.v<N>.bak (N its old format) and the new file take its place, and subagents/index.json is rebuilt by the next tree load. A failure leaves every original untouched.
  • cookie sessions upgrade converts the trees on disk up front.

Backups are kept until you delete them. The format bumps only for a change that cannot follow the additive rules below.

crates/engine/tests/fixtures/history/<format>/ holds session trees recorded from scripted runs against fake model providers, with snapshots of what the recording build read from them: every session's metadata, usage, events as clients receive them, and model history. Every later build must open them, read-only and owned, and read the same; they are never regenerated, and a build that bumps the format records its own directory beside them.

CI compares the generated EventPayload schema with the committed baseline in crates/protocol/compat/events/ (see Schemas). A new optional field must be safe to ignore, since its absence means the old behaviour; a field whose absence would be misread needs a new event type; and a new value of an open enum needs a fallback that is safe for older readers.

Terminal tool-result truncation and tool_output_elided references use the retained-output readback lifecycle.

docs.title: State and audit events
docs.text:
Every event type is a state event or an audit event. A state event is read by the projection, model history, delegation recovery, goals, producers, approvals, or usage; an audit event changes none of them, so an older reader may skip it. Writers stamp skippable on audit events. Live-only events are never stored.

Event Class Run scope Records session_created state runless The session's creation: origin, handle, workspace, selection, agent, revisions, history_format session_permission_overlay_set state runless The session's permission overlay runtime_attached, runtime_detached state runless The session's runtime attachments skill_loaded state either A loaded skill body skill_invocation_noted audit either A repeat of an identical skill load session_title_committed state either A title change agent_md_loaded state run The AGENTS.md context of one attachment memory_loaded state run The memory snapshot the model sees from this run on diagnostic audit either A notice about the engine, a plugin, or a runtime record_omitted audit either A record its writer deliberately did not carry over goal_activated, goal_checklist_revised, goal_lifecycle_changed state runless or run The session goal producer_message_accepted, producer_message_discarded state runless or run A producer message's body; its withdrawal producer_message_admitted, producer_messages_claimed, producer_messages_released, producer_message_consumed state run A producer message's delivery message_injected state run A message agent_before_start injected user_input_admitted state run or runless A steer waiting for the next turn user_input_submitted state run Input that became model history user_input_transformed audit run A user_before_input rewrite of direct input user_input_recalled state run or runless A withdrawn admission user_input_applied state run Where an admitted input took effect user_input_queued, user_input_queue_recalled, user_input_queue_voided state runless The queued-input lane session_model_selected state runless The session's model selection delegated_context_seeded state runless A child's inherited context run_started, run_finished state run A run's start and end model_attempt_started, attempt_abandoned, model_fallback state run A model attempt's lifecycle model_request_prepared, model_tools_published, model_output_started, model_replay_evaluated audit run Request and streaming bookkeeping model_turn_committed, model_usage_recorded state run A committed turn and its usage tool_call_started, tool_call_terminated, tool_output_elided, tool_call_linked state run A tool call's lifecycle delegation_reserved, delegation_progressed, delegation_finished state run A delegation on the parent delegate_child_terminated state runless A delegation ended the child before it ran approval_requested, approval_finalized, tree_approval_grant_committed state run An approval approval_step state; audit for doom_loop run An approval step internal_agent_started, internal_agent_usage_recorded, internal_agent_finished, internal_agent_fallback state run An internal agent invocation context_checkpoint_committed state run A compaction checkpoint text_delta, reasoning_delta, internal_agent_text_delta, native_compaction_started, native_compaction_finished, tool_call_progress live-only run Stream output

docs.title: Live-only stream output
docs.text:
text_delta, reasoning_delta, internal_agent_text_delta, native_compaction_started, native_compaction_finished, and tool_call_progress are live-only. The engine delivers them to event subscribers and plugins as they stream but never appends them to events.jsonl or to a session's in-memory log, and a stored record carrying one fails validation. Their durable record is the committed turn (model_turn_committed), the tool termination (tool_call_terminated, with its retained output), and the internal agent's terminal event. A replay or a reload therefore sees finished turns only.

A view that attaches while output streams does not start from a fragment: the daemon keeps each session's output still in flight in memory, and a tail registered by a subscription without a cursor (one that replayed the whole log) first receives it as live-only messages positioned after the durable tip it replayed to. A subscription that resumes from a cursor does not, since its reader may already hold part of that output; its later deltas continue it. Each open attempt's text and reasoning arrive as one text_delta or reasoning_delta per uninterrupted run of a kind, in order; each running tool as one tool_call_progress carrying its latest message and its live display so far as one replace delta (within the 64 KiB budget); a running provider-native compaction as its native_compaction_started; and a streaming compaction summary as one internal_agent_text_delta. Later deltas append as usual, and the durable record replaces it all as before. Output a daemon restart cut off is not kept.

internal_agent_text_delta (invocation_id, text) streams the compaction agent's summary text. Other internal agents do not stream. native_compaction_started and native_compaction_finished (resolved_model) bracket a provider-native compaction call, whether or not it succeeds; a committed context_checkpoint_committed is the durable record of a success.

model_output_started (attempt_id, kind: text or reasoning) is the durable trace of streaming. The engine appends it before the first delta of each streamed part: an attempt's first output and every switch between text and reasoning. Views use it to keep an attempt that is already streaming ahead of inputs admitted meanwhile, and to time thinking identically live and on replay (each reasoning part runs from its mark to the next mark or the commit).

A stored record of a live-only payload fails validation, so the reader skips it with a diagnostic like any other invalid record.

docs.title: Goal and producer contracts
docs.text:
Goal and producer state is projected independently from model summaries. The engine serializes mutations, message acceptance, and admission through the session actor. Goal activation and producer acceptance persist an otherwise buffered session, even before its first model request.

Event Payload fields Run scope goal_activated goal_id, objective, revision Runless allowed goal_checklist_revised goal_id, items, revision Runless allowed goal_lifecycle_changed goal_id, status, revision Runless allowed producer_message_accepted message_id, producer_owner, mode, idempotency_key, description, body (user content, text parts only); optional reminder, retained_output Runless allowed, including during an active run producer_message_admitted message_id Requires the destination run producer_messages_claimed Nonempty message_ids Requires the admission run; envelope seq identifies the claim producer_messages_released Positive claim_seq Requires the claimed run producer_message_consumed message_id, run_id Requires matching envelope run_id producer_message_discarded message_id; optional producer_owner, optional reminder Runless allowed

GoalId and ProducerMessageId are durable UUID identities. GoalItem contains only description and finished, with no item ID. Writer validation rejects blank objectives/descriptions. Revision is an engine-owned u64, including zero; strictly increasing revisions, overflow rejection, matching goal identity, and lifecycle transitions are enforced by the engine projection. Model updates replace the entire ordered checklist through the session actor: the last accepted update wins for the current/latest session goal at actor acceptance, without a model-supplied goal_id, expected_revision, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal; updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal. The engine records the selected goal's ID and revision in durable events. User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision, including stale-identity and stale-revision rejection. Empty checklist revisions preserve the active/paused lifecycle. Completion requires nonempty all-finished items, including while paused.

A stored checklist item carrying an id does not decode.

ProducerOwner is tagged by type: external { source, name } (a plugin's or a runtime's named producer), delegation { invocation_id }, goal { goal_id }, goal_control { goal_id }, agent { session_id }, tool { tool_call_id }, or subagent { session_id } (a child's <subagent_report>, keyed by its run ID). It identifies a specific stable owner, not a volatile registration or merely an owner kind. Accepted events are the sole authoritative message body/mode storage, including deferred queue sends while a run is active. Registration records are never session events. GoalControl { goal_id } owns engine-authored pause/cancel steering, not goal continuation reminders. These accepted messages survive goal-controller teardown and reminder invalidation. Accepted agent-owned messages carry agent_hop metadata for the messaging loop guard. It is present exactly on agent-owned messages, is not rendered in the agent-visible envelope, and does not participate in idempotency comparison. Tool { tool_call_id } owns the single <background_result> of that tool call once it ran in the background. Its accepted message carries the call's captured output as retained_output, the same shape a tool result uses, and the body previews it the way a tool result does. Recording the reference on the event is what keeps those artifacts alive; plugins cannot supply retained_output.

The optional accepted-event reminder: GoalReminderIdentity { goal_id, revision, kind } identifies a goal reminder; if present, its goal must match the goal owner. kind is the required started or continuation. Its body must contain the full objective and checklist, including finished items and revision. Each continuation attempt has a fresh message ID/idempotency key even at an unchanged revision. A consumed reminder cannot suppress later continuation. New goals use started until a same-goal reminder is covered by committed model input; acceptance, claims, discarded startup messages, and lifecycle-control notifications alone do not switch subsequent reminders to continuation.

Producer descriptions are compact, human-facing text; the full body remains model-facing. An absent description is empty, and clients then fall back to a truncated body.

producer_message_admitted links the accepted body to a run without duplicating user-input storage or changing existing input events. Its physical sequence is covered by model_turn_committed.input_through_seq. Admission is not consumption: append producer_message_consumed only after a committed turn covers the admission in that same run. Recovery repairs missing consumption markers from committed coverage; an uncommitted API attempt remains retryable. Queue acceptance does not create a forbidden runless pending user input during an active run.

producer_messages_claimed durably reserves admitted messages at the actor boundary before request preparation/dispatch. The claim's envelope sequence is its token, not evidence that the provider received input. Projection requires unique accepted, admitted, unconsumed, undiscarded message IDs belonging to the claim's run. Claims cover compaction, hooks, streaming, and model commit. producer_messages_released references the claim sequence in the same run and removes that claim. Failed or cancelled attempts release their reservation; recovery also releases surviving claims. Once all claims are released, an unconsumed, undiscarded message returns to waiting and the queue strip. Consumed messages remain consumed after release. Claim/release is not consumption and does not establish exactly-once model execution.

Discard is separate from consumption and is a generic durable producer-message event, not restricted to goal reminders. discard(session, message_id) checks the caller's ownership against the accepted message, including after its producer unregisters. Owned already-discarded retries are idempotent; cross-owner discard is rejected. Only unclaimed waiting messages qualify, including admitted messages not yet claimed. Consumed or claimed messages reject discard, even before actual provider dispatch; absence of a consumption marker is not proof that a message is retractable. The actor serializes discard against claim acquisition. Durable discard removes the message from pending delivery/readiness and the queue strip, and replay must not restore it as pending. Goal reminder invalidation still checks its identity; it does not authorize discarding another owner's real message.

Projection requires the discard's producer_owner to exactly match the accepted owner; a supplied reminder must also match. A discard of a consumed or claimed message is rejected. Claimed messages are hidden from the waiting strip until release makes them eligible again; in-flight input cannot be retracted.

Missing/corrupt optional reminder metadata follows the existing best-effort reader, with degradation diagnostics. Engine projection must quarantine invalid goal-owned reminder records rather than reclassifying them as real sends. Cross-event ownership, at-most-once consumption, and commit coverage are engine invariants, not properties a single-event decoder can verify.

Goal state and unconsumed messages must survive compaction. Fork copies durable branch data, never registrations; revert reconciles only the visible branch. Failed/disabled recovery notices are runless diagnostic events whose source is the producer source and whose kind is recovery_failed or recovery_disabled, not persisted readiness/registration records.

docs.title: Event details
docs.text:
model_replay_evaluated records, for one model attempt, the replay decision for each history entry of its request. Every attempt re-evaluates the whole history, so a long run would otherwise write a list that grows with every turn. When base_attempt_id is present, the event names an earlier attempt of the same run, with the same resolved_model, whose full list is an exact prefix of this attempt's list; ordered_decisions then holds only the decisions after that prefix. The full list is the base's full list followed by ordered_decisions. Without base_attempt_id, ordered_decisions is the full list, which is what a run's first evaluation writes, as does any attempt whose model changed or whose earlier decisions changed (compaction, a pinned turn, a late tool result). Readers that ignore the field see only new decisions for such an attempt.

agent_md_loaded is a run-scoped root-session event stamped engine:agent-md. It contains one or two AGENTS.md entries a coding runtime discovered in its workspace, each with a bounded display source, retained content, truncation flag, and original byte size, and the attachment naming that runtime's attachment. A run writes one event per attachment that returned a file. Missing or disabled context produces no event. History uses only the latest run's events, the latest per attachment, and replays their entries as one provenance-delimited user turn. Compaction pins that turn alongside loaded skill bodies. See System Prompt Composition.

docs.title: Memory snapshots
docs.text:
memory_loaded is a run-scoped event stamped engine:memory, appended at a run's admission (root or delegated, each in its own session's log) when the run's memory changed: the memory spec lists when. Its members, each left out when empty or false:

Member Meaning delegated The snapshot was taken for a delegated run and holds only agent writable The run could see the memory write tools user [{ category, description, keywords?, body }]: user categories, whole, in name order user_omitted Names of the categories that did not fit agent { agent, memory?: { description, keywords?, body }, omitted? }: the run's agent and its file; omitted when the file did not fit machines [{ machine, attachments?, memories?: [{ url, description, keywords? }], omitted? }]: the session's machines, each with an index of its memories, newest first, and how many more it has

An event without agent is empty: memory is no longer available, and the model sees no memory turn from then on. History renders only the latest memory_loaded of the log, as one user turn right after the AGENTS.md turn, and compaction pins it like that turn; the text depends on the event alone, so a replay shows exactly what the model saw. The stored event is at most 128 KiB of JSON; its rendered text stays within 64 KiB. See System Prompt Composition.

diagnostic { source, kind, message, count?, detail? } is a notice about the engine, a plugin, or a runtime: something it turned off, could not do, or dropped. source is engine:<area>, plugin:<name>, or runtime:<id>; kind is a snake-case label (at most 64 bytes) that readers show whatever it is; message is the nonempty text to show; count (at least 2 when present) says how many occurrences the record coalesces; and detail is display-only JSON of at most 16 KiB. Nothing but a view reads it. A diagnostic about a run belongs to that run; any other is runless. The kinds written today:

Source Kind Meaning plugin:<name> interception_timeout, interception_crash (the plugin was not connected or exited during the hook), interception_rejected (it answered with an error or a malformed result), hook_blocked, invalid_modification, oversized_event, event_drop, context_mismatch, rate_limited A plugin's operational notice, coalesced by count plugin:<name>, runtime:<id> recovery_failed, recovery_disabled A producer source cannot restore the external work it tracks; goal continuation is held engine:auto-compact auto_compaction_disabled Automatic context compaction failed three times in a row and stays off for the rest of the run engine:agent-md agent_md_too_large An AGENTS.md file is over the size limit and contributes no context; run-scoped, with detail { path, byte_length, attachment }

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
delegated_context_seeded is a runless creation event containing the bounded, text-only user/assistant turns copied by inherit_context; it must precede the child's first run and deterministically rebuilds the same initial model history after restart.

The delegation_* records are durable control events on the parent session, in the parent run. delegation_reserved contains the complete current delegate request, the child agent snapshot (whose selected suffix is the child's models), one cache strategy per entry of that suffix, its runtime revisions when they changed (see Runs and internal agents), the request fingerprint, and optional typed staged-skill provenance. The child records its attachments, the root session's, with runtime_attached events at creation. delegation_progressed { invocation_id, stage } records how far the delegation got; stage is started { child_session_id } (the child session was published), run_started { child_run_id } or run_attached { child_run_id } (a new child run, or attachment to an already-running resumed child), or queued { position? } (the child waits for a background slot). A stage this build does not know changes nothing.

delegation_finished { invocation_id, child_session_id, child_run_id?, status, reason?, short_id?, preview, total_lines } records the terminal status, the optional recovery reason, and the child references, together with the teaser transcripts render: short_id is the child's handle and preview the report as [subagent_output] previews it, whole or its first and last lines around an omission marker (at most 64 KiB; empty when no child run started). One record per invocation lets repeated resumes of one child each finish once. It is not model history: a foreground delegation's result reaches the parent's model as its tool result, and a background one's as the steer producer message the engine durably accepts for it (see Goal and producer contracts), so the result is in history exactly once. Full output remains available through get_subagent_result.

delegate_child_terminated is written runless to the child session when a delegation ends it before it ran (cancelled or failed); it sets the child's own status.

A fork does not take its source's subagents: they stay the source's. The fork keeps the conversation as it was (the delegate calls and their results, tool_call_linked, and the producer messages that brought the children's reports, which read as any other message), but none of the delegation_* records. Each is replaced, at its sequence and with its run, time, and origin, by record_omitted { omitted_type } naming its type, so the sequence stays contiguous. The fork has no children until it delegates itself, and get_subagent_result refuses the source's children. Runtime revisions that only a dropped delegation_reserved recorded go with it.

Engine startup projects delegation state while opening session logs. A reserved or started delegation without a terminal event resumes or rolls back according to its child and parent state. Recovery trusts the stored request fingerprint and never computes it again; it is compared only when the same invocation is reserved again. If best-effort reading skips a corrupt delegation event, that delegation is not recovered, the parent session records the diagnostic, and unrelated delegations remain recoverable.

docs.title: Runs and internal agents
docs.text:
run_started freezes the run's agent snapshot. The snapshot's fallback_chain lists the agent's models in fallback order, and selected_suffix_start is where the run starts in it: the run's model is that entry (its exact selection, variant included, equals the run selection's), and its fallbacks are the entries after it. session_created and delegation_reserved carry snapshots of the same shape, and the snapshot has no schema version.

session_created records the seven revisions of the runtime the session was created against as revisions (runtime_revision, catalog_revision, provider_state_revision, model_revision, agent_revision, recipe_registry_revision, and manifest_revision). run_started and delegation_reserved carry revisions only when the run or the delegated child was frozen against different ones than the latest the log recorded before it; without the field, an event was frozen against those latest revisions. Readers fold them in log order.

Each chain entry, like a model fallback of a frozen internal agent, is a stored model binding { selection, provider_id, provider_model_id, adapter, resolved, selection_fingerprint, blueprint_fingerprint, frozen }. adapter is the protocol adapter the binding speaks (such as oven.openai.responses), and resolved is the model reference the run's attempts record: model_attempt_started and model_fallback must name the resolved of the entry at their fallback index, counted from selected_suffix_start. frozen holds the complete binding (descriptor, request defaults, provider options, credential and setup bindings, static headers) as an opaque value. Loading a log never decodes it. The engine decodes it only to run the binding again: manual compaction, title generation, and the history view of the latest run, and the model fallbacks of that run's internal agents. When this build cannot read it, that operation fails with unreadable_model_binding; the session still opens, and a new run resolves its models afresh as always.

run_finished { outcome } ends a run. outcome is completed { final_text? }, failed { error, model_error?, resolved_model? }, cancelled { reason? }, or interrupted { reason? }; an outcome this build does not know reads as interrupted. internal_agent_finished { invocation_id, internal_run_id, kind, outcome } ends an internal agent invocation the same way, with completed { result }, failed { failure }, cancelled { reason? }, or interrupted { reason? }. run_started.internal_agents freezes the run's internal agent definitions, one per kind, and an internal_agent_usage_recorded of the run names the agent frozen for its kind.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text: approval_requested stores the request's tool_call_id, the call it gates, whose tool_call_started carries the call's presentation, and its operation_fingerprint, which the writer computes from the prepared operation and readers trust as written. An approval's lifecycle after its approval_requested is a series of approval_step { approval_id, step } records and one approval_finalized { approval_id, outcome }. step is evaluated { decision } (the internal decision pipeline decided), escalated { reason_code } (it waits for the user), user_decision { client_response_id, decision, feedback? } (a client answered; feedback only with reject), or doom_loop { operation_fingerprint, repetitions } (the same operation was requested at least four times in a row); a step this build does not know changes nothing. outcome is decided { decision }, the final decision of policy, a grant, the reviewer, or the user, or cancelled { reason_code }, the engine withdrawing the approval (request_cancelled, approval_expired, operation_changed, or prepared_capability_lost), which reads as a system decision that expired or cancelled the request. An outcome this build does not know reads as cancelled, so the operation is not approved.

docs.title: Runtime attachments
docs.text: The runless runtime_attached and runtime_detached events record the session's runtime attachments. runtime_attached carries the session-unique attachment name, the runtime_id, the capability attached, the kind label the capability declared (such as global or coding), and, when the instance has one, the canonical workspace it reported. runtime_detached carries the name it removes. The attachment set is the fold of these events in log order; a session's creation writes one runtime_attached per initial attachment together with session_created, so both reach disk with the session's first persistence. A session created with no attachment records no attachment event. Delegated children record their own attachments.

docs.title: Other events
docs.text:
record_omitted { omitted_type } stands in for a record its writer deliberately did not carry over, at that record's sequence, run (if any), time, and origin; omitted_type is the left-out record's type. Its run, when it has one, is a run the log started. Nothing reads it but a view; today only a fork writes it, for its source's delegation records.

The runless session_permission_overlay_set event's overlay contains the complete, validated set of unique (action, resource) rules for the session. The latest visible event wins. Because it is an ordinary branch event, restart replay, revert, and fork recover the same overlay without a sidecar file.

model_usage_recorded follows a committed provider turn and contains the positive model_turn_seq, agent ID, resolved model identity, and Oven's normalized usage fields: inclusive input/output totals plus optional uncached input, cache-read input, cache-write input, text output, and reasoning output counts. A reported reasoning count of zero on a turn that streamed reasoning text is recorded as unknown, together with the text output count derived from it. The required estimated_cost_pico_usd stamps the engine-selected price for that request: a number is priced, and null is unpriced. internal_agent_usage_recorded stamps its price the same way. Usage rollups preserve stamped prices exactly and never price a record again. Event-log validation requires its run, agent, model, and turn to match and rejects duplicate records for one turn. Session, agent, and global usage projections rebuild from these events after restart, revert, and fork.

model_request_prepared follows request assembly and all accepted model/provider request hooks. Its prompt_fingerprint hashes the authoritative normalized request sent to the provider, while model_attempt_started remains the earlier cancellation and lifecycle boundary.

model_tools_published comes just before model_request_prepared for the same attempt and lists the tool_names sent with the request, after request hooks. It is recorded only when the names differ from the session's latest visible record, so an unchanged tool set adds nothing to later attempts. Validation allows at most 1,024 names, each nonempty, at most 256 bytes, and free of control characters; a request whose names do not fit is still sent, without a record. The TUI shows the latest record as a collapsible tools block under the system prompt.

tool_call_started records the call's presentation: its title, an optional hint label (for icons and grouping), an optional primary_argument, arguments and preview display blocks (absent when empty; clients then show the raw model arguments), and tool, which the daemon fills: name (the name the tool's source knows it by), published_name (the name the model called), and source, tagged by type: base, runtime { runtime_id, attachment, capability }, plugin { plugin }, or mcp { server, runtime_id? }. source is absent for a call that names no tool the session offers. Today's runtimes report only the title and display argument. It also records the single/named output declaration, including arbitrary named streams, and background: true when the call's tool supports the background, so a client may offer to move the running call there (run.tool_background); the field is absent otherwise. tool_call_progress is live-only. It contains a control-free status message and an optional UI-only display delta, tagged by type:

  • append { index, text, stream? } appends text to block index of the live display, a text block, or a terminal block when the append names a stream (stdout or stderr), which extends that block's last segment of the stream or starts one. An append to the index just past the list creates the block. Today's tools send append to block 0.
  • replace { blocks } replaces the live display.

The terminal result.display replaces the live display. A live message and an append's text are each bounded at 1 KiB. A call's deltas share a cumulative 64 KiB budget (an append costs its text, a replacement its serialized size), and its messages another. TUI state is bounded and never reconstructs display by merging authoritative streams.

A result's display is a list of display blocks (see the compatibility spec), sanitized by the daemon and fit to 64 KiB serialized; blocks of a kind the daemon does not know are dropped. An empty list shows nothing.

events.jsonl stores display text that repeats the result's output as [start, end) byte ranges of output instead of a second copy, and the daemon expands them when it reads the log, so clients and plugins always receive whole blocks:

  • a display that is a single whole text block found in output (a single-output tool's whole output) is stored as the result's display_span in place of display;
  • otherwise a text, markdown, or code block's text, and a terminal segment's text (a shell's streams), may be stored as text_span, and a file_excerpt's lines as lines_span: a range of output holding the lines one per line, each after its file line number and :, as read numbers them.

The writer uses a range only when expanding it gives back the same text, and never inside a block of a kind it does not know.

The result a call commits when it moves to the background carries background { state, by, job? }: state is job (the call runs as background job job) or self_reporting (the work, such as a subagent, reports itself); an unknown state still means the call is backgrounded. by is model or user. Only the daemon sets it; it drops one a tool returns.

Authoritative output chunks go to runtime capture before completion, not into unbounded event records. Terminal retained_output contains ordered per-stream byte/line counts, truncation offsets, and an incomplete flag. Only a stream that outgrew its preview has an artifact (reference and sha256); a stream the result output holds whole has neither, and retained_output.reference (the single stream's artifact or the generic manifest) is absent when no stream needed one. Failed/cancelled calls retain accepted output with their terminal status and error. Self-paginating tools omit output retention and fail instead when a requested page exceeds the 2 MiB result bound. tool_output_elided records which retained output compaction elided.

During cancellation cleanup, a progress record is considered retained once its append command enters the session actor mailbox; actor FIFO then orders it before the later terminal command even if persistence has not completed yet. Cleanup deadline diagnostics count only display progress records that never entered that mailbox; authoritative chunks already accepted into capture remain retained.

For a batch of tool calls from one model turn, tool_call_started events are written in model content order before execution begins. Calls may then execute in parallel, so progress and tool_call_terminated events from different calls may interleave, and terminations commit in completion order. The ordering guarantee is per call: its start precedes all of its progress events, which precede its single termination. Consumers must correlate calls by tool_call_id rather than cross-call event position. A failed termination carries one of the tool failure codes.

internal_agent_usage_recorded attributes each completed internal model request to its internal run, internal agent ID, kind, and resolved model. It carries the same optional estimated_cost_pico_usd stamp. The same session, agent, and global projections include these records.

skill_loaded and skill_invocation_noted persist skill use. skill_loaded stores the rendered body, skill name, source path, arguments, base directory, and at most ten supporting-file paths. It is pinned across context checkpoints. An identical repeat uses the shorter skill_invocation_noted payload.

user_input_admitted normally belongs to an active run. A steer accepted for a queued delegated child is runless and requires that the session have no active run. It is persisted immediately and enters the next run's pending-input FIFO, including when a terminal child is queued for resume. A queued cancellation appends a runless user_input_recalled naming each such admission so those inputs cannot leak into a later resume. Promotion appends the ordinary run-owned user_input_submitted event, so transcript rendering and model history use the same path as interactive run steering.

Every input-lane event stores its input as content: UserContent, a nonempty list of parts tagged by type: text { text } or file { artifact: { sha256, byte_length, media_type, filename? } }. That covers user_input_admitted, user_input_submitted, user_input_recalled, and user_input_queued. Model history sends text parts as they are and file parts as files read from the session tree's artifact store, the way tool-emitted user messages carry theirs; a missing or damaged artifact becomes a short note. A part of a kind this build does not know is kept and never sent to a model. The content is what the client submitted (run.start, run.steer, session.submit_input), after any user_before_input transform. A writer rejects a file part whose artifact reference is malformed. The artifact a file part names stays in the tree's store for as long as an event references it, like a tool attachment: revert sweeps and fork linking count it.

message_injected is a run-owned role and content message accepted from agent_before_start. It is written during run setup and projected into model history, so reopen, fork, revert, and compaction use the injected message without consulting the plugin again. Its content, like a producer_message_accepted body, has text parts only. user_input_transformed is the run-owned audit record written immediately before user_input_submitted when user_before_input changes direct input; it contains both original_content and the non-blank committed content.

Running-resume rollback and session.recall_input append user_input_recalled with the exact user_input_seq of its admission (in the same run, or runless for a runless admission). Replay removes that specific pending input and preserves the others.

session_model_selected (selection) is the session-level model pick a client made with session.select_model; it is runless and its origin names the client. Later runs that name no selection of their own use it.

docs.title: The queued-input lane
docs.text: The queued-input lane is session-level, so its events are runless. user_input_queued holds an input waiting for the running run to complete, with the selection and client_run_id of the run it will start; its origin is the client that queued it. The entry leaves the queue when a run_started carries its client_run_id, when user_input_queue_recalled names its queued_seq, or when every entry is voided by a run_finished that did not complete, or by user_input_queue_voided (written when a queued input cannot start). A voided entry goes back to the client that queued it.

docs.title: Compaction checkpoints
docs.text:
context_checkpoint_committed carries a commit containing the text summary or opaque native checkpoint, boundaries, and budgets. Internal summaries cover the active pre-compaction history before the recent messages retained unchanged after the summary; the two do not overlap. Active history is the currently assembled context, not a reload of events replaced by earlier checkpoints. The original saved log is preserved; retained recent messages are replayed from it. System and tool context comes first, followed by pinned AGENTS.md, the latest memory snapshot, loaded skills, the summary, and the recent messages. See Compaction for selection and fit rules.

The retention fields:

Field within commit Type Meaning boundaries.recent_from_seq u64 or null Inclusive starting sequence of the retained original-message suffix. null means no retained suffix. budgets.keep_recent_tokens u64 Effective recent-history token budget for this checkpoint, not the raw configured request or a count of retained tokens.

The effective budget is at most min(configured keep_recent_tokens, input_budget / 4) and is further limited by actual post-checkpoint available space. Complete tool-call/result groups can leave the retained suffix smaller than that budget; an oversized newest indivisible group yields no tail rather than exceeding the budget. A reader never infers a suffix from current configuration.

Native compacted windows retain their existing replay behavior, with no independently appended recent-message suffix. Neither checkpoint path rereads files.

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
events.subscribe returns retained events after the optional cursor and starts events.subscription notifications. With limit, it returns at most that many events; when more remain it sets has_more: true and starts no notifications, and the client asks again with the last returned seq as the cursor. Only the final page (no has_more) subscribes, atomically with its snapshot, so events appended between pages arrive in a later page and none are missed. Without limit the first response is the final page. Paging a session this process does not own parses its log once and serves later pages from memory while the file is unchanged.

events.unsubscribe ends the connection's live tail for a session: no further events.subscription or events.plugin notification for it is sent, and the shared client drops messages already in flight and stops recovering it until it subscribes again. A session no connection has a tail on can be evicted from the daemon's memory, so a long-lived client releases sessions it no longer shows. The TUI keeps the sessions of its eight most recently viewed trees subscribed, so switching back is instant, and releases the others once they have no run and no pending or queued input; it keeps their last state and catches up from it when one is reopened.

A connection holds at most one live tail per session. Subscribing a session the connection already follows (reopening it, or a recovery replay) replaces its tail in the same step as the new snapshot: notifications the old tail had already queued are written first, then the new tail's, and nothing reaches both. Durable events carry a seq a client can drop a copy by, but transient output does not, so two tails would show every streamed delta twice.

A notification is tagged as a stored event:

{ "type": "event", "event": { "engine_version": "0.1.0", "seq": 43 } }

live-only stream output, which has no sequence of its own:

{
  "type": "transient",
  "event": {
    "session_id": "...",
    "run_id": "...",
    "after_seq": 43,
    "timestamp": "...",
    "payload": { "type": "text_delta", "attempt_id": "...", "text": "..." }
  }
}

or a gap indicating that the subscriber must rebuild its disposable projection:

{
  "type": "gap",
  "session_id": "...",
  "last_delivered_seq": 42
}

Stored sequences stay gap-free across a streamed turn, so replay cursors only ever point at durable events. A transient event belongs right after the durable event after_seq: it never advances the cursor, is never stored, and is never a reason to recover. A subscriber that starts from the beginning (no cursor, or 0) first receives the output streaming at that moment, coalesced into transient messages after the durable tip; one resuming from a cursor does not, since it may already hold part of it. The shared client delivers one only when its after_seq equals the subscription cursor, including output buffered while a replay is in flight; anything else is stale or outruns a durable event the view has not seen, and is dropped. The engine drops transient output for a subscriber whose queue is nearly full rather than spending the slot reserved for a gap.

A revert cuts the log and the next appends reuse the removed sequence numbers, so live subscribers receive a rewind:

{ "type": "rewound", "session_id": "...", "through_seq": 41 }

A subscriber drops everything it holds past through_seq; later events follow on from it. The shared client also replays the session in full. A reader that was not subscribed when the cut happened cannot tell a reused sequence from the event it replaced, so a replay request may carry cursor_timestamp, the timestamp of the event at cursor as the reader saw it. When the session's event at cursor has a different timestamp (or no longer exists), the response is { "events": [], "stale_cursor": true }, no tail is registered, and the reader must replay from the start. The shared client sends it on every recovery replay.

Tool stdout and stderr use separate snapshot, delta, and gap notifications. Offsets are byte offsets, and clients use a snapshot after a gap before applying later deltas. The ordinary event subscription also includes live-only tool_call_progress output chunks and the durable terminal events without a separate filter.

docs.title: Client Protocol Changelog
docs.text: The client protocol's version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (cookie_agent_protocol::CLIENT_PROTOCOL_VERSION). From 1.0.0 a minor only adds and a major breaks; before it, every minor could break the wire (see the compatibility spec section 3).

• memory.write results carry an optional notice: what the daemon kept in place of the text it was given. The daemon now keeps a memory file for every agent and owns its description and two keywords, so a write of an agent:// file that changes them keeps the daemon's and says so (see Memory). A 1.5 client ignores the member.

• Session deletion: session.delete { session_id, expected_last_seq } deletes a root session's whole tree from disk and returns the deleted session IDs, the root first; every connection gets sessions.changed removed for each (see Delete). It comes with the error codes not_a_root_session, session_tree_running, and session_changed, besides the existing session_not_found and session_owned_elsewhere. A 1.4 client sees only the removed changes; a 1.5 client calling session.delete on a 1.4 daemon gets method_not_found.

• Memory for clients: memory.list, memory.read, memory.write, and memory.delete list, read, and change the daemon's memory files for the user, with no session (see Memory). They come with the error codes memory_url_invalid, memory_not_found, memory_exists, memory_revision_mismatch, memory_invalid, memory_refused, memory_busy, and memory_store_failed. The memory.changed notification reaches every connection when a memory file changes through the daemon. A 1.3 client sees none of it; a 1.4 client calling a memory.* method on a 1.3 daemon gets method_not_found.

• A new state event, memory_loaded, records the memory snapshot a session's model sees from a run on: user categories, the run's agent's memory, and an index of the session's machines' memories (see Events). An event without agent records that memory is no longer available. A 1.2 client reads it as an unknown state event. The plugin protocol is 1.2.0 for the same event.
  • memory and memory_write join the built-in permission actions that session.permissions.get lists.

• Machines: the computers runtimes run on. machines.list, machines.rename, machines.assign, machines.unassign, machines.merge, and machines.forget read and change the daemon's machine registry (see Machines), with the error codes machine_not_found, machine_name_taken, machine_in_use, machine_memory_conflict, machine_merge_self, runtime_not_pinned, and machine_store_failed. The machines.changed notification reaches every connection when the registry changes, and each runtimes.list entry gains machine. A 1.1 client sees none of it; a 1.2 client calling a machines.* method on a 1.1 daemon gets method_not_found.

• A new audit event, record_omitted { omitted_type }, stands in for a record its writer deliberately did not carry over, at that record's sequence, run, and time. A fork writes one for each of its source's delegation_reserved, delegation_progressed, and delegation_finished records: the fork keeps the conversation but not the subagents, which stay the source's (see Events). It is skippable and changes nothing a reader projects; a 1.0 client reads it as an unknown event. The plugin protocol is 1.1.0 for the same event.

The client protocol is frozen: every later 1.x version reads and is read by this one. A 0.x build never interoperates with a 1.x one: the handshake refuses another major with -32002 unsupported_protocol, so a client and a daemon from before the freeze must be upgraded together. The plugin and runtime protocols froze at 1.0.0 too, and session history is history format 1.

What 1.x keeps:

  • Versions. The handshake carries "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH" strings and connects equal majors; each side sends a method, a member, or a display block kind only when the other's minor includes it, and the patch never matters.
  • Information is tolerant, commands are strict. Results, notifications, events, and the JSON-RPC envelope ignore members a reader does not know, and their enums are open, read as a documented fallback or as unknown; an event a client cannot read arrives as an unknown event, and a notification that does not decode fails no call. Params refuse an unknown member (unknown_field) or value (unknown_variant) with its JSON path.
  • Errors. Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a readable message, an optional hint, and detail on request (see Errors); clients branch only on data.code.
  • User content and media. Inputs are content: text and file parts naming artifacts uploaded with artifact.upload.*, admitted against the input_media each model of the catalog view advertises, and read back with artifact.read.
  • Tool display. Tool calls carry presentation v2 (title, hint, tool identity, argument and preview blocks), progress display deltas, and result display blocks of twelve kinds with a canonical text rendering; a connection receives only the kinds its version includes. A result always carries its whole display.
  • The catalog view. runtime.snapshot.get and runtime.changed carry a ModelCatalogView with one opaque revision.

Changed since 0.52.0: a tool result's display is always whole and required; display_span belonged to the session log's storage encoding and no longer reaches clients.

• Every model of the catalog view states input_media: the kinds it accepts in user input, with their media types and effective byte, dimension, pixel, and count limits.
  • run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input take content (text and file parts) in place of input, and a recalled outcome of session.recall_input returns content.
  • artifact.upload.begin, artifact.upload.chunk, artifact.upload.finish, artifact.upload.cancel, and artifact.read upload media into a session tree's store and read any of its artifacts back; new error codes upload_offset_mismatch, upload_size_mismatch, and too_many_uploads.
  • Input file parts are admitted against the model the input reaches: media_unsupported, media_type_unsupported, media_too_large, media_limit_exceeded, and artifact_not_found.

• The handshake's protocol_version is a semver string. A client of another major or, before 1.0, another minor is refused with -32002 unsupported_protocol, as is a build that sends the old integer.
  • The handshake takes an optional token and features, and its reply carries engine_version and features. The WebSocket upgrade no longer requires Authorization: a connection without it authenticates with the handshake's token, and gets -32003 for anything else until it does.
  • [server] allowed_origins lets web pages of listed origins connect.
  • Results, notifications, and the JSON-RPC envelope are information: a reader ignores members it does not know, and every enum in them is open, read as a documented fallback or as unknown (see Decoding). Params stay strict.

  • Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a message and hint from the registry, and the cause as data.detail (see Errors). The old codes -32011, -32012, -32020 to -32022, -32030, -32031, and -32040, the several meanings of -32602 for refusals, the typed error data (RunStartConflict, SessionRenameError, SessionRevertConflict, ApprovalRespondError, ProviderConnectError, ProviderDisconnectError, ConfigApplyError), and debug_code are gone.

  • runtime.snapshot.get and runtime.changed carry a ModelCatalogView (revision, catalog, providers, models, agents) in place of the runtime snapshot: one opaque revision replaces the snapshot schema version and the eleven revisions and counters, and descriptors lose their fingerprints. provider.connect and provider.disconnect take that revision as expected_revision; the disconnect receipt keeps its ID and time only. runtime.changed takes any number of reasons.

  • SessionMeta.short_id is required (nullable).
  • The daemon sends a connection only the display-block kinds its version includes, downgrading newer kinds to text and leaving out kinds it does not know.

docs.title: Before semver versions
docs.text: Builds before 0.51.0 sent the protocol version as an integer, from 34 to 50; the last of them was 50. They cannot connect to this build.

docs.title: Protocol Reference
docs.text: The daemon exposes JSON-RPC 2.0 over a WebSocket at /ws. This build speaks client protocol 1.6.0; the changelog lists what each version changed. A client and a daemon connect when their majors are equal: a minor only adds, so the two use what the lower minor includes, and the patch never matters. Compatibility states the rules every change to the protocol follows.

docs.title: Handshake and authentication
docs.text:
A client must call handshake before any other method:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "handshake", "params": {
    "protocol_version": "1.6.0",
    "client": { "kind": "web", "instance_id": "<uuid>" },
    "token": "<the daemon's token>",
    "features": [] } }

The reply:

{ "protocol_version": "1.6.0", "engine_version": "0.3.0",
  "origin": "client:web-<id>", "machine_id": "<opaque>", "features": [] }
  • protocol_version is the sender's semver version, a "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH" string. The daemon reads it from the raw params before anything else: a client of another major (a 0.x build from before the freeze included), or a build from before semver versions that sends an integer, is answered with -32002 unsupported_protocol, whose data names both supported_version and peer_version. A client only sends a method or a member the daemon's version includes.
  • client.kind names the client program: a lowercase letter followed by up to 15 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens (the shipped clients use tui, cli, and web). client.instance_id is a UUID identifying one running client; a client keeps it across reconnects so it can recognize events it caused. Any number of clients may connect to one daemon at once.
  • origin is client:<kind>-<id>, where <id> is the instance id as 32 lowercase hex digits. The daemon stamps that origin on every event the connection's requests cause, so each client can tell its own actions from another client's. A repeated handshake on the same connection keeps the first identity.
  • engine_version is the daemon's own version, for display and logs; machine_id an opaque identity of the daemon's machine when it has one, so a client can tell whether it runs on the same machine.
  • features list what each side's configuration enables. None are defined yet; an unknown feature is ignored.

Authentication. A client authenticates with the daemon's bearer token ([server] token) in one of two places:

  • the Authorization: Bearer <token> header of the WebSocket upgrade, which the native clients send; a wrong header is refused with HTTP 401;
  • or token in the handshake, which a browser must use, since it cannot set headers on a WebSocket.

Until a connection without the header has sent the right token, the daemon answers only handshake; any other request gets -32003 unauthenticated. A handshake with a wrong or missing token gets -32003, and the connection closes. A connection that has not authenticated within 10 seconds is closed. A connection that authenticated with the header but has not handshaken gets -32001 handshake_required for anything but handshake.

Web origins. /ws accepts an upgrade request from any web origin, or with no Origin header (every native client); the token is the guard. Dial-in runtimes on /runtime always authenticate with the header, and a request there with an Origin header is refused with HTTP 403. Refusals there name their reason in the response body or the close frame (see Dial-in refusals).

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
The daemon and its clients read what they receive by its role (see the compatibility spec section 4):

  • Results, notifications, and the JSON-RPC envelope are information. A reader ignores members it does not know, and request IDs may be integers or strings. Every enum in them is open: a value a newer daemon added reads as the fallback its type documents (for example an unknown permission effect as ask, an unknown approval status as cancelled), or as unknown for states a client only shows (session status, plugin state, MCP server state, runtime instance status, producer source status, runtime change reasons). An unknown sessions.changed change reads as resync, an unknown events.subscription message type is ignored, and an unknown session.submit_input or session.recall_input outcome fails that call with a readable error.
  • A notification a client cannot read is dropped. The shared client reports it as ClientDelivery::Diagnostic, and no call in flight fails. A response it cannot read fails only its own call. A frame that is not JSON, or not a request, notification, or reply, ends the shared client's connection; the daemon instead answers such a frame with parse_error or invalid_request and reads on.
  • Events. A client reads stored events with an open payload: an event of a type this build does not know, or one it cannot read, is delivered in its place as ClientDelivery::UnknownEvent, which advances the session's sequence and changes nothing else (the TUI shows a dim row in its debug view). A replay page does not fail for it.
  • Display blocks. The daemon sends each connection only the display-block kinds its client protocol version includes: a block of a newer kind arrives as a text block of its canonical text rendering, and a block of a kind the daemon itself does not know (from a log a newer build wrote) is left out of what it sends, while the log keeps it. Every kind of this build exists from the first minor, so today no block is downgraded.
  • Params are commands. An unknown or mistyped member fails with -32602 and data.code unknown_field (or unknown_variant for a value or tag), with data.field naming the JSON path. A client sends a method or member only if the daemon's version includes it; -32601 for a method the client expected reads as "the daemon is too old for" that method.

docs.title: Error diagnostics
docs.text: ModelErrorSummary.response_body is an optional DiagnosticText that preserves the supplied content, with terminal/Unicode format controls removed or replaced and a maximum of 4,096 UTF-8 bytes, including any truncation marker. Newlines and tabs are permitted. It is used for terminal, fallback, and internal-agent model failures. A failed run_finished keeps its short error and optionally includes model_error and resolved_model. Missing fields in old events default to null and are omitted when serialized; this is an additive event change without a protocol version bump.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Every application error is -32000 with a registry data.code, a message a user can understand, and optional data.hint and data.detail; the error reference lists every code with its fields. The daemon builds message and hint from the registry, so a code always reads the same way, and keeps its own description of the cause (bounded and terminal-safe, without secret-pattern redaction) as detail. Clients branch only on data.code, show message and then hint, and show detail on request; a code a client does not know reads as a generic error, whose message and hint are already readable. JsonRpcError Debug formatting redacts data. No request headers or credential dumps are added. See Error details for display and upstream limits.

docs.title: Tool-emitted messages
docs.text:
PersistedToolResult carries optional additional_messages, alongside its independent display and output references. The field is an ordered array of at most four messages. Each message has role system or user and one or more ordered text or file content parts. Empty arrays are omitted on the wire; event validation bounds text and attachment counts and validates every referenced artifact.

The engine materializes these messages from the persisted terminal result, so replay and restart are deterministic. The paired tool result is placed first, then messages are inserted in array order before the next assistant turn. User-role messages retain their role. System-role messages are represented as user turns whose first text part is the deterministic marker [tool-emitted system message; materialized as user history]; their original text and file parts follow in order. This translation keeps the initial system prefix and its cache breakpoint stable because provider families disagree on mid-history system semantics. Terminal result events use origin engine:tool-result.

Elision treats a tool result and its additional_messages as one unit. If the parent result is elided, none of its emitted messages enter model history and the marker reports how many were lost. Retried or replayed termination events replace the call record rather than applying first-attempt messages twice. Attachments in compacted history are not recoverable from the checkpoint.

docs.title: Session mechanics
docs.text:
The JSON-RPC session layer lives in the protocol crate so the server, the TUI, and the CLI share one implementation of the protocol mechanics.

  • Transport. protocol::Transport is a frame-level channel: send(MessageFrame) / recv() -> Option<MessageFrame>, with MessageFrame either a Text string or a Value. It carries no JSON-RPC semantics. The protocol crate provides the InProcessStream pair and, behind its websocket feature, the client WebSocketTransport; the daemon's axum accept path in the server crate implements the same trait server-side.
  • ServerProtocol. The server contract is one async method per RPC plus connected. The server crate implements it over Engine. protocol::serve drives one complete session over a transport: it authenticates the connection (by the transport, or by the handshake's token), rejects every method before the handshake with -32003 or -32001, correlates requests by id, dispatches to the implementation, and delivers notifications through a ServerContext. After the handshake, requests on one connection run concurrently (at most 64 in flight) and each response is written when it is ready, so responses can arrive out of request order. Notifications from work a request started, such as the live tail of events.subscribe, are written only after that request's response. A connection holds one live tail per session: subscribing again replaces it, and the replaced tail's queued notifications are written before the new tail's.
  • Client. The client side is the concrete protocol::Client. Its connection task correlates requests by id, demuxes notifications into an ordered ClientDelivery stream, injects cursor replays and gap recovery before buffered live notifications, fetches replays in pages of 2,000 events and delivers each replay whole once its final page arrives, wipes secret-bearing serialized frames, and fails outstanding calls on shutdown.
  • TUI and CLI. The TUI client is a thin adapter re-exporting the server's Client wrapper; the CLI uses the same client. Both still work without the tui feature.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Params are commands: a member a method's params schema does not list is refused with -32602 and data.code unknown_field, whose field is the member's JSON path (selection.model.extra). That holds inside types session history also stores, such as a run selection or a permission rule, which ignore unknown members when they are read as history.

run.start accepts optional reset_fallback (default false). The server normally trims a requested earlier model's suffix to the latest successfully committed fallback in this session, matching exact model/variant identity and agent/preset scope. Set reset_fallback: true for an explicit picker/model reset. The accepted effective selection and suffix are recorded in run_started; existing committed-turn events preserve progress without a new event type. Idempotent redelivery resolves against the state preceding the original run.

A refusal changes nothing and is the error config_apply_refused, whose reason is conflict, invalid_configuration, or invalid_change and whose detail says why config.reload Empty object status: applied_revision, restart_required (server, plugins, runtimes), and error when the configuration on disk failed validation and was not applied session.create Run selection, optional permission_mode, optional permission_rules (the initial session overlay, at most 256 rules), optional runtimes ([{ runtime_id, capability?, workspace? }]), optional global (default true), optional cwd (the client's directory) Session metadata with skipped-event diagnostics, and the session's runtimes session.list Optional cwd identity Root session metadata list with skipped-event diagnostics session.get Session ID Session metadata with skipped-event diagnostics, and the session's runtimes session.goal.get Session ID Required nullable goal: GoalState session.goal.set Session ID, objective, optional selection: RunSelection Activated goal: GoalState session.goal.lifecycle Session ID, goal ID, expected revision, pause/resume/cancel action, optional selection for resume only Updated goal: GoalState session.producers Session ID Runtime producers and sources (producer source recovery) inspection session.usage Session ID Token/request rollup, cache hit rate, optional estimated cost, and per-model breakdown session.tree_usage Session ID The rollup of the whole tree the session belongs to and session_count; docs.title: User content
docs.text:
run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input take the user's input as content, a nonempty list of parts, and session.recall_input hands the recalled input back the same way:

"content": [
  { "type": "text", "text": "What is wrong with this layout?" },
  { "type": "file", "artifact": { "sha256": "…", "byte_length": 482113,
      "media_type": "image/png", "filename": "screenshot.png" } }
]

A text part carries text; a file part names an artifact of the session tree's store by its ArtifactRef, as an upload returned it. The input-lane events store the same content (see Events).

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
A client attaches a file by uploading it into the session tree's artifact store and naming the result in a file part. A client that attaches before its first prompt creates the session first; the upload publishes a session that was still only in memory.

  1. artifact.upload.begin { session_id, byte_length, filename? } returns { upload_id, chunk_bytes }. chunk_bytes is 1 MiB. A byte_length above the largest attachment cap (25 MiB) is refused with media_too_large whose kind is file. The upload belongs to this connection: another connection cannot see it, it is dropped when the connection closes, and a connection may have at most 8 in progress (too_many_uploads). Its bytes stream into a temporary file of the store, never into memory.
  2. artifact.upload.chunk { upload_id, offset, data } appends data (standard base64, at most chunk_bytes decoded bytes) at offset, which must be exactly the bytes received so far (upload_offset_mismatch names expected_offset otherwise; the upload waits for the right chunk). A chunk past byte_length is upload_size_mismatch. Requests run concurrently, so send a chunk once the previous one is answered.
  3. artifact.upload.finish { upload_id, sha256 } checks the digest (digest_mismatch), recognizes the media type from the content alone (a filename never decides it), validates the content as tool attachments are validated (structure, the 20 MiB cap or 25 MiB for video, and for images at most 16384 pixels a side and 16 Mi pixels), and stores the blob under its digest. It returns { artifact: ArtifactRef, image? }; put artifact in a file part as it is. An upload whose digest or content is refused (digest_mismatch, media_type_unsupported, media_too_large) is dropped; one finished before all of its bytes arrived (upload_size_mismatch) stays in progress.
  4. artifact.upload.cancel { upload_id } drops an upload in progress.

An unknown or another connection's upload_id is upload_not_found.

Leases. A finished upload is kept for an hour while no event references it, then removed. Once an input that names it is submitted, its event keeps it, as tool attachments are kept: a revert that removes every reference removes it after its lease, and a fork takes it into the fork's tree. A daemon restart forgets leases; an upload no event referenced then stays in the store.

Admission. run.start, run.steer, and session.submit_input check every file part against the model the input reaches: the run's selected model (for a steer, the running run's; for a queued input, the model of the selection it will start with). The part must name an artifact of the tree's store whose content is what the reference says (artifact_not_found, or media_type_unsupported when the content is not that type), of a kind the model accepts (media_unsupported with kind and model), of a media type it lists (media_type_unsupported), within its byte and image limits (media_too_large, with the image's width and height and the model's limits), and the parts of one kind must not outnumber max_count (media_limit_exceeded). These are the model's input_media; a client that checks them first never meets these errors. A refused input records nothing. A model the input does not reach this way, such as a fallback or a model the session moves to later, sees a placeholder for each file it does not accept (Media reads describes the wording).

artifact.read { session_id, sha256, offset, length } returns { data, total_bytes, media_type }: up to length (at most 1 MiB) bytes from offset of any artifact of the session's tree (user uploads, tool attachments, and the full content of truncated display blocks), base64 encoded, fewer at the end, and none at offset = total_bytes. media_type is recognized from the content: a media type, text/plain for UTF-8 text, or application/octet-stream. A blob is verified against its digest when it is first read. An artifact the store does not have is artifact_not_found.

Model, agent, and catalog discovery uses runtime.snapshot.get. Skills use the session-aware skills.list and skills.get methods because visibility depends on the governing run policy and session overlay. session.list returns root sessions only: a delegated child is selected as part of its root's tree, not as a top-level entry, and stays reachable via session.tree, session.children, session.get, and session.resume.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
