A session uses the tools and workspace context of the runtime capabilities it is attached to. A RuntimeAttachment is { name, runtime_id, capability, kind, workspace? }: the session-unique attachment name (also the tool prefix on name collisions), the runtime_id, the runtime's capability the session uses, the capability's kind (a label the runtime declares, such as global or coding; the daemon never branches on it), and the canonical workspace the runtime reported, if any. The session create, get, and resume results carry the session's attachments in attach order; clients follow later changes through the runtime_attached and runtime_detached events of the session.

session.create attaches global unless global is false, then each entry of runtimes (runtime_id, optional capability, optional workspace) in order; without runtimes it attaches local's coding capability at cwd, or at the daemon's working directory without one. cwd is the client's directory as it names it: the session records it as its cwd_identity, so one daemon serves sessions of many directories and session.list with a cwd_identity shows one directory's. An empty runtimes list creates a session with no coding runtime. Instances that are not running are started first, and a failure creates no session and records no instance.

session.runtime.attach and session.runtime.detach are rejected while the session has an active run (session running). Attach connects the runtime and opens the capability's instance when needed, and records nothing when that fails: neither an attachment nor, for an instance that never opened, a failed instance in runtimes.list. The error says which step failed: runtime `<id>` failed to start: <reason> when the runtime could not be reached, and runtime `<id>` could not open `<capability>` for workspace `<workspace>`: <reason> with the runtime's own reason when it refused the workspace, such as one outside the directories it serves. Without capability it attaches the runtime's only capability; a runtime that offers several asks for one, naming them. The attachment's name is the name the instance reports (global, or <runtime ID>_<workspace basename> for a coding instance), suffixed _2, _3, ... when the session already has an attachment of that name; attaching an instance a session already has is an error. A capability that takes a workspace requires workspace, except local's coding, which opens at the daemon's working directory without one; a capability that takes none refuses one. Besides global and local, the runtimes are the configured [runtimes.<id>] tables and the dial-in runtimes that have connected since the daemon started; attaching any other runtime ID is an unknown runtime error, and attaching a dial-in runtime that is not connected now fails. The daemon passes workspace to the runtime exactly as given; the attachment records the canonical path the runtime reported, and two spellings of one workspace share an instance.

runtimes.list returns each runtime as a RuntimeListing: its runtime_id; its lifetime (builtin for global and local, spawned for a template, dial_in for a runtime that connected on its own); whether the daemon is connected to it now; its capabilities (name, kind, takes_workspace, description), empty until it has connected once; its platform; its machine (see Machines); and a message saying why its last attempt to connect failed, or, for a dial-in runtime that went away, runtime `<id>` disconnected: <reason>, where a runtime that stopped cleanly gives the other end closed the connection. Each instance has its runtime_id, capability, reported attachment_name, kind, workspace, and platform once started, its status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, or stopped), and a failure message.

runtimes.reconnect retries an instance now: a failed instance is started again, under a new generation, and keeps its identity; an instance that is not running is started; a ready or reconnecting one is left as it is. capability and workspace follow the attach rule, and for a failed instance it is the workspace that runtimes.list reports. A start that fails is an error with the reason, worded as for attach. An instance runtimes.list already showed stays failed with the new reason, which runtimes.changed reports; one it did not show stays unrecorded. Retrying global also retries its failed MCP servers.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Every runtime belongs to one machine, the computer it runs on (see the memory spec). The daemon keeps its machines in a registry, machines.json in its data folder, which only the machines.* methods change. A runtime is assigned when it connects, in this order: the machine that pins its runtime ID; the machine that stands for the machine ID it reported in the runtime protocol; a new machine for that ID, named after the runtime's sanitized host name with -2, -3, … added on a clash; and, for a runtime that reported no ID, a new machine pinning it, named after its runtime ID. global and local belong to the daemon's own machine. Machine names are a lowercase ASCII letter followed by up to 31 lowercase letters, digits, _, or -. runtimes.list gives each runtime's machine: the one it is assigned to while connected, else the one it is pinned to or last reported.

machines.list returns each machine as a MachineInfo: its name; the machine ids it stands for; the runtime IDs pinned to it; the connected runtimes assigned to it, each with its runtime_id, assigned_by (pinned or machine_id), and platform; the platform its connected runtimes agree on; and its number of memories, the memory files in its memory folder.

Each change answers with the machines afterwards, moves the connected runtimes it affects at once, and sends machines.changed; a session's system prompt names the new machine from its next run. A change holds the memory lock while it rewrites the registry and moves memory folders, and fails, changing nothing, when it cannot:

  • machines.rename fails with machine_name_taken when another machine, or a memory folder that belongs to none, has the name.
  • machines.assign removes the runtime's pin from any other machine.
  • machines.unassign of a runtime no machine pins is runtime_not_pinned.
  • machines.merge fails with machine_memory_conflict when both memory folders hold a file of one name, and with machine_merge_self for one machine.
  • machines.forget fails with machine_in_use while a connected runtime belongs to the machine or its memory folder holds anything.

An unknown machine is machine_not_found; a registry or folder that cannot be read or written is machine_store_failed.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The daemon's memory is Markdown files with description and keywords frontmatter, in four layers, each file addressed by a memory URL: user://<category>, agent://<agent>, machine://<machine>/<name>, and project://<project>/<name> (see the memory guide and the memory spec). The memory.* methods act on the files for the user, with no session; a change never refreshes the memory snapshot of an open session, which a later run takes when it would anyway.

memory.list returns each file as a MemoryInfo: its url, layer (user, agent, machine, or project), group (the machine or project of a machine:// or project:// memory), revision, size in bytes, and either its description and keywords or the reason it is invalid. An agent:// file whose agent the agent registry no longer has is orphaned. ignored lists, by path in the memory folder, what is not a memory file of the layout (a file without .md, a name that breaks the naming rules, something nested too deep) with the reason. layer keeps one layer; agent, machine, or project keeps one agent's file, one machine's memories, or one project's, and only one of the three may be given. A filter that contradicts layer or another filter is -32602.

A revision is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the file's bytes. memory.write takes the whole file text, frontmatter included, and checks it like the model's memory_write: it must parse, follow the file format, and fit [memory] max_file_bytes. Without revision it creates the memory, and fails with memory_exists when it exists; with revision it replaces the memory at that revision, and fails with memory_revision_mismatch when the file changed since, or memory_not_found when it is gone. Both errors carry the file's current revision. memory.delete needs the revision as well. Unlike the model, the user may create and delete user:// categories and delete agent:// files; an agent:// file is created only for an agent the agent registry has (memory_refused).

The daemon keeps an agent:// file for every agent that is not internal and owns its description and two keywords, the agent ID and its mode (see the memory guide). A memory.write of such a file keeps them: when the text gives another description or leaves a daemon keyword out, the daemon puts its own frontmatter in place, keeps the body and any other keywords, and says what it kept in the result's notice (since 1.6.0). A file whose agent the registry no longer has keeps the description it has.

A URL that is not a memory URL is memory_url_invalid; text that is not a valid memory is memory_invalid with the reason; a malformed revision is -32602. Another process holding the memory lock is memory_busy, and a file that cannot be read or written is memory_store_failed. Each change sends memory.changed to every connection; changes another daemon sharing the data folder makes are not announced.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
plugins.list returns every configured plugin in the order its hooks run. A PluginInfo is { name, state, reason?, tools, hooks, subscribe_events, subscribe_bus, publish_bus, producer_messaging, dropped_events, stderr? }: its state (disabled, starting, connected, reconnecting, failed, or stopped), why it failed or last disconnected, the tools it declares and the names of the hooks it intercepts, what it streams and publishes, whether its producer messaging is open, how many notifications it dropped for falling behind, and the tail of its standard error.

plugins.restart starts a plugin again now: a failed or reconnecting plugin is started at once, and a connected one is stopped and started. An unknown or disabled plugin is an error (plugin request rejected). Status changes arrive as plugins.changed.

docs.title: The catalog view
docs.text:
runtime.snapshot.get returns, and runtime.changed carries, a ModelCatalogView:

{ "revision": "<opaque>",
  "catalog": { "source": "network", "stale": false, "age": "current",
               "provider_quarantine_count": 0, "model_quarantine_count": 0,
               "last_error": null },
  "providers": [ … ], "models": [ … ], "agents": [ … ] }
  • revision is one opaque string: it changes whenever anything the view shows changes. Clients compare it and send it back, never parse it. provider.connect and provider.disconnect take the revision of the view their form was filled from as expected_revision; a view whose catalog (for a connect) or provider state (for a disconnect) has changed since is refused with catalog_revision_conflict or runtime_revision_conflict, and the client reads the view again.
  • catalog says where the model catalog stands: its source (network, cache, or bootstrap), whether it is stale, its age (current, older_than_seven_days, or older_than_thirty_days), the records it quarantined, and its nullable last_error.
  • providers, models, and agents are client-facing descriptors only: no frozen model bindings, recipe identities, fingerprints, compiler versions, or the internal revisions and counters the view's revision stands for. models lists only selectable models; an agent's resolved_fallback names model selections.
  • input_media on every model says what it accepts in user input, one entry per kind (an open label: image, pdf, audio, or video):
{ "kind": "image", "mime_types": ["image/jpeg", "image/png"],
  "max_bytes": 7864320, "max_dimension": 16384, "max_pixels": 16777216,
  "max_count": 20 }

The limits are effective: the lowest of the model's catalog capability, the delivery limits of its adapter family for a user turn, and the attachment caps (20 MiB, or 25 MiB for video). mime_types lists the model's types an upload can be recognized as from its content; max_dimension and max_pixels are present for images. A kind absent from the list is not accepted: clients offer attachments only for the kinds of the session's selected model and check sizes before uploading.

docs.title: Model availability
docs.text:
Unusable models are visible instead of silently dropped. Each ProviderDescriptor carries:

  • model_counts: available, quarantined, unsupported, needs_setup, and needs_credentials counts over the provider's catalog rows (deprecated, disabled, and non-text models are not counted).
  • unavailable_models: one entry per unusable model with id, display_name, kind (the four unavailable kinds above), and a nullable reason (the quarantine code or compiler reason). The list is strictly sorted by id and is populated only for configured (authored or stored) providers; unconfigured providers report counts alone.
  • documentation_url and environment: the models.dev doc URL and env variable names. They are display hints; cookie never reads those variables.

docs.title: Goal/producer integration handoff
docs.text:
The engine implements these methods through its per-session actor. Goal mutations are root-only; producer inspection is available for any owned session. Tool calls declare their output channels, and results carry terminal output references and a display independent of their output.

Surface Public contract Implementation owner Goal projection GoalState, GoalItem, GoalStatus, GoalId Engine; TUI renders durable events Goal read SessionGoalGetParams/Result, get_session_goal Engine; TUI/clients call async API Activation SessionGoalSetParams/Result, set_session_goal User-only root command, rejects active/paused goal Lifecycle SessionGoalLifecycleParams/Result, change_session_goal_lifecycle, GoalLifecycleAction User-only root pause/resume/cancel; reject stale/terminal goal Model tools GoalGetParams/Result, GoalUpdateParams/Result Root-only goal_get/goal_update, frozen at run admission Runtime inspection SessionProducersParams/Result, session_producers, ProducerRegistration, ProducerSourceState Session runtime snapshot, not global catalog snapshot or persistence Producer messaging Producer{Register,Send,Discard,Unregister}Params/Result producer/* requests of plugins and runtimes; SDK mirrors register/send/discard/unregister Recovery handshake RecoveryStartParams, RecoveryCompleteParams/Result, RecoveryOutcome producer/recovery/start daemon notification (no deadline/response); completion request

Goal activation accepts an optional selection: RunSelection, including agent, model, variant, and preset. The engine validates and persists this selection before scheduling a wake, so it survives waiting for producers and restarting. Lifecycle requests accept selection only with action: "resume"; pause and cancel reject a supplied selection. Resuming without it preserves the goal's previous selection. If activation omitted it and no later resume supplied one, automatic runs use the latest persisted run selection, falling back to the session's creation selection. None of these changes mutate an already-running turn's frozen selection or attribution.

GoalItem { description, finished } has no item ID. GoalUpdateParams { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist through the session actor: the last accepted update wins for the current/latest session goal at actor acceptance. Model updates have no goal_id, expected_revision, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal; updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal. Internal GoalId and engine-owned GoalState.revision remain for durable state and reminder identity. User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision and reject stale identities and revisions; no model tool can set an objective or issue lifecycle commands. Empty lists preserve the active/paused lifecycle and can bootstrap an active goal without completion. goal_get and goal_update declare no permission: they are published only to a root run whose session has an active or paused goal, and every call is allowed. There is no permission action or goal configuration for them.

To preserve strictly increasing event revisions, an all-finished update appends checklist revision r+1, then completion revision r+2, and returns the final state. Recovery repairs a missing completion event after a committed all-finished checklist. Empty checklists never complete through this rule.

See Events for admission/commit coverage and owned-message discard, and Plugin development for method names, idempotency, recovery, and the no-implicit-registration requirement.

docs.title: User steering
docs.text:
run.steer requires an active target run. It immediately appends user_input_admitted and returns { "accepted": true }; admission does not change model history. At each completed tool batch and no-tool completion boundary, all pending inputs are promoted FIFO as separate user_input_submitted events before the next request. A no-tool boundary with no pending input completes the run.

run.steer also returns the admission's user_input_seq. Terminal run events void anything still pending.

docs.title: The session's model selection
docs.text: A session has one model selection (agent, model, variant, preset) that every client shares. session.select_model validates a selection as a run start would and appends a runless session_model_selected event under the caller's origin; selecting what the session already has records nothing and returns { "changed": false }. cookie_agent_protocol::SessionModelState folds the session's selection from its events: the creation selection, then each run's selection and successful fallback, with an explicit pick replacing it and dropping any fallback the session had settled on. A run started without a selection (session.submit_input with selection omitted, or a queued input queued that way) uses it, and clients keep their drafts at it, so the latest pick from any client is what the next message runs on. A request that names its own selection still runs on that one.

docs.title: Submitting from several clients
docs.text:
session.submit_input is how clients send a message without first finding out whether the session is running. On the session's actor it either starts a run ({ "outcome": "started", "run_id" }), or, while a run is active, follows delivery:

  • steer admits the input as run.steer does: { "outcome": "steered", "run_id", "user_input_seq" }.
  • queue appends a runless user_input_queued event holding the input, its selection, and client_run_id: { "outcome": "queued", "queued_seq" }.

A run that starts or ends while the request is in flight only changes which outcome happens; the daemon retries a few times before answering with a session_running conflict. An omitted selection means the session's current selection. A plugin that handles the input yields { "outcome": "handled", "reason" }. Retrying the same client_run_id with the same input returns the original run or queue entry; different input is an idempotency_conflict.

When a run completes normally, the daemon starts a run with the oldest queued input under the origin of the client that queued it; that run's run_started carries the entry's client_run_id, which removes it from the queue. A failed, cancelled, or interrupted run voids every queued input, and the daemon appends user_input_queue_voided when a queued input cannot start at all. Clients reduce the queue with cookie_agent_protocol::QueuedInputs, as the daemon does.

session.recall_input takes back one pending steered input or one queued input by its seq. Only the client whose origin admitted it may do so: another client gets { "outcome": "not_owner" }. A pending input is withdrawn with user_input_recalled and a queued one with user_input_queue_recalled; both return { "outcome": "recalled", "content" }, the input's content for editing. An input that was already promoted, started, or voided returns { "outcome": "gone" }.

run.start on a session whose run is active fails with code -32602 and RunStartConflict data whose code is session_running, so a client can fall back to session.submit_input.

docs.title: Revert and fork
docs.text:
session.revert is idle-only. The target must be a positive existing sequence, and expected_last_seq must be the session's current last event sequence: a session that has moved on since the client looked (another client's turn, say) is refused with the error stale_revert, whose data carries current_last_seq, so a revert never deletes what the requester has not seen. The engine removes every event after it from the log (a run left with nothing but its run_started goes too), closes any run, tool call, internal agent, or approval the cut left open, and deletes the subagent sessions created by removed delegations; a running one refuses the revert. Later appends reuse the freed sequence numbers. Subscribers receive a rewound notification (see Subscriptions).

session.fork takes a client_fork_id: while the daemon runs, a retry with the same key and target returns the first fork instead of making another, and the same key with a different target is an idempotency_conflict. session.fork may read an active source but requires a persisted prefix that contains a submitted user message. The fork copies that prefix exactly under a new session ID, closes any copied in-flight run locally, appends (fork) to the title, and continues with new physical sequences.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
session.delete { session_id, expected_last_seq } deletes a root session's whole tree from disk: the root, every delegated session under it, their events and metadata, and the tree's artifacts. Nothing is kept for undo, so clients ask the user first. It is new in 1.5.0: a client sends it only to a daemon of minor 5 or later, and reads -32601 as "the daemon is too old to delete sessions".

expected_last_seq is the root's last_event_seq from the metadata the user confirmed. The delete is refused, changing nothing, when:

  • the session does not exist (session_not_found);
  • it is a delegated session (not_a_root_session, with its root_session_id): a tree is deleted through its root;
  • a session of the tree has an active run, a compaction, or a subagent waiting for a slot (session_tree_running, with the busy running_session_id);
  • another cookie process holds the tree's owner.lock (session_owned_elsewhere);
  • the root's last event is no longer expected_last_seq (session_changed, with current_last_seq).

The checks run in this order, so a running tree is session_tree_running even when its guard is stale too, as it is while a run streams past the listed last_event_seq; session_changed means the tree is idle and moved.

A tree this daemon does not hold is deleted under its lock without being opened, so nothing is appended to it first. The tree's background calls are stopped without a report and its uploads in progress are dropped. The daemon moves the tree's directory aside to a .deleted-<root>-<id> tombstone in the work directory, which commits the delete, forgets the tree, sends sessions.changed removed for each deleted session (the root first) to every connection, and removes the tombstone; a daemon that stopped in between removes the tombstone when it next opens the directory. Each connection's subscriptions to the deleted sessions end with them: no further events.subscription arrives for them and events.unsubscribe answers false. The result is { "deleted": [<root>, <descendants>…] }.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Notification Payload runtime.changed The previous view's revision, the complete new catalog view, and the change reasons, sorted and without repeats events.subscription One stored event, live-only stream output, a session sequence gap, or a rewind events.plugin Session-scoped non-durable plugin event sessions.changed One session index change: upserted, removed, approvals_changed, permission_mode_changed, or resync mcp.changed MCP server configuration or status changed; optional failures runtimes.changed A runtime template was registered or an instance's status changed; optional failures background.changed A subscribed session's background calls changed: session_id and its current calls plugins.changed A plugin's status changed; an empty object machines.changed The machine registry changed, or a runtime joined a new machine; an empty object memory.changed A memory file changed through the daemon; an empty object

A background call in session.background.list and background.changed is { job, tool, tool_call_id, display?, started_at, detached_at, by }: the job ID, the tool's name as the model called it, the call it came from, its display argument, when the call started and when it moved to the background, and who moved it (model or user). The list lives in the daemon, so it never shows a call a daemon restart killed. background.changed reaches only connections subscribed to the session; one that falls behind gets every subscribed session's list again.

docs.title: Daemon-wide changes
docs.text:
runtime.changed, sessions.changed, mcp.changed, runtimes.changed, plugins.changed, machines.changed, and memory.changed reach every connection from its handshake on, whether or not it subscribed to any session, so each client sharing a daemon stays current with what the others do. Clients ignore notification methods they do not know.

sessions.changed carries one change, tagged by change:

change Fields Sent when upserted session (SessionMeta) A session, root or delegated, is created, first persisted, or reverted, or its status or title changes removed session_id A revert deleted a delegated session, or session.delete deleted a session of a tree; the connection's subscription to it has ended approvals_changed root_session_id, session_id An approval in any session of the tree was requested, escalated, decided, or cancelled; approval.list for the root shows the result permission_mode_changed root_session_id, mode, changed_by session.set_permission_mode changed the tree's mode; changed_by is the caller's origin resync none This connection fell more than 256 changes behind and missed some; refetch session.list, approvals, and permission modes

The permission mode is runtime-only and has no event, so permission_mode_changed is the only way other clients learn of a change.

runtime.changed notifications form a chain through previous_revision. A connection that falls more than 64 notifications behind receives one with a null previous_revision, the current snapshot, and the reason resync; a client that holds a different revision refetches runtime.snapshot.get rather than trusting either. A status mcp.changed is an empty object; bursts coalesce into one notification, and a client refetches mcp.server.list. runtimes.changed and plugins.changed work the same way for runtimes.list and plugins.list, machines.changed for machines.list and runtimes.list, and memory.changed for memory.list.

docs.title: Connection failures
docs.text:
When an MCP server fails to connect, or drops and does not reconnect, and when a runtime instance fails to start, the daemon sends one notification for it with a failures list to each connection subscribed (events.subscribe) to a session that uses it. Each entry names the affected session_ids among that connection's subscriptions:

Notification failures entry mcp.changed runtime_id hosting the server (global for top-level [mcp]), workspace of the hosting instance when its runtime has one, server, reason, session_ids runtimes.changed runtime_id, capability, workspace when the capability takes one, reason, session_ids

Subscribing to a session also sends the failures that already affect it, so a client that opens a session after its servers failed still learns why their tools are missing. Failures are live notifications, not session events; the TUI shows each as an error row in every named session it displays. failures is omitted when empty.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
mcp.server.list returns the servers of every runtime: the global runtime's top-level [mcp] servers first, then those each running coding runtime instance hosts from its template's mcp table. Each entry has the hosting runtime_id, the hosting instance's workspace (absent for global), name, source, definition, state, tool_count, message, and auth_in_progress. state is connected, connecting, reconnecting, failed, needs_auth, disabled, or disconnected. A reconnecting server dropped and is being restarted: its tools stay published and calls fail with the runtime_unavailable failure code until it reconnects or, after every attempt failed, becomes failed and its tools are dropped (see MCP). The mcp.server.* mutations and mcp.auth.* act on servers of the global runtime. mcp.server.reconnect { name, runtime_id?, workspace? } reconnects a server of any runtime and waits for the attempt: without runtime_id (or with global) a top-level server, otherwise the one the instance of runtime_id at workspace hosts, as mcp.server.list names them.

The shared client maps these to ClientDelivery variants (Live, replay deliveries, PluginEvent, RuntimeChanged, RecoveryFailed), so a UI consumes one ordered stream and never parses raw JSON-RPC frames.

Tool display comes from tool_call_progress and tool_call_terminated events; retained output is read through its artifact references. Raw tool output is not streamed to clients.

text_delta, reasoning_delta, and tool_call_progress are live-only: events.subscription delivers them as transient messages carrying the durable after_seq they follow instead of a sequence of their own, and they are never stored or replayed. model_output_started durably marks where each streamed part began. See live-only stream output.

The MCP OAuth callback runs on the client, so a daemon reached through a tunnel or on another machine can still be authorized from the client's browser. mcp.auth.begin requires redirect_uri, the client's own loopback callback (http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path> or http://[::1]:<port>/<path> with no query, fragment, or credentials). The client then sends the browser's redirect to mcp.auth.complete { server, callback_url }; the daemon keeps the PKCE verifier, exchanges the code, and stores the tokens, which never cross the connection. A callback_url that is not a redirect to the pending redirect_uri with a code or error parameter is rejected and leaves the flow waiting. Any other completion ends it. A begin with the pending redirect_uri returns the same authorization URL; one with a different redirect_uri replaces the pending flow.

A client can configure permissions before a session exists. session.create accepts an optional permission_mode for the new tree and optional permission_rules, which are validated like any overlay (no duplicate action and pattern, at most 256) before the session is created and committed as its first session_permission_overlay_set event, so the first run already sees them. session.permission.preview { selection, rules } returns the effective permissions such a session would have, computed from the selection's frozen agent policy exactly as session.permission.get computes them for a live session.

Background jobs report through the tool { tool_call_id } producer owner (the completion report of a job a tool call started, such as a bash call with background: true), and producer_message_accepted may carry retained_output naming the job's captured output artifacts.

Tool output that fits its preview is stored only in the result's output: RetainedToolStream.reference and sha256 are absent for such a stream, and RetainedToolOutput.reference is absent when no stream needed an artifact. RetainedToolStream.dropped_bytes is present when output past the 128 MiB capture limit was not retained. A result always carries its whole display: the ranges of output a session log stores display text as (Events) never reach clients.

Session metadata includes additive skipped_events entries with the physical sequence (or source line number when no sequence was readable) and a safe reason. An empty array means the event log loaded without skipped records. Optional-field degradations remain available to the engine as load diagnostics but are not reported as skipped events.

See Events for event payloads and durability semantics.

docs.title: Runtime Protocol
docs.text:
The runtime protocol connects the daemon to a runtime: a source of tools and workspace context that runs outside the engine (see the runtimes specification). The daemon's built-in local coding runtime speaks it on a task of the daemon's own process over an in-memory frame pair; a configured [runtimes.<id>] template runs a command, typically ssh host cookie runtime serve --stdio, and speaks it over the child's stdin and stdout. The local and remote paths are one code path. The global runtime does not speak it; the engine calls it in-process.

The wire types live in the Apache-2.0 protocol crate's cookie_agent_protocol::runtime_protocol and the JSON-RPC peer both ends run in cookie_agent_protocol::peer, so the plugin SDK shares them; cookie_agent_runtime_api::protocol and ::rpc re-export them. The coding runtime's server is in cookie_agent_coding_runtime::server and the daemon's client in the engine's runtimes::remote module. Plugins declare and run their tools with this protocol's tool messages over their own connection (see Plugin development).

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The daemon reaches a runtime in one of two ways, and speaks the same protocol over either:

  • Spawned: it runs a template's command and frames the child's stdio, one message per line, as above.
  • Dial-in: the runtime opens a WebSocket to the daemon's /runtime?id=<runtime ID> endpoint with the daemon's bearer token in an Authorization: Bearer header, one message per text frame. The daemon then sends runtime/initialize exactly as for a spawned runtime, with no MCP servers: a dial-in runtime hosts its own. A dial-in runtime gets 30 seconds to answer runtime/initialize and each capability/open, and 3 seconds to answer runtime/shutdown. See Dial-in refusals for how the daemon refuses one. Either end that ends the connection sends a close frame, normal closure (1000), and waits up to 2 seconds for the other's answer; a runtime that stops does so before it exits. The daemon reads a normal closure, going away (1001), or a close frame without a code as the runtime disconnecting, and another code, or a connection that ended without a close frame, as a failure with that code or error.

docs.title: Dial-in refusals
docs.text:
Since 1.2.0 the daemon says why it refuses a runtime that dials in, and whether dialing in again can succeed (runtime_protocol::dial_in). A request it can refuse from the request alone is answered before the WebSocket upgrade with an HTTP status and the reason as the plain-text body:

Status Reason Permanent 400 The runtime ID does not match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}. yes 401 The bearer token is missing or wrong. yes 403 The ID is reserved (global, local) or names a [runtimes.<id>] template the daemon configures, or the request carries an Origin header. yes 409 A runtime is connected under the ID, or being accepted under it, now. The daemon may not have noticed yet that an earlier connection of the same runtime ended. no

A runtime that fails runtime/initialize after the upgrade, such as one of another major version or one that does not answer in time, sees the daemon close the connection with code 1011 and the reason as the close frame's reason, cut to the frame's 123 bytes. That refusal is not permanent.

A runtime stops dialing in after a permanent refusal and dials in again, after a wait, after any other, including a status this table does not list, such as one a proxy answers with. cookie runtime serve --daemon prints the reason either way, exits with an error on a permanent refusal, and checks its own ID first, so a malformed or reserved one never reaches the daemon. A daemon before 1.2.0 closes the connection after the upgrade without a reason for an ID it refuses, which a runtime can only treat as transient.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
• JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per frame: a frame of an in-memory transport, or one line of newline-delimited JSON over a byte stream such as a child's stdio (peer::LineTransport).
  • Both ends send requests. The daemon drives tools; a runtime reports progress back while a call runs. Request IDs are chosen by the sender and may be integers or strings, as JSON-RPC 2.0 allows; a reply echoes its request's ID. Both ends of this repository send integers.
  • The envelope is information. Members JSON-RPC does not define are ignored.
  • Bounded. No frame exceeds 48 MiB (runtime_protocol::MAX_FRAME_BYTES), which fits an execute reply carrying the largest attachment as base64 next to a full tool result. A sender refuses to send a larger message; a receiver that gets one closes the connection.
  • Information and commands. Every message is information except the ones a runtime sends that ask the daemon to act: tool/progress, tool/detachable, and the producer/* requests. Information ignores members its reader does not know, at any depth, and reads an enum value it does not know as that enum's fallback (see Open enums), so either end may be newer. A command is checked against its schema before it is decoded: a member, or an enum value or tag, the schema does not list is refused with -32602, data.code unknown_field or unknown_variant, and data.field set to its JSON path, such as progress.display.type. A sender gates new fields of a command on the receiver's version. The one exception is a display block of a kind the daemon does not know in a tool/progress replacement: it is only shown, so the daemon drops it with a diagnostic instead (see Display blocks).
  • Unreadable messages. A frame that is not JSON, or not a request, notification, or reply, closes the connection. A request whose params do not match its method is answered with -32602 (invalid_params, with serde's message as detail), and the connection stays up. A notification that cannot be read cannot be answered: the receiver reports it (the daemon in its log, a runtime on its standard error) and ignores it. The daemon also reports and ignores runtime/tools_changed from a runtime: only a plugin sends it.

docs.title: Open enums
docs.text:
An enum value a reader does not know reads as the fallback below. The fallbacks are chosen so that an older reader stays safe:

Value Where An unknown value reads as collision tool declarations prefix concurrency tool declarations exclusive, the most conservative result_truncation tool declarations bounded: the daemon still bounds the result tool error kind prepare, revalidate, and execute results; mcp/reconnect failed, a generic tool failure MCP server state capability/open results, mcp/changed disconnected: no tools, and no retry as a failure media delivery tool/prepare and tool/execute turns unknown: the tool does not attach that kind display block type prepare presentations, execute results, tool/progress replacements dropped, with a diagnostic (see Display blocks) media kind tool/prepare and tool/execute turns a label: a tool does not attach a kind it does not know

These are closed by design, since every reader must understand each value: a prepare result's and an execute outcome's status, an output's and an output declaration's kind, and a skill's source. The commands producer/send's mode and producer/recovery/complete's outcome are closed as every command is. The plugin protocol adds its own (see Plugin development).

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
The protocol version is a semver string, currently 1.2.0 (cookie_agent_protocol::RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION). The daemon sends its version in runtime/initialize and the runtime answers with its own. Each end reads the other's protocol_version from the raw JSON before it decodes anything else, so a peer of another version is answered with unsupported_protocol, naming both versions, rather than with a decoding error of a shape the two do not share; a hello without a readable version fails as invalid_params. Two versions are compatible when their majors are equal: a minor only adds, so the two ends use what the lower minor includes, and the patch never matters (see Compatibility). A 0.x build from before the freeze, and a build from before semver versions, which sends an integer, are refused the same way.

Both ends also send features: what their configuration enables, never what a version already implies. None are defined yet for runtimes; an end ignores a feature it does not know, and the daemon says so in its log.

Versions before 0.7.0 were integers. 3 removed tool/stdin and the stdin flag of tool/execute: tools no longer take input while they run. It also replaced the job/* messages and the background flag and launched_jobs of tool/execute with tool/detachable, and added background and background_default to tool declarations. 4 added producer messaging: the producer_messaging capability, the producer/* requests, and the recovery handshake (see Producer messaging). 5 added capabilities: one connection serves every workspace and capability of a runtime. runtime/initialize lost workspace and reports capabilities; capability/open opens an instance for a workspace and returns what runtime/initialize used to (identity, tools, skills, MCP servers); capability/tools_changed replaced runtime/tools_changed; and tool/prepare, runtime/context, mcp/changed, and mcp/reconnect name their instance (see the runtime capabilities spec). 6 removed the tool result's truncation, which nothing set: a result's retained output is retained_output. 0.7.0 made the version a semver string, added engine_version and features to the handshake, and moved errors to the registry's codes (see Errors). 0.8.0 replaced the turn's adapter family and model capabilities with turn.model (see tool/prepare). 1.0.0 froze the protocol: no 0.x build connects to a 1.x one. 1.1.0 added the optional machine of runtime/initialize's result, which the daemon groups runtimes into machines by. 1.2.0 made the daemon's answers to a refused dial-in part of the protocol: HTTP statuses with the reason before the upgrade, close code 1011 with the reason after it, and which of them are permanent (see Dial-in refusals). Its messages did not change; the version records the contract a runtime may now rely on to stop dialing in.

docs.title: Capabilities and instances
docs.text: A runtime offers capabilities, such as coding. Sessions attach each one separately, as { runtime_id, capability, workspace? }. The daemon opens a capability for a workspace (or none, for a capability that takes none) with capability/open; the result is an instance, under a runtime-chosen handle unique on the connection. One instance per (capability, canonical workspace) is shared by every session attached to it, and stays open for the connection's life. Tool calls, context, and MCP reports name the instance they belong to; prepared IDs are unique per connection, so the messages about one prepared call need no instance.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: Every runtime belongs to one machine, the computer it runs on. The daemon assigns a runtime to a machine when it connects, from the machine it reports in runtime/initialize: a machine the user pinned the runtime ID to comes first, then the machine that stands for the reported ID, then a new machine named after the host name. A runtime that reports no machine gets a machine of its own, named after its runtime ID. The user regroups, renames, and merges machines from any client; a runtime never learns its machine's name. See the memory spec.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. The daemon connects (in-process: a new frame pair and a server task; a configured template: it runs the command in its own process group, a job object on Windows, with the daemon's environment plus the template's env) and sends runtime/initialize, all within the template's startup_timeout_ms. It connects once per runtime, when a session first needs one of its capabilities. Every other request before it is answered with not_initialized; a second initialize with already_initialized. A child's stderr is kept as a bounded tail (the last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB) that failure reasons end with; nothing but protocol messages may appear on its stdout.
  2. The daemon opens an instance with capability/open for each capability and workspace its sessions attach, each within startup_timeout_ms.
  3. Sessions use the instances: the daemon prepares, executes, and releases calls, and asks for AGENTS.md context at each root run's admission. A coding runtime reports each instance's MCP servers' status as it changes (mcp/changed) and a changed tool list (capability/tools_changed).
  4. The daemon sends runtime/shutdown when it shuts down, waits up to the template's shutdown_grace_ms for the answer, and closes the transport (a child's stdin); a child that has not exited after another grace is killed with its process group. The runtime answers, cancels every running call, backgrounded ones included, and stops. It also stops when its transport ends.

When the connection is lost while it is in use, every call in flight fails with runtime_unavailable; a backgrounded call reports that failure as its background result. Every instance of the runtime becomes reconnecting: its tools stay published, calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable, and the daemon connects the runtime again up to 3 times, after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s, and opens each instance again with the canonical workspace it reported. One new connection serves them all. An instance that comes back with the same identity (runtime ID, capability, kind, attachment name, workspace) is revived under a new generation: its tools are listed again, and a call published before the restart fails as operation_changed. When every attempt fails, the instance becomes failed, its tools leave the session's tool list, and clients are told the reason. A failed instance starts again when a session that uses it is created or opened, or on runtimes.reconnect. A runtime that dials in is not dialed by the daemon: an attempt succeeds only once the runtime has connected again, and a runtime that dials in after its instances failed reopens them. Calls are never retried transparently.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Direction Kind Purpose runtime/initialize daemon → runtime request Version, runtime ID, settings; returns the capabilities capability/open daemon → runtime request Open a capability for a workspace; returns the instance's identity, tools, skills capability/tools_changed runtime → daemon notification An instance's whole new tool list runtime/context daemon → runtime request An instance's AGENTS.md context for a run's preset runtime/shutdown daemon → runtime request Stop gracefully tool/prepare daemon → runtime request Prepare one turn's calls to an instance tool/revalidate daemon → runtime request Check a prepared call can still run as approved tool/execute daemon → runtime request Run a prepared call; returns its terminal result tool/release daemon → runtime notification Discard a prepared call that will not run tool/progress runtime → daemon request Display and output deltas of an executing call tool/cancel daemon → runtime notification Cancel an executing call tool/detachable runtime → daemon notification An executing call reached its detach point mcp/changed runtime → daemon notification The status of an instance's MCP servers, and the ones that failed mcp/reconnect daemon → runtime request Reconnect one of an instance's MCP servers, or retry every failed one producer/recovery/start daemon → runtime notification Producer messaging is open; restore tracked work, then report producer/recovery/complete runtime → daemon request The runtime's recovery outcome producer/register runtime → daemon request Register a named producer for an attached session producer/send runtime → daemon request Send a message through a registered producer producer/unregister runtime → daemon request Close a registration; its messages stay producer/discard runtime → daemon request Discard one of the runtime's waiting messages

An unknown request is answered with -32601; an unknown notification is ignored.

docs.title: runtime/initialize
docs.text:
Params field Meaning protocol_version The daemon's protocol version (see Version). engine_version The daemon's own version, for logs. features What the daemon's configuration enables for the runtime; none are defined yet. runtime_id The runtime's ID, [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}. settings.tool_output The [tool_output] preview limits: max_lines, max_bytes, head_lines, tail_lines. settings.agent_md max_bytes: files larger than this are skipped. At most the AGENTS.md event bound. settings.mcp_servers The template's MCP servers: name and config, the server's table as the [mcp.servers.<name>] schema reads it. Each instance of a capability that hosts MCP servers runs them in its workspace.

A runtime rejects settings it does not support with initialize_rejected; a runtime that hosts no MCP servers rejects a nonempty mcp_servers. A coding runtime parses each server strictly and rejects the request when one does not parse or enables OAuth, which stays with the daemon's global runtime.

Result field Meaning protocol_version The runtime's protocol version. features Optional: what the runtime's configuration enables; none are defined yet. platform Optional: the operating system, as Rust's std::env::consts::OS names it, for a runtime where it matters. Shown in the system prompt with the runtime's machine. machine Optional, since 1.1.0: the machine the runtime runs on, { id, host_name? }. id is a stable, opaque ID of 1 to 128 printable ASCII bytes; runtimes reporting one ID belong to one machine. host_name (at most 255 bytes) names a machine the daemon has not seen. cookie runtime serve reports the digest cookie uses as its machine ID and the host name; a runtime that cannot tell leaves it out, and the daemon reads a malformed one as left out. See Machines. capabilities What the runtime offers: name ([a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}, unique within the runtime); kind, a self-declared label such as coding (a lowercase ASCII letter followed by up to 15 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens) that the daemon shows to clients and in approval reviews and never branches on; takes_workspace; and an optional description. The coding runtime offers coding, which takes a workspace. producer_messaging Optional, default false: the runtime sends producer messages to the sessions attached to its instances (see Producer messaging).

docs.title: capability/open
docs.text:
Params field Meaning capability One of the runtime's capabilities. workspace The workspace path, exactly as a session gave it, required exactly when the capability takes one: the runtime expands a leading ~ and resolves it on its own machine. A runtime started with --root refuses one outside its roots.

The runtime answers capability_open_failed for a capability it does not offer or a workspace it cannot open. Opening an instance that is already open (the same capability and canonical workspace) returns it. A coding instance connects every enabled MCP server before it answers: the reply comes once each server's first connection attempt and tool listing have finished, successfully or not, so the template's startup_timeout_ms must cover them. A server that fails publishes no tools; its status says why. The servers' tools join the declared tools as <server>_<tool>, with permission mcp, after the runtime's built-in tools, which keep their names: a server whose tool would take another tool's name fails, as in the global runtime. OAuth is never used: a remote server connects with its static headers only.

Result field Meaning instance The instance's handle on this connection. attachment_name The name sessions attach the instance under: <runtime ID>_<workspace basename>, sanitized, for a coding instance. workspace The canonical workspace on the runtime's machine; absent for a capability without one. AGENTS.md is loaded only from instances that report one. tools.tools Tool declarations: name, collision (prefix, override, or fallback; see collisions), permission, description, parameters (JSON Schema), concurrency, result_truncation, output, and optionally background and background_default. background says the tool supports the background: the daemon adds a background argument to its schema, strips it before tool/prepare, and may detach its calls (see Background calls); background_default is that argument's default and is only valid with background. permission is the action the tool is checked under: a label matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}, either one the daemon's own tools use (such as bash or read, which takes file paths) or the runtime's own (such as browse). An action no rule names is denied, so its tools stay hidden until an agent grants it. A tool without permission needs none: it is always published and every call is allowed without rules or approval, and its prepared calls report no permission either. Version 1 allowed only the nine built-in actions, and versions before 3 required permission. tools.prompt_sections System prompt sections (title, body) the tools contribute. skills.skills Project skills: the SKILL.md text, source, absolute path and base_dir on the runtime's machine, and a sample of supporting_files. The daemon parses the text with the same rules as local discovery. skills.discoveries Every SKILL.md found, with precedence_winner. mcp_servers The status of each MCP server after its first connection attempt, in name order: name; state, one of connected, connecting, reconnecting, failed, disabled, or disconnected; message, why it failed; and tools, its tool names. Absent when the instance hosts none.

docs.title: capability/tools_changed
docs.text: Params: instance and its new tools object as in the open result. The daemon uses it from the next model turn on. (A plugin, whose connection has one implicit instance, sends runtime/tools_changed with the tools object alone.)

docs.title: mcp/changed, mcp/reconnect
docs.text:
mcp/changed carries instance; servers, the status of every MCP server the instance hosts as in the open result; and failures, the servers that failed to connect or dropped and did not reconnect since the last report, each with server and reason. The runtime sends it after its open reply, whenever a status changes; a failure may arrive in a report of its own. The daemon shows the statuses in mcp.server.list and passes each failure to the clients viewing a session attached to the instance.

When a connected server drops, the runtime restarts it up to 3 times, after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s. Meanwhile it is reconnecting, its tools stay declared, and calls fail with runtime_unavailable. A successful attempt restores the server with its current tool list; when every attempt fails, it becomes failed, a capability/tools_changed drops its tools, and mcp/changed reports the failure.

mcp/reconnect params: instance, and server, optional. With a name, the runtime closes that server's connection and connects it again; without one, it retries every failed server of the instance. It answers {} once the attempts have finished, or {"error": …} for an unknown or disabled server or a failed attempt; the new status follows in mcp/changed. While one of the instance's servers is failed, the daemon sends it without a name when a session that uses the instance is created or opened, or when the instance is attached or retried, and the session's next run waits for the answer; it names a server for mcp.server.reconnect.

docs.title: runtime/context
docs.text: Params: instance, and preset, the run's agent preset (optional; must be a valid agent ID). Result: agent_md, the AGENTS.md entries in prompt order, and skipped, files over the size limit. The runtime applies the lookup to the instance's workspace: the preset's .cookie-agent/agents/<preset>/AGENTS.md, else .cookie-agent/agents/AGENTS.md, then <workspace>/AGENTS.md. A file that exists but cannot be read fails the request with context_failed and data.path.

docs.title: tool/prepare
docs.text:
Params: instance, the instance whose tools the calls name; session, run, turn; and calls (id, name, arguments; at most 256). turn is { agent, model }, where model is { model, adapter, input_media }: the model's key, its adapter label (such as openai-responses), and the media kinds a tool may return to it. Each input_media entry is { kind, mime_types, max_bytes, delivery }: kind is image, pdf, audio, or video; the limits are effective, already the lowest of the model's capability and its adapter's delivery limit; and delivery is tool_result (an attachment of the result) or user_message (a user message after the result, for an adapter whose tool results cannot carry the kind). A kind not listed is not accepted: a tool reports that it cannot attach the file. A plugin's prepare carries no instance. The runtime prepares a turn's calls together, so calls on one target chain. The result has one entry per call, tagged by status:

  • prepared: prepared_id; normalized_arguments, the arguments as the call will run them (not null); permission, the permission action, which must be the one the tool declares, absent for a tool that needs none; permission_resource, the resource of the normalized arguments, absent for a call checked under the action alone; presentation, how clients show the call (see below); and serialization_key, lowercase hex, when calls sharing it must run one at a time.
  • failed: error and the presentation to show for the failed call.

presentation is { title, hint?, primary_argument?, arguments?, preview? }: the title, an optional hint label for icons and grouping (such as shell or file_edit; see the compatibility spec), the argument clients show next to it, and display blocks for the arguments and for what the call will do. The daemon adds the tool's identity and fits the blocks to the display budget.

The runtime keeps a prepared call under its prepared_id until it is executed or released. Concurrency is declared per tool, not per call.

docs.title: Approval identity
docs.text:
The daemon builds each prepared call's approval identity; a runtime never states one, and a member it sends for one is ignored. The identity binds what the runtime declared to the tool the daemon knows the call goes to, the runtime attachment, plugin, or MCP server and the name it knows the tool by, so no runtime can state another tool's identity:

  • the normalized arguments' digest, over their JSON with object members in key order;
  • one capability: the permission action (tool for a tool that needs none) with operation <tool name>:call;
  • one resource of that action, <action>:<SHA-256 of the resource> (<action>:unscoped without one), bound to the tool's identity. A bash resource approves by command prefix and every other resource exactly. A bash command's and a path action's (read, write) binding lasts only for the daemon's process, since the runtime resolves it against its own machine at preparation; every other binding survives a restart, so a call of such a tool may be approved for its whole session tree;
  • the execution context: the tool's identity and the instance's workspace.

Two calls are the same operation, for tree grants and the doom-loop guard, exactly when these agree.

docs.title: tool/revalidate, tool/release
docs.text: Both take prepared_id. Revalidate answers {} or {"error": …}; release is a notification.

docs.title: tool/execute
docs.text:
Params field Meaning prepared_id The call to run; executing consumes it. session, run, turn As for prepare. background true when the model started the call in the background; omitted otherwise. A tool may use it to word its own results; it detaches the same way either way.

The result's outcome is tagged by status: failed with an error the call could not run past, or completed with the call's result:

Member Meaning output What the model reads, tagged by kind: single with the whole text, named with one text per declared stream, or streamed when the call's progress already sent it. title Optional: the result's title, at most 1 KiB without control characters; the tool's name when absent. display Optional: what clients show, a list of display blocks (see Display blocks). A single output without one shows its text. metadata Optional: structured data the model reads with the output. attachments Optional: files the result carries, each { mime_type, filename?, byte_length, sha256, reference }, at most 256 with the files of additional_messages. additional_messages Optional: at most 4 messages added to the model's history after the result, each { role, content }. failed Optional, default false: the call failed, and the model reads its output as the failure.

The daemon builds the result a session stores from it: it captures the output, previews and retains it, records whether the call moved to the background, and fits the display. Next to the outcome:

  • media: the bytes of every attachment the result references, as sha256 and base64 data, at most 25 MiB in all. The runtime gives each retained attachment the reference the daemon's content-addressed artifact store will give it; the daemon stores the bytes, checks each digest and reference, and rejects a result that references media it did not receive.

While a call runs, the runtime sends its progress with tool/progress (prepared_id, and progress: tool_call_id, message, an optional display delta, append { index, text, stream? } or replace { blocks }, and output chunks, under the 64 KiB and 8-stream delta bounds). It waits for each answer, so output reaches the daemon's capture in order, the daemon's capture limits reach the tool, and every chunk precedes the execute reply. The daemon owns capture, previews, and artifact retention.

tool/cancel cancels the call; it still answers its execute request. The runtime registers an execution as the request arrives, so a cancellation sent right after execute reaches it.

docs.title: Display blocks
docs.text: A prepared call's presentation, an execute result's display, and a tool/progress replace carry display blocks, typed units such as text, code, diff, or terminal that clients render as they choose (see the compatibility spec). The daemon strips control characters a block may not carry and fits each list to 64 KiB, cutting whole lines, hunks, or rows. A runtime sends only the kinds the daemon's version includes: a block of a kind the daemon does not know is dropped, and the session records a diagnostic of kind unknown_display_block whose source names the runtime (runtime:<id>) or plugin (plugin:<name>), once per call for its progress and its result.

docs.title: Background calls
docs.text:
The daemon owns the background (see the background tool calls spec); a runtime only says when a call may be detached. When an executing call of a tool declared with background reaches its detach point, the runtime sends tool/detachable (prepared_id, an optional note for the immediate result, such as a process ID, and reports_itself, omitted when false). The daemon may then detach the call: it commits an immediate result for it and keeps waiting for its tool/execute reply, whose result it reports to the session as a <background_result>. Nothing changes for the runtime: the call keeps running, its progress keeps arriving with tool/progress, and tool/cancel stops it, which is how a revert, a deleted session, or stop_background reaches it. A detached call does not outlive the runtime's connection.

A call whose work reports its own results once detached sets reports_itself (the daemon's delegate_subagent does, since its subagent reports every turn). The daemon then only stops waiting: it drops the call instead of awaiting its reply and sends no <background_result>, and cancelling the run that waited for it ends the call without cancelling the work. For a runtime's call, the daemon then sends no tool/cancel: the call keeps running in the runtime, and whatever it reports later goes through its producer messaging.

docs.title: Producer messaging
docs.text:
A runtime that declares producer_messaging may put messages into the model input of the sessions attached to its instances, as plugins do (see the external producers spec). It produces as external { source, name }: the daemon derives source, runtime:<runtime ID>, from the connection, and the runtime names each producer it registers.

  1. After runtime/initialize, the daemon sends producer/recovery/start. The runtime may send producer requests from then on; earlier ones are rejected. It restores whatever external work it tracks and answers producer/recovery/complete with outcome {"status": "ready"} or {"status": "failed", "message": …}. Until then its source is starting, and goal reminders of the sessions attached to it wait.
  2. producer/register (session_id, name: [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}) returns producer_id. producer/send (session_id, producer_id, mode steer or queue, idempotency_key, description, body) returns message_id once the message is durably accepted; an identical retry returns the same receipt. producer/unregister (session_id, producer_id) and producer/discard (session_id, message_id) return {}. The params and results are the protocol crate's Producer* and Recovery* types, which the plugin protocol shares.
  3. Every request may only address a session attached to one of the runtime's instances; any other fails with producer_rejected. The body must be non-empty and at most [producers] max_body_bytes.
  4. Registrations belong to the connection. They end when it does or when the session detaches the runtime; a reconnected runtime registers again, and its retried sends deduplicate against what it sent before.

The coding runtime declares producer messaging when started with ServeOptions::producer_messaging; its tools then reach these requests through ToolExecutionContext::producers.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors follow the scheme of the compatibility spec, in both directions. A protocol error uses a standard JSON-RPC code; every other error is -32000 with a stable snake-case data.code. Each carries a message a user can understand, and in data an optional hint (what to do next) and detail (technical detail, such as a serde error or a path). Receivers branch on data.code, never on message. The codes come from the protocol crate's registry (cookie_agent_protocol::errors):

Code data.code Meaning -32601 method_not_found Unknown method; data.method names it. -32602 invalid_params Params do not match the method; detail says why. -32602 unknown_field, unknown_variant A command carried a member, or an enum value or tag, its receiver does not know; data.field is its JSON path (see Framing). -32603 internal_error The receiver failed in a way it cannot describe further. -32002 unsupported_protocol The peer speaks an incompatible version; data.supported_version and data.peer_version name both (see Version). -32000 already_initialized A second runtime/initialize. -32000 initialize_rejected The runtime rejects the initialize request or its settings. -32000 not_initialized A request before runtime/initialize. -32000 capability_open_failed capability/open for a capability the runtime does not offer or a workspace it cannot open; data.capability and data.workspace name what was asked. -32000 unknown_handle Unknown prepared call or instance. -32000 context_failed Reading the runtime's context failed; data.path names the file. -32000 reply_too_large The reply would exceed the frame bound. -32000 producer_rejected The daemon rejected a producer request: messaging is not open on the connection, the session is not attached to the runtime, or the operation failed.

When the daemon shows a runtime's error to a user, such as a runtime that fails to start or a call whose tool/execute request fails, it keeps the runtime's message (and detail) and names the runtime.

Tool-level failures travel inside results as {"kind": …, "message": …}, where kind is the tool error kind (failed, operation_changed, resource_limit, permission_denied, timeout, runtime_unavailable, …).

docs.title: Schema Compatibility
docs.text:
Runtime configuration and agent documents are unversioned authored files parsed against the current shape. They reject schema and schema_version fields as hard errors rather than migrating or ignoring them. Session event history is also versionless and read best-effort. Versioned persisted and wire surfaces emit only their current version and reject unsupported versions.

Surface Current write Accepted reads Runtime configuration unversioned unversioned current shape Agent document unversioned unversioned current shape Client protocol 1.6.0 1.x Plugin protocol 1.2.0 1.x Runtime protocol 1.2.0 1.x Session history (events JSONL) history format 1 format 1; older formats are converted Session metadata unversioned unversioned current shape Catalog cache 2 2 Provider store 3 3 Family recipe registry 1 1 In-memory model manifest (recorded run bindings) 1 1

The three protocols have semver versions, as the compatibility specification describes: the client protocol CLIENT_PROTOCOL_VERSION (1.6.0), the plugin protocol PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_VERSION (1.2.0), and the runtime protocol RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION (1.2.0), all in cookie_agent_protocol. All three froze at 1.0.0. Each handshake sends its side's version and accepts a peer of the same major; the two use what the lower minor includes, and the patch never matters. No 0.x build from before the freeze connects to a 1.x one. The client protocol's versions are listed in its changelog.

Session history is versioned apart from the protocols, by the history_format that session_created records (format 1 in this build). It bumps only when a change cannot follow the additive rules of Events; a log of a lower format is converted when a newer build opens it, and one of a higher format opens only to be viewed. The catalog view that runtime.snapshot.get returns carries no schema version, only one opaque revision.

Agent snapshots embedded in events are read in their current shape only (schema 7); earlier shapes are rejected. Delegation lifecycle records are ordinary parent session events; the removed delegations.jsonl surface and its schema versions are not read.

docs.title: Published schemas
docs.text:
The three protocols' schemas are published with this documentation, exactly as crates/protocol/compat/ commits them (see below):

Surface Methods Schemas Version Client protocol methods.json schemas/client/schemas/<Root>.schema.json, such as RuntimeSnapshotResult version Plugin protocol methods.json schemas/plugin/schemas/<Root>.schema.json, such as PrepareResult version Runtime protocol methods.json schemas/runtime/schemas/<Root>.schema.json, such as ExecuteResult version

methods.json names each method's params and result roots; each root's file holds its schema and its definitions ($defs). A plugin or runtime written in any language can validate what it sends against them. The reference plugin does so in CI. The client protocol's error data is not described by schemas: the error reference lists every code and its fields.

docs.title: Baselines and the checker
docs.text:
crates/protocol/compat/ holds one baseline per surface: client, plugin, runtime, and events (the EventPayload set, which the client and plugin protocols both deliver; its version records the client version). Each holds:

  • version: the surface's version when the baseline was taken;
  • methods.json: every method and notification with its direction (to_daemon or from_daemon), its kind (request or notification), the names of its params and result schema roots, and params_role (command or information), plus information: roots that flow as information without a method of their own, such as the stored event set;
  • schemas/<Root>.schema.json: the JSON Schema of every root.

cargo run -p cookie_agent_protocol --example generate -- --output <directory> writes the same layout from the current code; the method registry it reads is surface_methods in crates/protocol/src/bindings.rs.

crates/protocol/scripts/check-schema-additive.sh generates the set into a temporary directory and compares it with the baselines using crates/protocol/scripts/check-compat.py, then runs the checker's mutation test, test-check-compat.py. The checker gives each type a role from methods.json: params sent to the daemon are commands, except a peer's declarations of what it has (runtime/tools_changed, capability/tools_changed, mcp/changed), while params the daemon sends and every result are information. It walks nested definitions and computes the version bump each change requires under the rules of section 7.1 of the specification; open enums are marked "x-open": true.

Every rule is enforced: the version constant must carry at least the required bump against the baseline's version, an information type with additionalProperties: false fails outright, and new event tags are recorded only through the update script. After a change to a wire type, a method, or a version constant, run crates/protocol/scripts/update-compat-baseline.sh, which refuses an insufficient bump, and commit the result. The update replaces only the surface directories; the frozen corpora in crates/protocol/compat/corpus/ are never regenerated.

docs.title: Corpora
docs.text:
The baselines show what a schema allows; the corpora in crates/protocol/compat/corpus/ show what peers actually sent, and the tests replay them against the current code:

  • <surface>/<version>/*.jsonl, for client, plugin, and runtime: conversations recorded at that version, one JSON-RPC message per line as {"from": <side>, "message": <message>}, in the order they crossed the connection. client/1.0.0/session.jsonl is a TUI-like session against a daemon with a scripted model: handshake, catalog, session, subscription, an image upload, a run whose bash call waits for approval while two steers arrive, the approval, and reads of the session and the artifact. runtime/1.0.0/coding.jsonl is the daemon and its local coding runtime during that session. plugin/1.0.0/reference.jsonl is the scripted conversation of check_reference_plugin.py with the reference plugin.
  • future/*.json: what a newer peer may send each reader: unknown members, enum values, event tags, display block kinds, methods, and notifications.

The replays prove that a new build accepts old data. Recorded client requests are answered by a fresh daemon as they were (a session, run, upload, or approval ID the replay's own replies hand out replaces the recorded one); recorded replies and notifications read with the current client without a diagnostic or an unknown event; the daemon's plugin and runtime messages drive a plugin built with the Rust SDK and the coding runtime; and what plugins and runtimes sent reads as the daemon reads it. Each test also reads the recorded information with an unknown member added to every object, which must change nothing, and the future/ fixtures of its reader.

A recorded version directory is frozen: the tests check it against a digest pinned in cookie_agent_protocol::corpus::FROZEN and fail when it changed, and no COOKIE_UPDATE_* switch applies to it. A later minor records its own <surface>/<version>/ directory beside the earlier ones and pins it. The recorders write the current versions and refuse a directory that exists:

COOKIE_RECORD_CORPUS=crates/protocol/compat/corpus \
  cargo test -p cookie_agent_server -- --ignored record_the_client_and_runtime_corpora
python3 examples/plugins/python/check_reference_plugin.py --record crates/protocol/compat/corpus

The module documentation of cookie_agent_protocol::corpus (behind the crate's test-support feature) lists the tests of every crate.

The Rust API documentation describes the public Rust types; the protocol reference summarizes the active method surface.

docs.title: System Prompt Composition
docs.text: Cookie Agent keeps the system prompt deliberately small and inspectable. The Markdown body of the selected agent document is the base prompt. Parsing removes only trailing newlines and restores one final newline; frontmatter configures the agent but is not copied into prompt text.

docs.title: Composition order
docs.text:
For a root or delegated run, the engine composes the model request in this order:

  1. The selected agent document body becomes AgentSnapshot.composed_prompt.
  2. Where the session's runtimes work is appended (see Runtimes): the working directory, or the list of runtimes when there are several. The prompt and document fingerprints are updated.
  3. Tool providers may append bounded behavioral-policy sections. Sections retain provider provenance and update both prompt and document fingerprints.
  4. If skills are visible to the model, a generated available-skills listing is appended to that prompt. The prompt and document fingerprints are updated.
  5. agent_before_start plugins run in configured order. A plugin can replace the composed prompt or append an addendum, subject to the 128 KiB prompt limit. Each accepted change recomputes the prompt fingerprint.
  6. History assembly puts the final composed prompt in history[0] as the sole system turn.
  7. Root runs may then add a durable AGENTS.md context user turn. The memory snapshot follows when the session's latest snapshot is not empty, then loaded skill bodies as user turns, followed by normal session history.

Appended blocks are joined by a markdown horizontal rule ( --- ) so the boundaries between the authored body, the runtimes block, tool-provider sections, the skills listing, and a plugin addendum are visible. The authored body is first and carries no leading separator; a plugin replace_system_prompt replaces the whole prompt instead of appending to it.

The resulting agent snapshot is frozen in run_started. Model retries and fallbacks reuse that run policy and prompt fingerprint; configuration refreshes cannot alter an admitted run. Request assembly reuses the first event snapshot for the first attempt and refreshes session events only when a later attempt needs current history.

docs.title: Fingerprints
docs.text:
The document fingerprint covers the agent identity, strict frontmatter, and body. The prompt fingerprint covers prompt text only. The runtimes block, tool-provider sections, skill listings, and plugin composition update the effective fingerprints before run_started is persisted. Model-attempt events record the prompt fingerprint, and replay validation rejects attempt attribution that contradicts the frozen run snapshot.

AGENTS.md context and the memory snapshot are intentionally excluded from the system-prompt fingerprint. Each has its own durable event, provenance, and user-role boundary.

docs.title: Tool-provider sections
docs.text:
Tool providers can contribute cross-tool behavioral policy at run admission: built-in providers, plugins, and runtimes over the runtime protocol. Each section is normalized, validated, and rendered with an engine-derived identity:

<tool_instructions provider="builtin.delegate">
Available subagents:
- sub-fixer: Coder for anything that touches code
</tool_instructions>
