docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Use /sessions to search and open saved sessions, or /new for a fresh root. Selecting a saved session restores its visible transcript; submitting another message continues it. A headless continuation uses:

cookie run --resume-session <session-id> "Continue the investigation"

See Command line for selection overrides. For shortening model context without removing the saved log, see Compaction.

docs.title: Lifecycle and persistence
docs.text:
A new empty session exists only in memory. Its directory, metadata cache, and event JSONL are created atomically when the first user message is submitted. Closing an empty session leaves no persisted session.

Persisted sessions use an append-only JSONL history. New events are stamped with the writing engine version for diagnostics, but opening a session does not require an exact version match. The engine reads what a newer build wrote tolerantly: it ignores members it does not know, skips unknown audit events, quarantines records that do not agree with the rest of the log, reports what it skipped in session metadata, and tolerates the resulting sequence gaps (Event Reference). The derived metadata file is only a cache: missing, stale, mismatched, or unreadable cache content is rebuilt from the event history. Streamed text, reasoning, and tool progress are live-only: they reach attached views but are never written to events.jsonl, whose history holds finished turns and tool results. Reattaching to a session while a reply streams shows its finished turns, then the reply from the next live output on; a daemon that dies mid-reply leaves no partial reply on disk, and the run reopens as interrupted. Every stored event is written before it is published, and every event recovery depends on is also synced first. Per-attempt bookkeeping (model_attempt_started, model_tools_published, model_request_prepared, model_replay_evaluated, model_output_started, model_usage_recorded) is synced by the next event that is, so a system crash can drop only such records at the end of the log. While a run is in flight, fold-ignored records do not rewrite the metadata tip (last_event_seq, last_activity); it catches up at the run's next projection change or terminal event, on eviction, and on shutdown.

Shutting the daemon down cleanly cancels whatever runs are in flight and waits, under a short bound, for them to record RunCancelled; a run only comes back as interrupted by daemon restart when the process died without that chance.

Reopening a session adopts it: the engine reconciles that session's interrupted work and then waits, under a short bound, for the delegation recovery the adoption scheduled. Background subagents whose runs died with the previous process are therefore already settled — marked interrupted, reported to their parent, and their concurrency slots released — by the time the session is usable again.

Use /new to create a fresh root session and /sessions to search and switch between sessions. Delegated sessions form a tree beneath the root that created them. The Agents panel lists each session's subagents by their latest user-initiated activity, newest first: a user input submitted or admitted, or a delegate_subagent call started. Output and tool results never reorder it. Session metadata carries this time as last_agent_activity, so a reopened session orders its subagents the same way before any of them is replayed. Accepted runs retain their frozen model binding even if catalog, configuration, or provider-store state changes later.

Several cookie processes may share one project directory, but a root session and every delegated session beneath it are written by one process at a time: ownership is taken for the whole tree, not for a single session. Reopening any session of a tree another process still has open reports session is owned by another cookie process, for the root and its subagents alike. Such a session is still readable — the TUI shows it as a read-only snapshot with input disabled — and becomes writable once the process holding the tree exits. Adopting one session of a free tree claims the tree, while each session in it still reconciles its own interrupted work the first time it is written.

docs.title: History formats
docs.text:
A session log records its history format. A build that reads a newer format cannot open the session and asks for a newer cookie. A build that reads an older one converts it the first time it takes the session's tree for writing, keeping each original log beside the new one as events.jsonl.v<N>.bak; a read-only view converts in memory only. To convert every session up front instead:

cookie sessions upgrade        # the sessions of this directory
cookie sessions upgrade --all  # the sessions of every directory

It reports each tree it converted, each it skipped because another cookie process holds it (that process converts it itself), and each session it cannot convert, such as one written before history formats, and exits nonzero when there was one. The backups stay until you delete them.

docs.title: Titles
docs.text: Root sessions may generate a title from their opening user messages according to the Session Title configuration. A delegated session is titled immediately from the delegate_subagent description instead. The description is bounded by session_title.max_chars, and the delegated child does not run the title internal agent.

docs.title: Revert
docs.text:
Revert is available only while the session is idle. It removes every event after the selected positive sequence from events.jsonl; new events reuse the freed sequence numbers. A run left holding nothing but its start goes with it, and a run the cut falls inside is closed as interrupted, along with its open tool calls, internal agents, and approvals. Subagent sessions created by the removed delegations are deleted, together with their own subagents; a revert that would delete a running subagent is refused. A revert cannot be undone: fork first to keep the current branch.

In the TUI, click a past user message, choose Revert, and confirm. The TUI targets the sequence immediately before that user message and restores the message text to the composer for editing.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
Deleting a session removes its whole tree from disk: the root session, every subagent session under it, their events.jsonl and metadata, and the tree's artifacts (uploads and retained tool output). Only a root can be deleted; a subagent goes with its root. Its background calls are stopped without reporting. A delete cannot be undone: fork first to keep a copy, since a fork holds its own copy of the artifacts.

The daemon refuses while any session of the tree is running or compacting, while another cookie process owns the tree, and when the root gained events since the client showed it, such as another client's new turn. It moves the tree's directory aside first and then removes it, so a crash in between leaves only a .deleted-… directory, which the next start removes. Every client is told the sessions are gone.

In the TUI, open /sessions, highlight the session, press Ctrl+D (or Delete while the list has focus), and confirm with y. In the web client, use the trash icon on the session's row. See session.delete.

docs.title: Fork
docs.text:
Fork copies a persisted prefix containing at least one submitted user message into a new independent session. It may read an active source session. Copied events retain their sequence numbers, timestamps, run IDs, and payloads, while their envelope is rebound to the new session ID. Shared content-addressed artifacts remain resolvable without copying their bytes.

A fork does not take its source's subagents. The conversation comes along, including what the subagents reported, but the subagents stay the source's: the fork starts with no children, get_subagent_result refuses the source's, and the fork creates its own when it delegates. Each delegation record the fork leaves behind is replaced by a record_omitted event (see Events).

A fork of a root session is a new root, with a tree of its own, and may be taken from a session another process owns. A fork of a delegated session stays inside its source's tree, so it is published into that root's directory and needs that tree's ownership: forking a subagent of a tree another process holds fails with session_owned_elsewhere ("This session is open in another cookie process.").

In the TUI, choose Fork from a user message. That message is included in the copied prefix, the new title receives (fork), and the new session is selected.

docs.title: Compaction
docs.text:
Compaction reduces a long session history to a checkpoint. Internal compaction keeps a budgeted tail of recent messages unchanged and summarizes everything before it; the summary replaces those older messages in model context, and the original saved log is preserved. Provider-native compaction instead stores an opaque provider window.

Active history means the currently assembled context before compaction, including any existing summary and the messages after it. It does not reload historical events already replaced by earlier checkpoints.

docs.title: Native provider compaction
docs.text:
OpenAI Responses and Azure OpenAI Responses models can opt into provider-native compaction. The native operation runs first. If the adapter rejects the assembled request, the provider call fails, or the returned opaque window is invalid, Cookie Agent automatically runs the existing internal compaction agent.

Enable it on a managed provider model override with compaction = "openai-responses-compact" or compaction = "azure-responses-compact". Cookie Agent derives the native model capability from that setting. Other adaptors reject the setting. Azure also requires the managed provider identity azure.openai plus model, version, and deployment_type in the provider setup table so the window is scoped to an explicit deployment.

This deployment-metadata requirement is specific to native compaction, not ordinary Azure replay. Native windows retain their exact scope checks; the portable-block replay rules do not permit moving a compaction window to an incompatible provider or deployment.

A native checkpoint stores a bounded opaque provider window rather than summary text. Events through the checkpoint boundary are omitted from normal history, no framed summary message is inserted, and the window is attached to the next request. Later native compactions are seeded with the previous window. The window has a 32 MiB cap; max_summary_bytes applies only to text summaries. Native windows remain unchanged by recent-history retention: the engine does not append an independent recent-message tail to them. Neither native nor internal compaction rereads files.

docs.title: The trigger threshold
docs.text:
Triggers are measured against the model's input budget, the number of tokens a request may occupy:

input_budget = model_input_limit                     when the model declares one
input_budget = model_context_limit - output_reserve  otherwise
output_reserve = min(max_output_tokens, 32000, model_context_limit / 2)

Catalog models take the input limit from models.dev limit.input when it is narrower than the context window (for example gpt-5: 400,000 context, 272,000 input); custom models declare it as capabilities.input_tokens. max_output_tokens is the output cap the run sends (see agent limits), by default the model's full output limit. The reserve is capped at 32,000 tokens so a large output limit does not claim a big share of the window, and at half the context so a model whose output limit equals its context window keeps a usable budget.

By default, compaction uses a proportional trigger:

trigger_tokens = input_budget * percent / 100

percent defaults to 70, so a model with a 200,000-token context window and a 64,000-token output limit triggers at 117,600 tokens, and gpt-5 at 190,400. Valid percentages are 1 through 99; 100 is rejected because compaction at the model limit does not preserve useful request headroom.

The fixed-buffer form preserves the earlier behavior:

trigger_tokens = input_budget - buffer_tokens

This subtraction saturates at zero. If the buffer equals or exceeds the input budget, the trigger becomes 0 and automatic compaction is disabled for that model.

Before each model request, the engine compares the input + output tokens the provider reported for the latest model turn against the threshold, and compacts when they reach it. Usage recorded before the latest checkpoint is ignored, so a fresh checkpoint waits for the next reported turn. Messages added since the latest turn, such as a new prompt or steering input, are not counted until the provider reports them, and they are kept verbatim only when they fit the recent history budget (see step 4 below). If a request still exceeds the provider's context length, the engine compacts once regardless of the threshold and retries.

docs.title: What happens when it triggers
docs.text:
1. Native attempt. An opted-in Responses model first attempts native compaction. A successful native window goes directly to checkpoint commit, without selecting independent recent messages. Otherwise, or after any native failure, the engine uses internal summarization. Native compaction uses the bound model's context limit minus the effective compaction output allowance. If that allowance is unknown, the engine reserves 20,000 tokens as conservative summary-output headroom.
  2. Recent-history selection. For internal summarization, the engine first selects a contiguous suffix of original messages to keep unchanged. Its effective token target is at most min(keep_recent_tokens, input_budget / 4), using integer division, and is further limited by actual available space in the post-checkpoint request. System and tool context, pinned context, the summary, and the output reserve must still fit. Tool calls and their results are retained as complete groups, never split at the suffix boundary. If the newest indivisible group exceeds the target, no tail is retained; the engine does not exceed the target or substitute an older, noncontiguous group. keep_recent_tokens = 0 disables the tail.
  3. Replaced-span trial. The summarizer receives only the span the checkpoint replaces: the active, unpruned history up to the selected suffix, including any earlier summary. The suffix itself is never sent. The request keeps the session's own system prompt, pinned context, and tool definitions, so it is a cache-friendly prefix of the latest conversation request; the compaction agent's prompt rides along in a trailing instruction message instead of replacing the session system prompt. A tool-call answer is rejected as non-text output and counts as a compaction failure. The provider is authoritative for internal-agent input size; there is no byte-based pre-flight admission gate. The session's calibrated estimator still sizes the retained recent history and the post-checkpoint budget.
  4. Context-fit retry. A provider context-length failure permits one pruned retry. Other failures do not trigger pruning. Internal model bindings are tried in order, advancing after provider failures. The retry uses an in-memory copy of the same replaced span and drops the session tool definitions (cache affinity is already lost once tool outputs are rewritten): tool results are retained with ArtifactStore::retain and replaced by reference markers with a structured read_artifact hint carrying artifact="<digest>". Saved ArtifactReference URIs remain unchanged. The session tree can read the retained artifact back with read_artifact. Structured tool content is retained as serialized JSON, not flattened into original output; the marker labels this format. All outputs of read_artifact calls are replaced with [artifact read output omitted for compaction] in the private retry input, including named-stream reads. Detection uses the tool name; ordinary filesystem read results follow normal tool-output pruning. This does not emit durable tool_output_elided (ToolOutputElided) events or change the original saved log or the retained recent messages, even if the retry fails.
  5. Summary. The internal compaction agent (see Internal agents) writes a structured checkpoint with fixed sections (objective, requirements, decisions, work state, files, commands and errors, next step, important context). When the replaced span starts with an earlier internal summary, the prompt asks it to merge that summary into one updated checkpoint instead of starting fresh. An authored compaction.md can extend or replace this prompt with placeholders, and the user's focus text is added to it. It must return summary text only, at most max_summary_bytes (256 KiB by default); non-text output is rejected. The built-in compaction document sets no output cap of its own, so it inherits the owner run's max_output_tokens, bounded by the model's own output limit; the same inheritance applies to any authored internal-agent document that omits the limit. A nonzero limits.max_output_tokens in compaction.md overrides the inherited value. The suffix-selection output reserve equals that same effective cap. The built-in compaction document uses a flat 3-minute timeout. An authored compaction.md can override limits.timeout_ms; the configured value is honored exactly, while zero or omission uses the 30-second internal-agent default.
  6. Checkpoint commit. A context_checkpoint_committed event records the text summary or opaque native window, source and recent-suffix boundaries, and the budget math, including the effective recent-history token budget. Retained messages come from saved history, not new file reads.

docs.title: Context after an internal checkpoint
docs.text:
The next request assembles context in this order:

  1. System prompt and tool definitions.
  2. Pinned AGENTS.md context.
  3. Pinned loaded skill bodies.
  4. Summary of everything before the retained suffix.
  5. Recent original messages retained unchanged, followed by any new messages.

Pinned context is preserved separately from the suffix. With retention disabled, or when the newest complete group cannot fit, the recent suffix is absent and only the summary remains alongside pinned context. The summary and the retained suffix do not overlap. Native checkpoints continue to use their opaque provider windows rather than this summary-and-tail layout.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: See Context Compaction for settings, defaults, trigger forms, and inheritance.

docs.title: Manual compaction
docs.text:
Choosing /compact in the command palette forces a checkpoint for the selected idle session. The palette then asks for an optional focus, for example:

preserve the parser decisions and failing test evidence

Press Enter with the prompt empty to compact without a focus. The focus text is added to the compaction prompt (appended, or placed where an authored compaction.md puts {{focus}}) so the summary emphasizes the areas you care about. Steering remains available while compaction runs; admitted pending inputs are promoted only after the checkpoint, honoring any recalls made during compaction. A message sent to an idle session that is compacting, from this or another client, waits for the compaction to finish and then starts its run.

To stop a manual compaction, press Ctrl-C (or Esc twice) while the session shows compacting, as you would to cancel a run; session.compact.cancel does the same over the protocol. A cancelled compaction commits no checkpoint.

session.compact returns whether a checkpoint was actually committed. Manual compaction follows the same recent-history selection, replaced-span trial, and context-fit retry rules.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Compaction produces these event payloads:

  • internal_agent_started / internal_agent_finished / internal_agent_fallback — the compaction agent invocation
  • internal_agent_text_delta (live-only) — the summary as it streams
  • native_compaction_started / native_compaction_finished (live-only) — a provider-native compaction call

While compaction runs, the TUI shows a 🧹 compacting context… row and the bottom bar reads compacting. Expanded, the row streams the summary, or reads calling native compaction endpoint (model) during a native call. When compaction finishes, the row is replaced by the context compacted checkpoint row, or removed if compaction failed. A failed native call hands the row to the summarizer fallback. - context_checkpoint_committed — the checkpoint with boundaries and budgets

The internal summarizer's in-memory pruning retry does not produce tool_output_elided events.

See the event reference for checkpoint retention fields.

docs.title: Goal Mode
docs.text:
Goal mode lets you give a root session a durable objective and a checklist the agent maintains while it works. It is activated explicitly: the engine never infers a goal from prompt content, and only root sessions can have one.

The goal mode design spec describes the runtime, plugin, and persistence contracts behind this workflow.

docs.title: Activation and goal bar
docs.text:
Activate goal mode in the root session by choosing /goal in the command palette and entering the objective in the prompt that follows. An empty objective is refused in place, and Esc returns to the command list. Outside a root session, or in a read-only one, the palette explains why instead of prompting.

A persistent one-line goal bar appears above the message composer whenever the selected session has a goal. Click its objective description to open a detail modal with the full objective, checklist, and lifecycle status. The checklist view is read-only; the root agent maintains it through its items-only update tool.

Use the bar's Pause or Resume button and Cancel button to control an active or paused goal. From the keyboard, F6 focuses the bar, Left/Right or Tab move between its controls, Enter activates one, and Esc returns to the composer. Completed and cancelled goals keep a read-only bar and detail view; the bar is hidden when no goal exists. The producer queue strip is separate and appears above the goal bar and composer.

Setting a new objective errors if a goal is already active or paused; cancel or complete the current goal first.

A goal moves through four lifecycle states: active, paused, completed, and cancelled. Completed and cancelled are terminal. Only you control the lifecycle: the agent can read and revise the checklist through its tools, but it cannot activate, pause, resume, or cancel a goal.

docs.title: Checklist and tools
docs.text:
While a goal is active or paused, the root run gains two extra tools, goal_get and goal_update. They are root-only: delegated child sessions never see them, and there is no goal inheritance into subagents. They are also not a configurable capability; they cannot be granted to anything else. The tools appear or disappear at the next run start after a lifecycle change, never mid-run.

goal_get and goal_update declare no permission. Setting the goal is what makes them available, and they act on that goal alone, so permission rules do not govern them and every call is allowed.

Each checklist item contains only a description and a finished flag, with no item ID. goal_update { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist of the current/latest session goal when the engine actor accepts the update. The engine serializes updates: the last accepted replacement wins, with no model-supplied goal ID, revision check, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal. Updates reject if the current goal is absent, completed, or cancelled. The engine still numbers durable state revisions for reminders and user lifecycle controls; those controls retain their goal-ID and expected-revision checks. The root checklist is the authoritative record of progress: the agent is instructed to verify work directly or through subagents before marking an item finished, and to trust its own checklist over any subagent's self-report.

Completion has one automatic rule. When a checklist update leaves the checklist non-empty and every item finished, the goal is recorded as completed. An empty checklist preserves the current active or paused state and never completes a goal: activating a goal with no checklist yet still starts work, and the initial goal message asks the agent to establish the checklist.

Checklist updates are also preserved while a goal is paused, including an all-finished update, which records completion without scheduling any further work.

docs.title: Continuations
docs.text:
While a goal is active, the engine can wake an idle session with a message carrying the full objective and the entire checklist. The first delivery says Goal started and asks the agent to establish the checklist if it is empty. Later reminders say Continue the root goal.

The distinction comes from committed model input, not from merely accepting or claiming a queued reminder. If the startup message is discarded before delivery, the next eligible message still says Goal started. A consumed introduction survives restart and pause/resume, while activating a new goal starts fresh.

A goal message is scheduled only when all of the following hold:

  • the goal is active, and the checklist is empty or has unfinished items;
  • the session is idle (no active run);
  • no pending user, steer, or queued messages exist;
  • no other live producer registration (background delegation or plugin) exists;
  • no goal reminder is already pending.

The condition is rechecked when the run actually starts, so real work that arrives in between always wins. Because the reminder re-injects the objective and checklist, compaction cannot strand the goal.

docs.title: Pause, cancel, and interruption
docs.text:
Pausing or cancelling a goal stops future goal continuations. The engine also durably queues a steering notification before closing the producer registration if the root has an active run, other live producers (excluding the goal's own registration), or queued real messages. This includes an idle root waiting for subagent results or plugin work. At the next safe model API request, the model is told that the goal was paused or cancelled, to stop autonomous pursuit of that old goal, and to follow your directions. These are durable lifecycle-control messages, separate from continuation reminders, so closing the goal controller does not remove them.

Because the notification uses steer delivery, it can wake a normal root run when the root is idle but has other producers or queued real messages. That wake does not resume goal reminders: the goal remains paused or cancelled. A fully idle root with no other live producers and no queued real messages saves the lifecycle change without starting an announcement run. The goal's own registration or pending reminder alone does not trigger one.

This does not cancel an in-flight request, abort active delegations, or undo actions already emitted. The existing explicit interrupt (/cancel) remains unchanged and separate from goal lifecycle controls. Checklist updates still target the current session goal at actor acceptance; the notification does not bind an older run's updates to its former goal.

docs.title: Producers: plugins and background work
docs.text:
Background delegation results and plugin-originated messages reach the session through runtime producer registrations. Registrations are runtime-only: they vanish on restart. Messages that were accepted before a restart are durable, and accepted-but-unconsumed messages that have not been discarded are delivered after recovery even if their producer never re-registers.

Each message is sent in one of two modes, chosen per send:

  • Steer — inserted into the next model API request, including mid-run at a tool boundary. It never cancels an in-flight request. Background subagent results always steer; a steer to an idle session starts a normal run.
  • Queue — starts a subsequent normal run. While a run is active it is persisted and deferred, then delivered when the session is idle.

Pending and admitted producer messages in either mode appear in the existing queue strip above the goal bar and composer, which automatically shows and hides with its contents. Messages reserved for a model request are hidden while claimed; release after a failed/cancelled attempt returns them to the strip unless already consumed or discarded. Discarded messages are removed from the strip. Producer messages cannot be recalled into the user composer; displaying them does not make them user-authored input.

The producer's owner can discard its own waiting message through the producer discard API, even after unregistering, because accepted messages are independent of runtime registrations. Discard is durable and retrying an owned already-discarded message is idempotent; another owner cannot discard it. Only unclaimed waiting messages qualify, including admitted messages not yet reserved by the engine. Reservation happens before provider dispatch, so a claimed message cannot be discarded even if the provider has not received it yet. Releasing all claims makes an unconsumed, undiscarded message waiting again. In-flight or consumed input cannot be retracted, and discard cannot undo actions already taken.

After a restart, producer-capable plugins reconstruct their own pending work from their own storage or the external services they front; the engine does not replay plugin state for them. A goal's automatic continuation waits until all tracked producer-capable plugins report ready, so recovered external work can register before the agent resumes. A failed or disabled producer is surfaced as a notification and holds goal continuation; it is not silently treated as work done. Already accepted real messages can still be delivered.

There are no watchdogs or deadlines for producers. A producer that registers and then stalls stays visible in the runtime inspection API (a read-only snapshot of registrations) and blocks automatic goal continuations, but no TUI command manufactures a wake around it. A plugin that never finishes startup recovery can likewise keep the readiness barrier waiting indefinitely. The engine also makes no exactly-once claim: a producer that does not see an acknowledgment retries with the same sender-chosen idempotency key, and the engine deduplicates the retry, but external side effects of a repeated attempt are the producer's own concern.

docs.title: Attaching Media
docs.text: A message can carry images, PDFs, audio, and video alongside its text, when the session's model accepts them. The daemon stores each attachment in the session's artifact store and sends it to the model as a file.

docs.title: What a model accepts
docs.text:
Every model in the catalog view states its input_media: the kinds it accepts in a message, the media types of each, and the limits that apply (see The catalog view). The limits are the lowest of the model's own, its provider's for a message, and the daemon's caps: 20 MiB per file, 25 MiB for video, and at most 16384 pixels a side and 16 Mi pixels for an image. A client offers attachments only for the kinds the selected model accepts and checks a file before sending it.

For example, an Anthropic model that accepts PNG and JPEG images and PDFs takes images of up to 7.5 MiB and PDFs of up to 20 MiB, and no video; a Gemini model takes each kind it accepts up to 14 MiB, which keeps the whole request within the Gemini API's limit.

docs.title: Attaching a file
docs.text:
A client uploads the file into the session first, then names it in the message:

  1. artifact.upload.begin with the session, the file's size, and its name.
  2. artifact.upload.chunk for each piece of at most 1 MiB, in order.
  3. artifact.upload.finish with the file's SHA-256. The daemon recognizes the file by its content (the name never decides its type), checks it, and returns the reference to send.
  4. run.start, run.steer, or session.submit_input with content holding the text and a file part with that reference.

The protocol reference lists every rule and error. An upload the connection leaves unfinished is dropped when it closes.

The daemon checks every attachment again when the message arrives, against the model the message goes to. An attachment the model does not accept, one over its limits, or more of a kind than it takes refuses the message, and nothing of it is recorded; the error says which limit, so a client can offer to downscale an image that is too large.

docs.title: In the terminal UI
docs.text: /attach asks for a file's path and attaches the file to the next message, and pasting the path of one existing file (what a terminal pastes when a file is dropped on it) offers to attach it. Both appear only while the selected model accepts some kind of file. The TUI checks the file's kind, size, and an image's pixels against the model's limits before it uploads, and shows the limit when a file is refused, by the TUI or the daemon; it does not downscale. Attachments show on the composer's border as 📎 name · type · size, and Backspace at the start of the draft removes the newest. See Terminal UI.

docs.title: When the model changes
docs.text:
A session can move to another model, or a run can fall back to one. A model that does not accept a file in the history is sent a short note in its place, such as:

[image omitted: acme/text-model does not accept images (screenshot.png, 471 KB)]

The saved history keeps the file, so a later model that accepts it sees it again. Compaction summaries never see media: the summarizer reads notes in place of every file.

docs.title: How long a file is kept
docs.text:
An uploaded file no message references is kept for an hour, then removed. Once a message names it, it lives as long as the session history references it: a revert that removes every message naming it removes the file once its hour is up, and a fork takes it into the forked session. A daemon restart forgets the hour; a file no message referenced then stays in the store.

Any artifact of a session, an uploaded file, a tool's attachment, or the full output behind a truncated tool display, can be read back with artifact.read.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Memory is what Cookie Agent keeps between sessions: Markdown notes that the agent and you write, which later sessions see or find again. It belongs to the global runtime, so a session has memory while global is attached; detaching global turns it off for that session. Memory is gathered context: reading or writing it never changes a session's attachments, runtimes, or workspaces. The memory spec has the full design.

docs.title: Layers and files
docs.text:
Each memory is one Markdown file with a short frontmatter, in ~/.cookie-agent/memory (the memory folder of the data root):

memory/
  user/<category>.md            user://<category>
  agents/<agent>.md             agent://<agent>
  machines/<machine>/<name>.md  machine://<machine>/<name>
  projects/<project>/<name>.md  project://<project>/<name>
Layer About Created by Deleted by user You, in every task: profile, preferences, feedback, references You only (the agent may edit existing categories) You only; the agent's delete clears the body agent One agent's way of doing its job, such as what you want from reviews The daemon, one for every agent (Agent memory) You; the daemon removes an empty one it made when its agent goes; the agent's delete clears the body machine One machine: OS quirks, toolchains, paths, rules such as "read-only unless asked" The agent or you The agent or you project One body of work: conventions, decisions, gotchas The agent or you; the first memory creates the project The agent or you; the project goes with its last memory

The first time the daemon starts without a memory folder, it creates the four layer folders and the categories profile, preferences, feedback, and references with empty bodies. Add a category by creating a file in user/.

---
description: Build and test conventions for cookie-agent
keywords: [cargo, clippy, msrv, no-fail-fast, cookie-agent]
---
- Run `cargo test --no-fail-fast`; plain `cargo test` stops at the first
  failing crate.

description is required (one line, 1 to 200 characters); keywords is an optional list of up to 32 search terms. Names are a lowercase letter or digit followed by up to 63 lowercase letters, digits, or -; machine folders use machine names. A file that breaks these rules, or is larger than [memory] max_file_bytes (Memory [memory]), is invalid: search and the snapshot skip it. You may edit the files with any editor; a session that writes a memory you changed since it read it gets an error naming the current revision instead of overwriting your edit.

docs.title: Agent memory
docs.text:
The daemon keeps one agents/<agent>.md for every agent of the shared agent set and of every preset, internal agents (approval, compaction, title) aside. It makes the missing ones at start and after every configuration reload or config.apply, with an empty body, and writes nothing when there is nothing to do.

The daemon owns two things in each file:

  • The description: Memory of the `<agent>` agent: <description>, with the agent document's description on one line and the whole cut to 200 characters. When an ID is in the shared set and in presets, the shared document is used; otherwise the preset that comes first alphabetically. Changing the agent document's description rewrites it.
  • Two keywords: the agent ID and the agent's mode (primary, subagent, or all; one keyword when the ID is the mode's name). You and the agent may add more; the daemon keeps them and puts its two back first when they are removed.

So a write of an agent's file, by the agent or by you, keeps the daemon's description and keywords: memory_write and memory_edit say what they kept, and /memory and cookie memory edit show the daemon's notice after saving. The body is the agent's: it starts empty, and an empty one is left out of the model's memory turn entirely.

When an agent leaves every agent set, its file is removed only if the daemon made it and nobody touched it: the body is empty, and the description and keywords are exactly the daemon's. A file with notes stays, and /memory and memory.list mark it as belonging to no current agent.

docs.title: Managing memory
docs.text:
In the TUI, /memory lists every layer: the user categories, each agent's file, and the machine and project memories grouped by machine and project, with invalid files marked and, at the end, anything in the memory folder that is not a memory, each with the reason. Enter opens the selected memory in $VISUAL or $EDITOR, frontmatter included; saving writes it at the revision it read. n creates a memory, starting from the URL of the selected layer, machine, or project, and d deletes the selected one after you confirm. Every action is also a button under the details. When the text you saved is not a valid memory, e reopens it as you left it; when the memory changed since you opened it, nothing is overwritten: r reloads the current version into the editor, and o overwrites it with your edit. The panel refreshes when a memory changes through the daemon, by you, another client, or the agent.

From a terminal, cookie memory lists, edits, and deletes memories through the daemon, so it works against a remote daemon as well (--url and --token, or [server] in config.toml, as for cookie config):

cookie memory list                      # every layer, invalid files with the reason
cookie memory list project              # one layer: user, agent, machine, or project
cookie memory edit project://web/build  # in $VISUAL or $EDITOR; created when absent
cookie memory rm machine://labpc/gpu    # asks first; --yes does not

edit opens the whole file, frontmatter included, and saves it at the revision it read. Text that is not a valid memory is offered again as you left it; a memory that changed since you opened it is not overwritten, and you can reload it and edit the current version. You may add and remove user:// categories and remove agent:// files, which the agent cannot. An agent:// file can be created only for an agent that exists; a file whose agent was removed or renamed stays and is listed as belonging to no current agent. Your edits never change the snapshot of an open session; it sees them when it next takes one.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: The machine layer is keyed by machine names, the computers runtimes run on, which the daemon assigns on its own and you can rename, merge, and forget from the Machines view of /runtime or with cookie machine (see Machines). A machine's memories live in memory/machines/<machine>/ and move with it when it is renamed or merged into another; machines.list and cookie machine list count them.

docs.title: What the model sees
docs.text:
At the start of a run that has memory, the model gets a snapshot as one user turn after the AGENTS.md turn: every user category, the run's agent's own file, and an index of the memories of the machines the session's attachments run on. Project memories are never shown; the model searches for the project a task belongs to. An agent file with an empty body adds nothing. The system prompt reference shows the exact text.

The snapshot is taken once and kept, so the provider's prompt cache survives writes. It is taken again only at a run's start when the session has none yet, after a compaction, when the session's machines or the run's agent changed, or when the run gained or lost memory or write access. Edits you make to the files reach open sessions at those points, and new sessions at once.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
The global runtime offers five tools (Tools):

Tool Does memory_search Searches every memory by keywords, names, descriptions, and bodies, and shows each result as far as the memory rules for its URL allow memory_read Reads one memory with its revision memory_write Creates a memory, or replaces one at the revision it read; keywords may be left out, and description too for the agent's file, whose description the daemon sets memory_edit Replaces one occurrence of a text in a memory's body memory_delete Deletes a machine:// or project:// memory. A user:// or agent:// memory cannot be deleted: its body is cleared, and the file stays with its description and keywords

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The tools use two permission actions with the memory URL as resource: memory for searching and reading, memory_write for writing, editing, and deleting. An agent document that names neither gets defaults by mode: primary and all agents may read and write all memory, subagent agents may read all memory and write their own agent:// file, and internal agents get none. A declared key replaces the default, so memory: deny turns memory off for an agent. See Memory defaults.

permissions:
  memory:
    "agent://reviewer": deny
    "*": allow
  memory_write:
    "user://*": ask
    "agent://self": allow
    "project://*": allow

agent://self in a rule stands for the run's own agent. An agent without a memory rule gets neither the snapshot nor any memory tool, even with memory_write rules.

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text: A delegated run sees only its own agent's memory in its snapshot and may write only its own agent://<agent> file, whatever its rules say; it can still search and read every layer its memory rules allow. Only the root agent decides what to keep about you, machines, and projects.

docs.title: Usage and Cost
docs.text:
Cookie agent records normalized provider usage after every committed model turn and completed internal-agent model request. Records include inclusive input and output token totals and cache read or write counts when the provider reports them. Anthropic cache creation maps to cache writes and cache reads map directly; OpenAI cached_tokens maps to cache reads. GPT-5.6+ can additionally report cache_write_tokens, which maps to cache writes when supplied by the provider adapter. Cohere cached_tokens similarly records server-side automatic cache reads. Providers that omit a field leave it unknown rather than estimating it.

The event log is the source of truth. Session rollups and their per-model rows are rebuilt from the session's log when it is loaded and obey revert/fork visibility. Session-tree rollups combine the selected session with all of its delegated descendants, including descendants that have been evicted from memory. There are no rollups across sessions: usage is always read for one session or one session tree.

Open /usage in the TUI to compare the selected session with its session-tree totals. Programmatic clients can call session.usage and session.tree_usage. Cache hit rate is cache-read tokens divided by inclusive input tokens. It is unavailable unless every included request reports both fields; an explicitly reported zero remains a 0% hit rate.

Each TUI section shows formatted totals and a per-model table. Models are sorted by descending estimated cost, with unpriced models last, then by input tokens and model name. Token counts use thousands separators, cache hit rates use one decimal place, and costs use two decimal places at or above one cent and four below it. Use the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, or the mouse wheel when the panel content exceeds its viewport.

When a request is priced, the assistant block's closing footer includes its estimated cost after generation speed and context usage. The bottom bar shows the selected session total; clicking it opens /usage. Unpriced costs are omitted from both locations.

Cost is always optional. Managed models use the selected models.dev catalog price tier for each request's reported input-token context size. Model-specific entries under [providers.<provider>.models.<model>.pricing] supply prices for custom models or override catalog prices, as described in the model pricing reference. The precedence is config override, catalog, then no cost. An aggregate remains unpriced when any used model lacks a required rate or when a provider omits a usage split needed to apply a distinct cache or reasoning price.

Cache economics are model-specific. In particular, current GPT-5.6+ pricing charges reads and writes differently, while earlier OpenAI models use model-tier-dependent cached-input discounts. The selected catalog model's cache_read and cache_write rates, or explicit pricing overrides, are the authoritative inputs to Cookie agent's estimate; do not assume a fixed cached discount.

Usage events stamp the request price selected when the request completes. Footers and rollups preserve those stamps, so later pricing changes do not rewrite already stamped costs. An unpriced stamp also remains unpriced after configuration or catalog changes, and a rollup containing such a record has no complete estimated-cost total.

To evaluate prompt caching, compare equivalent workloads before and after changing [providers.<id>.cache]. Track cache_hit_rate after the first turn and estimated_cost_usd over the whole session. Providers that expose writes may report them when a prefix is first cached and reads on later matching requests; compare totals only after enough repeated-prefix turns to amortize any write and storage charges. Use the provider's off configuration as the baseline: set all Anthropic or Bedrock system, tools, and rolling values to "off"; for OpenAI GPT-5.6+, use mode = "explicit" with both placements false. Gemini caching is always implicit and has no off control. Disabling authored cache placements is not a guarantee that provider-managed cache activity or billing stops; use the reported usage rather than assuming zero reads or writes.

docs.title: Agent Messaging (Subagent-to-Subagent Communication)
docs.text: Status: implemented. This page is the governing contract for agent-to-agent messaging through the send_message tool. User-facing settings live in Agent Messaging [messaging]; the tool contract is summarized in the tool reference.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Let any agent in a delegation tree send a durable message to any other agent in the same tree (parent ↔ child, sibling ↔ sibling, child → grandparent).
  • Delivery semantics: all delivery is producer-backed. The recipient receives the message either steered into its next safe model-request boundary (if running) or queued durably (if idle or queued). Messaging an idle or finished agent wakes it through the producer reconcile path: the message is admitted durably and the session resumes with it as input.
  • Model-visible tool surface, permission-gated, observable by the TUI and plugins.

docs.title: Non-Goals (v1)
docs.text:
• Cross-daemon / cross-process agent mesh. The engine is in-process; one daemon owns all sessions.
  • Arbitrary cross-session messaging outside the delegation tree. No discovery or authorization basis exists for that yet.
  • Request/response RPC between agents. Async mail only; replies are new messages.
  • Broadcast topics / pub-sub. Can be layered later on the same envelope.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
send_message accepts either a full session UUID or the recipient's short handle (explore_1a2b3c4d) — the same raw-session addressing model the removed steer_subagent tool used. A non-UUID reference is resolved as a handle against the sender's tree only; if it matches no live tree peer the send fails with a self-repairing candidate list, and a handle from another tree never resolves. No labels, aliases, or special targets (parent, root).

There is no discovery mechanism. An agent learns a peer's session ID only because the parent disclosed it — in the delegation prompt, in a steering message, or via delegation tool results (a parent naturally knows its children's IDs from delegate_subagent). The parent therefore controls the communication graph: siblings can only talk if the parent chose to introduce them, and an agent cannot enumerate the tree to find targets on its own.

Every inbound message envelope carries the sender's handle when one exists, so a recipient can reply directly with send_message. Older sessions without a handle use the full sender UUID in the reply hint. Mail from a parent to its own child is the exception: every turn a child finishes already reaches its parent as a <subagent_report> (or as the foreground delegation's result), so the child answers in its final answer, and a send_message reply would arrive twice.

docs.title: Message Envelope
docs.text:
The durable body (ProducerMessageAccepted.body) is readable text rendered into the recipient prompt as a user-turn materialization (repo convention: tool-emitted system input materializes as a user turn):

<agent_message from="explore_1a2b3c4d">
Message written by the sending agent

[use `send_message(to="explore_1a2b3c4d", ...)` to reply]
</agent_message>

Mail from the recipient's parent carries this hint instead, whether or not the recipient can send messages:

<agent_message from="main">
Also check the tests

[reply in your final answer: it reaches `main` when this turn ends]
</agent_message>

The from attribute identifies the sender in every variant. The send_message hint appears only when the recipient's send_message tool is exposed. The original body is preserved as written; the engine adds only the envelope and optional hint. The recipient is implicit — the envelope only ever appears in the session it was delivered to. Message IDs, sender UUIDs, agent hop counts, and other delivery metadata remain in the durable event record and are not rendered into the model-facing body.

docs.title: Tool Surface
docs.text:
MessageToolProvider (provider id builtin.message), modeled on DelegateToolProvider, is registered via try_register_tool_provider in crates/cookie_agent/src/main.rs after engine open.

Tool Args Behavior send_message to: <handle or session_id>, body, mode? (steer/queue, default steer) Resolve the recipient reference (UUID, or handle within the sender's tree), check permission, register/find the sender's agent-producer on the recipient session, send with idempotency key derived from (sender session, run, tool_call) (same derivation pattern as invocation_id)

Model-facing arguments are exactly to, body, and mode; the argument object is strict. The recipient argument is named to; it was renamed from recipient_session_id during implementation with no alias — see Migration notes.

Delivery is fully described by mode: steer (default) joins the recipient's in-flight run at the next safe boundary through producer delivery; queue admits the message durably and it is claimed into the recipient's prompt at the next safe boundary. There is no inbox tool — agents never need to poll.

docs.title: Results, errors, and retries
docs.text:
A successful send_message result means durably accepted (decided): the ProducerMessageAccepted event is persisted in the recipient's event log, so delivery survives a daemon restart. It does not mean the recipient has seen or consumed the message. The result carries:

  • message_id — the durable producer message ID,
  • mode — the effective delivery mode,
  • recipient_state — the recipient's state at send time (running, queued, waking_finished).

Failures are explicit tool errors with stable codes in the send_message: namespace, one per case, so the sending model can react predictably (retry, give up, or report to its parent):

  • send_message:disabled — [messaging] enabled = false, even when permission rules allow the send,
  • send_message:invalid_arguments — missing, unknown, or wrongly typed arguments, including the removed recipient_session_id spelling,
  • send_message:invalid_body — empty or over max_body_bytes,
  • send_message:unknown_session — a well-formed session UUID that names no session,
  • send_message:not_tree_peer — a well-formed session UUID whose root_session_id differs from the sender's,
  • a non-UUID recipient is treated as a subagent handle: a handle that matches no live peer in the sender's tree fails with the self-repairing unknown subagent reference … tool error, whose candidate list renders each addressable peer as handle — description — status (session_id <uuid>) (pre-handle peers print their UUID once),
  • send_message:self_send — sender targeted its own session,
  • send_message:inbox_full — recipient has max_pending_per_session pending agent messages (see Configuration),
  • send_message:max_hops_exceeded — the hop guard rejected the send (see Guards),
  • send_message:inflight_full — the per-pair in-flight window is full (see Guards),
  • send_message:engine_shutdown — send raced daemon shutdown.

Permission failures are not messaging-specific: a denied send follows the generic permission-denied flow, and an ask rule routes through the existing approval flow instead of erroring.

Retries are safe: the idempotency key derives from (sender session, run, tool_call), so a retried call returns the original message_id instead of delivering twice (existing producer dedup behavior).

docs.title: steer_subagent removal
docs.text:
send_message is a strict superset of the removed steer_subagent tool (decided): steering a running child is send_message(mode=steer); steering a queued child durably accepts the message and it is claimed when the child's run starts; finished children, unreachable by steer_subagent, are reachable via wake. The model-visible steer_subagent tool is removed from DelegateToolProvider; delegate_subagent and get_subagent_result remain. (cancel_subagent remained too until 0975445c1 removed it; stop_background given a subagent's handle now stops its turn.) The engine's steer_subagent method is gone too; user steering (run.steer) keeps its own admission path, which send_message does not use. Consequences:

  • Parent→child authority is expressed entirely through message permission rules on the child relationship (e.g. "child": allow in the agent doc).
  • Intentional breaking change (decided): combined with deny-by-default, the out-of-box default agent can delegate subagents but cannot steer them until the user adds message: { "child": allow } to their agent doc. This is accepted as-is; see Migration notes. There is no built-in exemption.
  • Agent docs, prompt sections, and guides were updated in the same change.

send_message uses bounded result truncation and ToolConcurrency::Parallel; guard checks and acceptance are serialized inside the recipient actor.

docs.title: Engine Behavior
docs.text:
1. ProducerOwner::Agent { session_id } variant (protocol/src/producer.rs). Additive payload change; the versionless, best-effort event log tolerates it and old readers degrade gracefully.
  2. Authorization predicate beside ensure_subagent_owned: ensure_tree_peer(sender, recipient) — both sessions are tree peers iff their stored SessionOrigin metadata carries the same root_session_id. That is the entire contract (decided): no live-registry walk, no ancestry or taint validation. Known, accepted limitation: after a parent reverts history, "ghost" sessions from the reverted branch remain reachable by agents that hold their session IDs. Sender identity is always derived from the executing tool context, never from model-supplied arguments. The recipient may be in any state, including finished. Running recipients get steer/queue delivery; Queued/idle recipients get a durable admission claimed at start; Finished/Completed recipients are woken.
  3. Engine API: engine.send_agent_message(invocation) -> AgentMessageHandle in messaging_api.rs, internally accepting the message atomically on the recipient's session actor. Sender-side auto-registration of its Agent producer on the recipient mirrors how background monitors register ProducerOwner::Delegation on parents.
  4. Wake and delivery are producer-backed everywhere. Idle and finished recipients wake through the producer reconcile path — the same reconcile that restarts delivery of accepted-but-unconsumed producer mail after idle eviction or restart — never through user steering or a runless UserInputAdmitted. Messaging an idle-evicted actor therefore reuses the existing producer wake machinery (spawn_actor) with no special casing.
  5. Guards — see Guards.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
Two loop-safety guards reject sends at send time; both are opt-out:

  • Hop guard. The engine tracks an internal hop count per message chain, carried in producer metadata and never rendered in the agent-visible envelope. A send that would exceed messaging.max_hops fails with send_message:max_hops_exceeded. The default is unlimited: max_hops <= 0 disables the guard.
  • Per-pair in-flight window. At most max_inflight_per_pair unacknowledged messages per directed pair (default 4) to stop ping-pong storms between two agents. A pair message is unacknowledged while it is accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, and acknowledged once it is consumed or discarded. A full window rejects the send with send_message:inflight_full. max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disables the guard.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
A dedicated PermissionAction::Message gates send_message (decided) — messaging is not overloaded onto Delegate, so steering a child and messaging an agent remain independently controllable.

Rule shape (agent-doc frontmatter):

permissions:
  message:
    "child": allow      # my delegated children
    "parent": allow     # the agent that delegated me
    "sibling": ask      # other children of my parent
    "*": deny           # any other same-tree peer (grandparent, uncle, ...)
  • The permission resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender: parent, child, sibling, or * (catch-all for any other same-tree peer). The label is derived from stored SessionOrigin metadata at send time and matched by the existing PermissionPipeline + WildcardPattern. This is purely a labeling step — there is no relationship-based authority check anywhere; permissions alone decide.
  • Deny by default, including built-in agents. Built-in agent definitions ship without message rules, so deny-by-default applies and the send_message tool is not even visible to the model (tool_visible requires an allow/ask rule). Messaging is strictly opt-in: an agent doc must declare rules for the tool to appear.
  • ask routes through the existing approval store and TUI approval flow.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[messaging]
enabled = true
max_hops = 0                  # <= 0 disables the hop guard (default); hop counting is internal metadata
max_body_bytes = 32768        # tighter than the 256 KiB plugin cap; agent mail should be terse
max_pending_per_session = 32  # pending agent mail per recipient; overflow → send rejected
max_inflight_per_pair = 4     # 0 disables the per-pair in-flight window

Inbox overflow (decided): max_pending_per_session counts only pending agent mail (accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, but not yet consumed or discarded) — plugin, delegation-notification, and goal producer messages do not count against it, and no agent message is ever discarded to make room. When the cap is reached, send_message fails with the send_message:inbox_full tool error and the new message is not admitted; the sender may retry later. No silent drops.

docs.title: Observability, TUI, Plugins
docs.text:
• TUI: message lifecycle events are durable, so events.subscribe already delivers them. Both delivery modes surface as producer events — steer and queue sends alike appear as ProducerMessage* rows (owner == Agent) in the transcript, so users see steering and queueing exactly like existing producer traffic.
  • Plugins: zero new hooks — plugin/event observes all mail traffic; tool_before_call can gate/audit sends; plugin/producer/send already lets external systems inject into any session (precedent for external→agent mail).
  • Audit: bodies are durable in the recipient's event log, so full mail history is reconstructable per session.

docs.title: Migration notes
docs.text:
There is no separate changelog; these notes are the migration record for the messaging rollout.

  1. steer_subagent is removed. The model-visible tool no longer exists. Its replacements:
Former call Replacement Steer a running child send_message { to, body, mode: "steer" } (the default mode) Steer a queued child send_message { to, body }; the message is durably accepted and claimed when the child's run starts Reach a finished child Newly possible: send_message wakes finished sessions through producer reconcile

Parent→child authority moves from the delegate action to the message action with relationship labels. Agents that previously steered children need an explicit rule such as message: { "child": allow }; the default agent ships without one, so out-of-box subagent steering is denied until the rule is added. User steering through run.steer is unchanged. 2. Recipient argument renamed without an alias. The send_message recipient argument is to; the earlier recipient_session_id spelling is not accepted and fails with send_message:invalid_arguments. Because tool argument objects are strict, old calls fail closed, and prepared-operation grants issued under the old argument identity do not carry over — a previously granted "allow for the session tree" must be approved again under the new identity. 3. Protocol version 19. ProducerMessageAccepted gained the optional, internal agent_hop field in live RPC responses and durable events, so PROTOCOL_VERSION was bumped and the TS/JSON-schema bindings regenerated in the same change, per the repo's version-bump ritual.

docs.title: Resolved Decisions
docs.text:
1. Scope: tree-only, equality check only. Two sessions are tree peers iff their stored SessionOrigin.root_session_id values are equal. No live registry walk, ancestry validation, or taint reconciliation; sessions left over from a reverted branch remain messageable by agents holding their IDs. Any-session addressing is out of scope (it would need a global agent registry and new ownership rules) and conflicts with the no-discovery model.
  2. Permission action: dedicated Message action. Messaging gets its own PermissionAction variant rather than reusing Delegate, so messaging permissions are controlled independently of delegation.
  3. Finished agents are messageable. Sending to a Finished/Completed session wakes it through the producer reconcile path: the message is admitted durably and the session resumes with the message as input, enabling follow-ups without the parent re-delegating with resume_session_id.
  4. steer_subagent is removed. send_message is a strict superset: it covers steering running and queued children and additionally reaches finished children (wake), siblings, and ancestors. Only the model-visible tool is removed; the engine's steer machinery stays for user steering. Parent→child authority moves to Message permission rules.
  5. Permissions: relationship labels, deny by default. The message resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender (parent, child, sibling, *), matched by ordinary wildcard rules — no relationship-based authority checks in the engine. Built-in agents ship without message rules: deny-by-default hides the tool entirely, so messaging is opt-in per agent doc. Combined with decision 4, the default agent loses out-of-box subagent steering until the user adds message: { "child": allow } — an accepted breaking change, documented in Migration notes.
  6. Send result = durably accepted. Success means the message is persisted (ProducerMessageAccepted) and returns message_id, effective mode, and recipient_state; failures are explicit send_message:-namespaced tool errors plus the generic permission-denied flow; retries return the original message_id via idempotency dedup.
  7. Inbox overflow rejects the sender. max_pending_per_session counts pending agent mail only (including claimed and released mail until it is consumed or discarded); overflow fails the send with send_message:inbox_full and nothing is admitted or silently discarded.
  8. Guards are enforced and opt-out. The hop guard (max_hops) and the per-pair in-flight window (max_inflight_per_pair) reject overshooting sends with send_message:max_hops_exceeded and send_message:inflight_full. max_hops <= 0 and max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disable their guard. Hop counting is internal metadata, never part of the delivered envelope, and a pair message counts as unacknowledged from acceptance until it is consumed or discarded.

docs.title: Phased Rollout
docs.text:
• Phase 1 (implemented): ProducerOwner::Agent, send_message with both steer (default) and queue modes, tree-scoped auth, relationship-labeled Message permissions (deny-by-default, tool hidden without rules), steer_subagent tool removal with doc/prompt migration. TUI read-only visibility.
  • Phase 2 (implemented): the hop guard and per-pair in-flight window are enforced with the semantics under Guards; ask approvals use the existing approval flow.
  • Phase 3 (future): plugin mediation recipes, optional broadcast-to-children (to: "children"), cross-daemon story if it ever becomes real.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
The implementation is correct when all of the following hold, covered by tests:

  1. An agent with message: { "child": allow } can send_message a running child (steer joins the next safe boundary) and a queued child (durable admission claimed at run start); an agent without message rules does not see the tool.
  2. Sibling→sibling and child→parent sends work when rules allow them; parent/child/sibling/* labels resolve correctly from origin metadata.
  3. A message to a finished session wakes it through producer reconcile: the session resumes with the message as input; the completed delegation is untouched.
  4. Tree authorization: equal root_session_id succeeds; mismatched roots fail with send_message:not_tree_peer; self-send fails with send_message:self_send.
  5. Result contract: success returns message_id, effective mode, and recipient_state; a retried tool call returns the original message_id and delivers once; restart before delivery still delivers.
  6. Limits and guards: send_message:invalid_body at size boundaries, send_message:inbox_full at max_pending_per_session (agent mail only), send_message:max_hops_exceeded and send_message:inflight_full at their configured limits with max_hops <= 0 / max_inflight_per_pair = 0 disabling each guard, and deny-by-default visibility.
  7. steer_subagent is gone from the tool surface; docs, prompt sections, and guides no longer reference it; the breaking change is in Migration notes.
  8. TUI renders steer and queue deliveries as ProducerMessage* mail rows in both live and replayed streams.
  9. PROTOCOL_VERSION bumped to 19; check-bindings.sh and docs stay in sync.

docs.title: Implementation Notes
docs.text:
Deliberately shallow — the mechanisms already exist; do not re-specify them:

  • Wake lifecycle: waking an idle or finished session reuses the producer reconcile path: accepted-but-unconsumed mail makes the session deliverable, the actor is spawned if evicted, and a fresh run starts on the same session with the message as input. No user steering or runless UserInputAdmitted is involved. The completed delegation is not reopened; no new completion notification fires unless the woken agent sends one.
  • Delivery semantics: steer and queue follow the existing producer machinery unchanged in all recipient states. Races with completion or compaction resolve the same way they do for other producer traffic.
  • Revert and fork: mail events follow the event log's existing revert and fork behavior. No special handling, no cross-branch dedup or wake suppression.
  • Hop counting: meaningful only when max_hops > 0; the count travels as internal producer metadata between chained sends and is rejected at send_message:max_hops_exceeded when it would exceed the limit.
  • Compatibility: ProducerMessageAccepted gained the optional, internal agent_hop field in live RPC responses and durable events, so PROTOCOL_VERSION was bumped to 19 and TS/JSON-schema bindings regenerated in the same change, per the repo's version-bump ritual.

docs.title: Background Tool Calls
docs.text: Status: implemented (decisions of 2026-10-16; all three phases landed 2026-10-16). Sections 1, 7.1, and the "today" notes describe the design this replaced. This document is the governing specification for running supported tool calls in the background, whether the model asks for it or the user moves a running call there. Section Decisions records what review settled.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Two tools can run in the background today, each its own way:

  • bash (coding runtime) takes a background argument and runs a separate code path (execute_background). It reserves a job through ToolExecutionContext::start_background, and the job reports a <background_bash> element whose body (Command:/Status: lines and an output preview) differs from the foreground result.
  • delegate_subagent (daemon base layer) takes a background argument too, but reports through the delegation machinery as <subagent_notification>, whose body is the same text the foreground result carries.

Neither lets the user background a call that is already running, and each tool owns its own flag, its own notice, and its own completion format.

After this work:

  • A tool declares that it supports the background. It runs one code path, its foreground one; the host decides whether and when to stop waiting.
  • The host adds the background argument to every supporting tool's schema and strips it before the tool sees the call.
  • The model starts a call in the background with background: true; the user moves a running foreground call there with one key.
  • A background call reports with one element, <background_result>, wrapping exactly the result the foreground call would have returned.
  • The model stops a background call with one base-layer tool, stop_background.

  • Subagents report every finished turn to their parent (section 7).

  • Clients list a session's background calls and let the user stop one; the model is told the user stopped it.

Out of scope: hotkeys and UI for clients other than the TUI, persistence of background calls across a daemon restart (unchanged: shutdown kills them), and any replacement for interactive stdin, which this work removes (section 8).

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Background-capable tool A tool whose spec sets background: true. Detach The host stops waiting for an executing call: it commits an immediate result for the call and keeps the call's execution running as a background call. Background call A detached call, from detach until its execution ends or is stopped. Identified by a job ID. Job ID The handle the model uses for a background call: job_<8 hex> taken from the tool call ID, or the subagent handle for delegate_subagent. Immediate result The tool result committed at detach. Background result The producer message a background call sends when its execution ends.

docs.title: 3. Tool declaration
docs.text:
ToolSpec, and ToolDeclaration in the runtime protocol, gain two fields:

Field Type Default Meaning background bool false The tool supports running in the background. background_default bool false Whether a call runs in the background when the model omits the argument. Only valid with background: true; true without it is a declaration error.

For a background-capable tool the host:

  • adds "background": {"type": "boolean", "default": <background_default>} to the tool's parameters before publishing it to the model, with a description saying what the background does. A tool whose own schema already has a background property is a declaration error.
  • removes background from the arguments before prepare. The tool never sees it, and it is not part of the prepared operation's identity, so an approval covers a call in either mode.

bash and delegate_subagent declare background: true, background_default: false and drop their own background arguments.

docs.title: 4.1 Triggers
docs.text:
• Model. A call whose effective background is true detaches as soon as its execution starts, after preparation and approval.
  • User. A client asks the daemon to detach one executing call (section 9). Only calls of background-capable tools in the execute phase can be detached; a call awaiting approval, still preparing, or already finished cannot, and the request answers accepted: false.

docs.title: 4.2 What the host does
docs.text:
The engine already awaits each executing call in one select! loop (runtime/tool_execution.rs). Detach is one more branch of that loop.

A background-capable tool marks its detach point: once it has started its work (bash right after spawning its command), it calls ToolExecutionContext::detachable(note) with an optional detach note, a line for the immediate result (bash: the process ID; delegate_subagent: the subagent handle). A remote runtime forwards it as tool/detachable (section 8). The engine detaches only at or after that point: a call the model started in the background detaches as soon as it reaches it, a user's request waits for it, and a call that finishes first simply returns its result in the foreground. Detaching:

  1. Reads the detach note. The call's execution is otherwise untouched.
  2. It commits the call as completed with the immediate result (4.3).
  3. It moves the call's execution future, its output capture, and its progress channel into a background call under the existing background-job rules (runtime/background_tasks.rs): the background result is held until the immediate result is durably committed, and the background call is killed if that commit fails, a revert removes the call, its session is deleted, or the daemon shuts down.
  4. It releases the run: the call no longer blocks the turn, and later calls of the same batch proceed as if it had returned.

The background call's cancellation is no longer the run's. Each call gets its own cancellation token, linked to the run's only until detach, so cancelling the run (Esc) after detach leaves the background call running.

docs.title: 4.3 Immediate result
docs.text:
The tool result committed at detach, model-visible as the call's result:

  • Model-started: Started in the background as job <job>. You will get a <background_result job="<job>"> with its result when it finishes; do not wait for it or run it again. Stop it with stop_background(<job>).
  • User-moved: User manually moved this call to the background; it is still running as job <job>. You will get a <background_result job="<job>"> with its result when it finishes; do not wait for it or run it again. Stop it with stop_background(<job>).

The detach note, when present, follows on its own line. The result carries background: {"state": "job", "job": "<job>", "by": "model" | "user"} so clients can show the call as backgrounded (state is self_reporting, with no job, for work that reports itself). The compatibility spec replaced the earlier metadata.background key with this typed field.

docs.title: 5. Background result
docs.text:
When a background call's execution ends, the host finishes its output capture and renders the result exactly as it would have for the foreground call: same output preview, same truncation, same metadata, same failure text. It sends that, wrapped, as a Tool-owned producer message with steer delivery:

<background_result job="job_1a2b3c4d" tool="bash" status="completed">
…the foreground result…
</background_result>

status is completed, failed (the execution returned an error; the body is the failure text and any partial output), or stopped (section 6). The notification row's summary is <tool> <status> plus the call's display argument.

<background_bash>, BackgroundReport, ToolExecutionContext::start_background, and the BackgroundJobs/BackgroundLauncher traits are removed: no tool starts its own job any more.

docs.title: 6. Stopping: stop_background
docs.text:
A base-layer tool:

Name stop_background Arguments job (string, required): a job ID from an immediate result. Permission None (6.1): it can only reach the session tree's own background calls. Published Only while the model can see at least one background-capable tool.

docs.title: 6.1 Tools that need no permission
docs.text:
Today a base-layer tool that needs no permission declares the reserved permission name unconditional, which the permission pipeline special-cases: always visible, always allowed, never named by a rule. This work makes it part of the tool interface instead of a magic string:

  • ToolSpec.permission becomes optional. None means the tool needs no permission: it is published whenever its own publication rule says so, and every call is allowed without evaluating rules or asking.
  • The reserved unconditional name goes, both as a permission name and as the reserved PermissionAction label; read_artifact and stop_background declare None.
  • Its prepared operations still carry an approval identity, as unconditional tools' do today; it is never evaluated.

Runtime tools may declare no permission too: permission on a runtime protocol tool declaration becomes optional (section 8). Such a tool runs without any rule or approval, and the user cannot restrict it through permissions, only by detaching its runtime.

A tool's own publication rule stays separate from permissions: stop_background declares no permission, and is published only alongside a background-capable tool.

It cancels the background call's execution (for a remote runtime, the existing tool/cancel) and returns once the call has ended. The background result is still sent, with status="stopped" and whatever output the call produced, so the model sees one result per job either way.
