  • C8. Grant invalidations move from the work-dir grant-invalidations.jsonl into each root's directory and load with that tree. A session revert rebuilds grants only for its own tree.
  • C9. Delegation runtime state (records, admission queue, inflight bookkeeping, recovery claims) is keyed by root; every lookup, promotion, and limit is evaluated within one root. Background concurrency is already per root (background_slot_unavailable).
  • C10. delegation.max_resident_subagents applies per tree: idle-eviction candidates are chosen within the tree whose resident child count exceeds the cap.

docs.title: D. Artifacts are per tree
docs.text:
• D1. Artifact reads resolve only inside the reading session's own tree. The process-wide digest index, the directory-scan fallback into other trees, and the cross-refs.jsonl ledger are removed.
  • D2. A fork into a new tree copies every artifact its copied history references — and the streams a named-stream manifest lists — into the new tree's artifacts/ before the fork returns, so a forked tree never depends on its source. A fork of a child stays in its root's tree and copies nothing.
  • D3. Every artifact write is attributed to a tree; the artifacts.shared/ store is removed. Production writes are already routed through the tree resolver installed by Engine::open, which always yields a root.
  • D4. Garbage collection stays per tree and needs no information from any other tree.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• The fixed ~0.7 s of catalog loading (0.19 s) and model-manager compilation (0.47 s), tracked separately.
  • Event-log and metadata formats.
  • The TUI tree panel for an unloaded root, which keeps reading that root's subagents/index.json only when the tree is shown.
  • Existing on-disk artifacts.shared/, cross-refs.jsonl, and work-dir grant-invalidations.jsonl data: breaking changes are acceptable, and old cross-tree references stop resolving.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Engine::open and session.list open zero event logs (store log-open counter) in a work dir containing roots with delegations, grants, and producer state.
  • A tree load opens each of its logs exactly once and opens no file under any other root.
  • Lazy consumers work after a cold start: resuming a prior child, run cancellation cascading to children, session.children, adoption recovery of a nonterminal background delegation, missing-child recovery, and a pre-restart grant applying after its tree is resumed.
  • A grant invalidation survives a restart when only its own tree is loaded.
  • Producer reconciliation with no producer plugin opens no log.
  • A fork's artifacts still resolve after the source tree is deleted.
  • session.usage and session.tree_usage totals are unchanged; agent.usage and usage.global return method-not-found.
  • Launching in the 22-root project takes about as long as in an empty project.

docs.title: Implementation order
docs.text:
1. Rollup removal and the protocol bump (A).
  2. Metadata-only discovery and listing, with the known-session set separated from summaries (B).
  3. Per-tree delegation index, registry, grants, grant journal, producers, and delegation runtime state (C1–C9).
  4. Per-tree artifacts and fork copying (D).
  5. Per-tree residency cap (C10).

docs.title: Tree-Scoped Session Ownership Lock
docs.text: Status: implemented on 2026-09-21. This document records the decision to move cross-process session ownership from a per-session lock to a single lock per root session tree. It amends the ownership rules described in Architecture and the session guarantees in Sessions; it does not touch the ~/.cookie-agent store locks covered by Store lock retention.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Ownership is keyed per session today. SessionStore carries ownership: HashMap<SessionId, StoreOwnership> (crates/engine/src/session/mod.rs, around lines 216 and 255), and every session — each root and each delegated child — acquires a lock of its own. A lock is taken at publication (the fork path around lines 1367-1395, the buffered-publish path around lines 1446-1478) or at adoption (begin_write_locked, around line 833).

On unix that lock is <session-dir>/owner.lock. On Windows it is a <session-id>.owner.lock sidecar placed next to the session directory (crates/engine/src/ownership.rs, owner_lock_path), because a handle held inside the directory would block the publication rename. A tree with N children therefore litters <root>/subagents/ with N sidecars, plus one beside the root.

The per-child locks buy nothing:

  • A child never has a different writer than its root. Delegation only creates and resumes children from a process that already owns the parent.
  • A tree is loaded, folded, reconciled, and published as a unit.
  • Residency and eviction already retain locks for the lifetime of the process, so the per-child locks are never released early anyway.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• One lock per tree. A root tree is guarded by exactly one ownership lock: <root-dir>/owner.lock on unix, and a <root-id>.owner.lock sidecar beside the root directory on Windows. The Windows sidecar stays a sidecar so the temporary-directory rename at publication is not blocked by the open handle. Children have no lock file of any kind. Holding a root's lock guarantees that only its holder writes anywhere under that root's directory, children included.
  • The ownership map is keyed by root. SessionStore.ownership holds TreeOwnership::{PendingPublish { authority }, Adopting { lock, authority }, Owned { lock, authority }, Foreign} (the StoreOwnership enum is renamed). There is one WriteAuthority per tree, and every EventLog::open_owned in the tree is handed that tree's capability, so dropping the tree lock invalidates every log in the tree at once.
  • Per-session adoption bookkeeping stays. A session is writable only when its tree is owned by this process and the session was either created in this process or adopted in it — reconciled by Engine::reconcile_session and committed. WriteOpen::{AlreadyOwned, Adopting} keeps its per-session meaning; the created/adopted sessions are tracked in a per-store set beside the tree map.
  • begin_write(id) resolves root = root_of(id) first. If the tree is unowned it try_acquires the root lock; a foreign or unreadable lock is cached per root and reported as SessionLocked(id) for every session in that tree, exactly as the per-session cache does today. If the tree is already owned there is no lock activity at all. The per-session step follows: a created or adopted session reports AlreadyOwned (reopening its log as today), and any other session has its log opened for adoption and reports Adopting. Acquiring the tree lock through a child does not reconcile the root; the root reconciles when it is first written, through its own adoption.
  • Publication. A new root or a fork of a root acquires the root lock as it does today — inside the temporary directory before the rename on unix, from the sidecar path derived from the final directory on Windows. Publishing a child creates no lock of its own; it requires the tree to be PendingPublish or Owned by this process and fails with SessionLocked otherwise. A fork of a delegated session is the one publication that can be the first write in a tree — nothing else in the tree has to be open for it — so it acquires the root lock when the tree is free, the same way an adoption reached through a child does, and fails as foreign-owned when it is not. Its temporary directory is prepared inside the root's directory, so the lock is taken before it is created.
  • is_owned(id) is answered from the tree of id, and from the per-session record: it is true when the tree is held and settled here and id was created or adopted here. That keeps its meaning at the call sites that use it as a write gate, while a foreign root answers false for every session in its tree. release_ownership drops every tree lock the store holds. Eviction is unchanged: a tree lock is retained for the lifetime of the process even after every session in the tree has been evicted.
  • Legacy child lock files (<child>/owner.lock and <child-id>.owner.lock) are ignored. The tree's single load pass removes them best-effort. There is no migration and no compatibility decoding.
  • Errors are unchanged. SessionError::SessionLocked, EngineError::SessionOwnedByAnotherProcess, and the server's error mapping keep their current shape; a foreign root simply makes every session in its tree report that error.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text: Cross-tree locks, work-dir-level locks, any change to the artifact or provider-store locks (see Store lock retention), and any change to adoption reconciliation semantics.

docs.title: Web Client and Local Daemon Use
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-20), in phases L and W0 to W5; what landed and where it differs from the plan is in section 17, with a summary of the deviations at its end. The decisions in section 1 come from the planning discussion of 2026-10-19, and no questions are open (section 15). The spec builds on the compatibility spec, which froze the client protocol and added browser authentication, and on the runtime capabilities spec, which added the listening daemon. The addendum of 2026-10-21 (section 16) adds web layout v2 and session deletion, implemented on 2026-10-21. On 2026-10-21 the user also reversed the "no service worker" decision of section 9: the page installs as an app, with a network-only service worker. On 2026-10-21 the user also reversed the origin allowlist (sections 1 and 7.1): [server] allowed_origins is gone, and /ws takes a connection from any origin, with the token as the guard.

docs.title: 1. Goal and scope
docs.text:
Before this spec the TUI was the only interactive client. This spec adds a browser client that does everything the TUI does that a browser can do. It works on a phone and on a desktop, against a daemon on the same machine or on another one.

It also makes plain cookie use a daemon already running on the machine instead of starting a private one beside it (section 13). Once a persistent daemon holds the machine's sessions, every client should see the same ones.

Decided 2026-10-19:

  • Use. One client serves the desktop browser on the daemon's machine and remote access from a laptop or phone. The layout is responsive, and every action works by touch.
  • Stack. The client is Rust compiled to WebAssembly with Leptos, using client-side rendering. It reuses the Rust protocol client and a reducer shared with the TUI. No TypeScript client and no generated TypeScript types are written.
  • Hosting: both.
  • The daemon serves the built page.
  • The same bundle also works from any static host, connecting to a daemon whose allowed_origins lists that host. (Since 2026-10-21, any daemon: the allowlist is removed, see the next decision but four.)
  • Who serves the page. cookie daemon always serves it. Plain cookie never does: it either connects to a running daemon (section 13) or runs one in-process with no port. There is no configuration key or flag for this.
  • Highlighting. Code is highlighted by highlight.js shipped inside the bundle, not by syntect compiled to WebAssembly and not by Shiki (several times larger). The web and TUI colours may therefore differ slightly.
  • Editors. /config and /memory edit in a plain text area in version 1. A code editor can come later.
  • No project-site hosting. The bundle is not published on cookie-agent.github.io. Releases attach it as an archive.
  • MSRV. If the chosen Leptos release needs a Rust newer than 1.88, the workspace MSRV rises to match.
  • Origins: no special case. Every browser connection, the embedded page's included, must come from an origin [server] allowed_origins lists. Whoever sets up the daemon decides which addresses reach it. The user reversed this on 2026-10-21: [server] allowed_origins is removed. /ws accepts an upgrade from any Origin, or none, because a reverse proxy makes browser-origin gating pointless and the token is the real guard; /runtime still refuses any request with an Origin. A config that still has the key fails as an unknown key.
  • One listener. The page and /ws share the daemon's one TCP listener. Forwarding that one port (with cloudflared, Tailscale, an SSH tunnel) forwards both, and the connect screen fills in the daemon URL from the page's own address.
  • Styling. The page uses standard tooling: Tailwind CSS through Trunk's built-in Tailwind support, as the Leptos documentation describes. No hand-written stylesheet framework.
  • No conformance client. No Python or Node smoke client is added. The compatibility checker and the frozen corpora stay the guard for third-party clients.
  • Milestone. The milestone is full TUI parity, phases W0 to W5. Two exclusions stay with the TUI and CLI:
  • MCP OAuth, whose redirect must reach a loopback listener;
  • offering this machine as a runtime, as cookie attach does when the daemon is remote.
  • Plain cookie and a running daemon (section 13):
  • When a daemon is running on this machine, plain cookie connects to it.
  • It then checks whether the daemon has a coding runtime on this machine. If so, sessions use the daemon's runtime. If not, plain cookie provides its own local coding runtime.
  • When no daemon is running on this machine, plain cookie behaves as today: it runs the daemon in-process.
  • cookie attach and cookie --standalone override the automatic choice.
  • There is no discovery file. Plain cookie finds the daemon at the address [server] configures (section 13.1).
  • cookie run stays in-process.
  • A daemon running as another OS user on the same machine is not detected. It reports the same machine ID, so its local runtime is used, with that user's file permissions. Users who run the daemon under a service account use --standalone or a dial-in runtime.

Out of scope: - protocol changes, beyond any small additions phase W0 finds it needs (section 11); - a TypeScript SDK; - hosting the bundle on the project's Pages site; - offline use; - push notifications.

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Bundle. The built web client: index.html, the WebAssembly module, its JavaScript glue, the highlighter, styles, and icons.
  • Embedded page. The bundle served by cookie daemon from its own listener.
  • Hosted page. The same bundle served by any other web server.
  • Shared client. The Rust code the TUI and the web client both use: the protocol client in cookie_agent_protocol and the state crate of section 5.

docs.title: 3. Architecture
docs.text:
crates/protocol            wire types + Client (now also wasm32)
crates/client_state        NEW: reducer and view state, shared by TUI and web
crates/tui                 ratatui rendering over client_state
crates/web                 NEW: Leptos CSR app over client_state (wasm32)
crates/web_assets          NEW: the prebuilt bundle as bytes, for the server
crates/server              serves /ws, /runtime, and now the bundle
  • crates/web is a workspace member.
  • It builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown with trunk.
  • It also compiles natively, so cargo build --workspace and the unit tests keep working without the wasm target.
  • Natively, only its pure logic is tested. Browser APIs are not called in native tests.
  • crates/web_assets includes the bundle at compile time.
  • When no bundle has been built (a fresh checkout, or the regular CI jobs), it includes a placeholder page: "the web client was not built; run scripts/build-web.sh".
  • So cargo build --locked --workspace never needs trunk or the wasm target.
  • Dependency direction. web and tui depend on client_state. client_state depends only on cookie_agent_protocol and plain crates. Nothing in it renders.

docs.title: 4. Protocol client on WebAssembly
docs.text:
cookie_agent_protocol builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown with the client side only.

  • Features. The native-only parts are gated by target:
  • the server (session/server*);
  • the stdio transport and codecs;
  • oauth-callback;
  • StopSignals;
  • process helpers.

On wasm, tokio is limited to sync (and macros where needed). uuid and jiff enable their browser features for randomness and the clock. The core oven-sdk crate already has no tokio or HTTP dependency. - Executor shim. Client calls tokio::spawn, tokio::time::timeout, sleep, and interval today. A small internal module provides spawn, timeout, sleep, and interval: - native: tokio, unchanged; - wasm: wasm_bindgen_futures::spawn_local and browser timers.

The client's logic, its limits (2,000-event replay pages, the 5 s page timeout, 6 recovery attempts) and its tests stay one copy. - Browser WebSocket transport. - The web_sys::WebSocket is not Send. It lives in one local task that exchanges frames with the client over channels, so the client's own futures keep their bounds. - The transport sends no Authorization header (browsers cannot set one). The token goes in ClientHello.token, as the protocol reference describes. - A close before the handshake reply is reported like a refused native upgrade. A browser exposes no HTTP status for a refused upgrade (Firefox reports close code 1006), so an origin refusal cannot be told from others: the page shows every refusal before the handshake with the allowed_origins hint naming its own origin. - Reconnect uses the same backoff (500 ms rising to 10 s) and the same ClientIdentity across reconnects, so this tab's origin stays stable. The instance id lives in sessionStorage, so each tab is its own client, the same as each TUI process. - CI. A job runs cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown for cookie_agent_protocol (client features) and cookie_agent_client_state, and clippy over them; the web job runs the browser tests (section 12).

docs.title: 5. Shared client state
docs.text:
The reducer and view state move from crates/tui/src/state/ into crates/client_state, and the TUI uses them from there. Their tests move with them (state/tests.rs).

  • Moves:
  • StateStore, SessionState, and reduce_event/reduce_transient (event attribution, pending and queued lanes, approvals, goal, live tool display deltas);
  • the runtime snapshot revision chain (state/runtime.rs);
  • model display names (state/model_names.rs).
  • Markdown.
  • Today the state stores a MarkdownDocument already styled with ratatui.
  • The state will keep only markdown that any client can use: the source text plus a pulldown-cmark event list, or the source alone if parsing in each client proves cheap enough.
  • The ratatui styling moves to crates/tui/src/markdown.rs, and the web client renders the same markdown to HTML.
  • Phase W0 picks the representation by measuring the TUI's redraw cost on a long session.
  • Moves too, where it separates cleanly:
  • the subscription policy (keep the 8 most recently viewed trees subscribed, release settled ones, retry a failed recovery after 2 s);
  • treating a session.resume "owned by another process" error as a read-only snapshot;
  • the model-selection draft: publish after 300 ms, and yield to a session_model_selected from another origin;
  • upload chunking.

These are client behaviour, not rendering. Pieces too tangled with App stay in the TUI, and the web client reimplements them. Phase W0 records which. - Stays in the TUI: - rendering, pointer targets, hover; - tui.toml and the theme; - $EDITOR editing; - the OSC 52 clipboard; - the terminal-only debounces (approval hotkey grace).

docs.title: 6. The web client
docs.text:
• Shape.
  • Wide screens: a session sidebar (list and subagent tree), the transcript, and a composer docked at the bottom. Panels (approvals, /runtime, /mcp, /config, …) open as side sheets.
  • Narrow screens: the sidebar and panels become full-screen sheets, and the transcript fills the screen.
  • Commands. The composer accepts the same slash commands as the TUI, with the same names and aliases. Every command is also reachable from a menu, because phones lack a convenient /. Superseded on 2026-10-21 (section 16.3): the web composer has no slash commands; the ⋮ menu has them all.
  • Keys and touch.
  • Keys: Enter steers, Alt+Enter queues, Shift+Enter and Ctrl+J insert a newline, Escape cancels, Up recalls.
  • Touch: Send steers, and long-pressing Send (or its menu) queues.
  • Every clickable element has a visible hover on pointer devices and a visible pressed state on touch, mirroring the TUI's rule that every click target hovers.
  • Transcript rendering.
  • Markdown: rendered to sanitized HTML. Raw HTML in model output is escaped, never rendered.
  • Display blocks: every kind gets its own renderer: text, markdown, code, file_excerpt, diff, terminal, key_value, table, json, media, link, session_ref.
  • Diffs show real file line numbers and their five context lines.
  • Terminal blocks turn SGR sequences into styled spans.
  • Tool names: no renderer branches on a tool's name.
  • Unknown blocks use their text fallback, and unknown events render as nothing.
  • Media.
  • Attachments come from the file picker, drag and drop, paste, and the camera on phones.
  • They are offered only for the media kinds the selected model's input_media accepts.
  • On a too-large rejection, the client offers "downscale and attach?". Images are re-encoded through a canvas; video is not downscaled.
  • media blocks and attachments are shown inline from artifact.read through Blob URLs.
  • Highlighting.
  • A JavaScript highlighter is shipped in the bundle (no CDN, since a daemon may run with no internet) and called through wasm-bindgen.
  • It is loaded lazily on the first code block.
  • The highlighter is highlight.js.
  • Editors. /config and /memory edit in the page.
  • They keep the TUI's revision and conflict handling: config.apply reports configuration errors, and a memory edit that conflicts with a newer revision asks what to do.
  • Version 1 uses a monospace text area.
  • Clipboard.
  • Copy uses navigator.clipboard. Browsers offer that only in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost).
  • Elsewhere the client falls back to selecting the text and asking the user to copy it.
  • Preferences.
  • Theme (light, dark, or system) and the /events level filter live in localStorage.
  • There is no server-side preference store.
  • Styling.
  • Tailwind CSS, wired in through Trunk's rel="tailwind-css" asset. Trunk runs the standalone Tailwind CLI at a version pinned in Trunk.toml, so the build needs no npm or node_modules.
  • Components use Tailwind utility classes in their view! markup. Tailwind finds them by scanning crates/web/src/**/*.rs (an @source entry), so class names are always complete string literals, never assembled from pieces at runtime.
  • The palette is defined once as Tailwind theme tokens (CSS variables): the landing site's colours, which are the TUI colours from crates/tui/src/theme.rs. Light and dark variants use Tailwind's dark: variant, following the system setting or the user's override.
  • Other web assets come in through Trunk's standard asset pipeline too: the highlighter script, fonts, icons, and the manifest are copied by Trunk, not by hand. Copied files keep their names (the manifest names its icons by path), so they are revalidated rather than cached forever (section 7.1).
  • JetBrains Mono for code. Fonts are bundled, not loaded from Google.
  • Icons are Font Awesome Free (CC BY 4.0, credited on the connect screen and in the connection panel) from the icondata crate, rendered by leptos_icons as inline SVG that takes the text colour. Only the icons the page names are in the bundle; there is no icon font. Icon-only buttons have an aria-label and a tooltip.

docs.title: 7.1 Embedded page
docs.text:
• cookie daemon serves the bundle on its listener, over TLS when TLS is configured.
  • GET / returns index.html.
  • The bundle's files are served at their paths.
  • /ws and /runtime keep their meaning, and any other path is a 404.
  • Files whose names carry Trunk's content hash (the WebAssembly module, its glue, the stylesheet) are sent with Cache-Control: immutable. index.html and the files Trunk copies under their own names (fonts, highlighter, manifest, icons, screenshots, the service worker) are sent with no-cache and an ETag, so a restarted daemon's page always matches its own build.
  • A compressible file is sent gzip-compressed to a browser that takes gzip; there is no Brotli.
  • Serving the page needs no token. The page holds no secret. Every connection it opens still authenticates in the handshake.
  • One listener for both. The page and /ws share the daemon's TCP listener. Anything that forwards that one port forwards both, and the page finds the daemon at its own address (7.2).
  • Origins have no special case.
  • The page's /ws connection is a browser connection like any other. It carries the page's Origin, and the daemon accepts it only if [server] allowed_origins lists that origin or is ["*"].
  • The default list is empty, so the embedded page cannot connect until the user lists the origins they open it from. Examples: http://127.0.0.1:7419, http://192.168.1.5:7419, or a tunnel's https://cookie.example.com.
  • The daemon trusts no headers to work out where it is reachable from.
  • The user reversed this on 2026-10-21: [server] allowed_origins is removed. /ws accepts an upgrade from any Origin, or none, because a reverse proxy makes browser-origin gating pointless and the token is the real guard; /runtime still refuses any request with an Origin. A config that still has the key fails as an unknown key.
  • Telling the user what to add.
  • A refused connection gives the page no reason to show. When the handshake never happens, the connect screen names the likely cause: "add "<location.origin>" to [server] allowed_origins in the daemon's config.toml and restart it". It quotes its own origin exactly.
  • When allowed_origins is empty, the daemon says, in a log line after its ready line, that the web page needs an entry before it can connect.
  • Since 2026-10-21 (the allowlist's removal) the connect screen says only that the daemon refused or closed the connection before its handshake, and to check the daemon URL and that the daemon is running. The daemon prints the page's address after its ready line and nothing about origins.
  • Plain cookie opens no port and serves nothing.

docs.title: 7.2 The connect screen
docs.text:
The same page runs embedded in the daemon or from any other static host, and both open on one connect screen.

  • The daemon URL is filled in from the page's own address.
  • The scheme changes from http to ws, or from https to wss.
  • Host and port stay the same.
  • ws is appended to the page's directory: https://abc.efg/ gives wss://abc.efg/ws, and https://abc.efg/cookie/ gives wss://abc.efg/cookie/ws.
  • What the fill covers.
  • The embedded page, reached directly or through any forward of the daemon's port, always gets the right URL.
  • A page on a static host without a daemon gets a URL to edit. The edited URL is remembered in localStorage.
  • When the page connects by itself. It connects without a click when it has both a URL (filled in or remembered) and a token (from #token= or localStorage, section 7.3). Otherwise the screen waits for input.
  • Relative paths. The bundle uses relative paths only, so it works from any path on any static host.
  • HTTPS pages. A page served over HTTPS can only reach wss:// daemons. The web clients section already says so, and the fill keeps the page's scheme.
  • Version skew between page and daemon is handled by the handshake: same major required, and the page gates methods on the daemon's minor.
  • Archive. The release attaches the bundle as an archive, so it can be hosted anywhere.

docs.title: 7.3 Getting the token to the page
docs.text:
• cookie web is a new CLI command. It prints the page URL with the token in the fragment: http://<host>:<port>/#token=<token>, or https when the daemon uses TLS.
  • URL and token resolve like cookie attach: --url and --token flags first, then [server] url and [server] token in this machine's configuration.
  • --open opens the system browser.
  • The URL is derived from the client URL: ws→http, wss→https, and the /ws path dropped.
  • The fragment never reaches a server or its logs. On load, the page reads #token=, stores the token in localStorage under the daemon URL, and removes the fragment from the address bar.
  • Fallback: a paste box on the connect screen.
  • The daemon's ready line is unchanged, since supervisors parse it. The page URL, without the token, follows it as a log line.
  • Forget: a "Forget this daemon" action deletes the stored token.

docs.title: 8. Feature parity
docs.text:
Everything in the TUI except the two exclusions. Rows marked as phases name where each feature lands.

Area TUI surface Web phase Sessions create, /sessions list filtered by cwd, resume, read-only snapshot, live sessions.changed W2 Transcript markdown, every display block, live tool progress, diffs, terminal SGR, full-content artifact.read W2 Composer submit (steer/queue/start), queue strip, recall, cancel W2 Approvals panel, respond with revision and fingerprint W2 Models and agents /model, /agent, /preset, debounced session.select_model W2 Permissions mode toggle; /permissions overrides and preview W2 (toggle), W3 (overrides) Usage /usage, cost in the status bar W2 Subagents tree panel with fold modes, session_ref navigation W3 History edits fork, revert, /compact and its cancel W3 Goal goal bar, /goal set, pause, resume, cancel W3 Background backgrounding a running call, the bar, /background list and stop W3 Media /attach, chips, upload, downscale offer, inline media W3 Skills /skills search and run W3 Runtimes /runtime attachments, draft runtimes, reconnect W4 Machines rename, assign, unassign, merge, forget W4 MCP list, add, edit, remove, enable, reconnect, persist (no OAuth) W4 Providers /connect forms, disconnect W4 Configuration /config documents, apply, reload W4 Memory /memory by layer, edit at revision, delete W4 Plugins /plugins status, restart, plugin status lines W4 Diagnostics /events level filter W2

Excluded:

  • MCP OAuth. mcp.auth.begin requires a loopback redirect_uri (crates/mcp/src/oauth.rs). The web client shows the server as needing authorization and tells the user to run cookie mcp auth or use the TUI.
  • This machine as a runtime. A browser has no workspace to offer.

docs.title: 9. Phones
docs.text:
• Layout. Layouts work from 360 px wide. Touch targets are at least 44 px, nothing scrolls sideways, and long lines in code, diff, and terminal blocks scroll inside their block.
  • Home screen.
  • The bundle has a web app manifest and icons (any and maskable, 192 and 512 px, an SVG, and an Apple touch icon), display: standalone, and a theme colour for light and dark, so it can be added to the home screen.
  • The spec first left a service worker out: it would need a secure context and adds caching the daemon's version matching does not want. The user reversed this on 2026-10-21: the page advertises itself as an installable app, with a service worker that caches nothing (below).
  • Installable app (user decision, 2026-10-21). Users opening the page in a browser, typically over tailscale serve HTTPS (https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/ in front of the loopback daemon), can install it to a phone or desktop.
  • Manifest. name, short_name, and id, start_url, and scope of ./ (relative, so the page installs from any path), display: standalone, background and theme colours, the icons above, and a narrow and a wide screenshot for Chromium's richer install dialog.
  • Service worker, network-only. sw.js beside index.html, so its scope is the page's directory without Service-Worker-Allowed. It caches nothing: no Cache Storage, and its fetch handler passes the page's own GET requests to the network (respondWith(fetch(request))) and leaves every other request, and /ws and /runtime, to the browser. The page must always match its daemon's build, which is why caching stays out. It calls skipWaiting and clients.claim, and scripts/build-web.sh stamps the build on its last line, so a new build replaces it on the next load. The page registers it only in a secure context, with updateViaCache: "none".
  • Serving. sw.js keeps its name, so it is sent with no-cache and an ETag like index.html, as text/javascript. The Content-Security-Policy adds worker-src 'self' and manifest-src 'self'.
  • Advertising it. An inline script keeps Chromium's beforeinstallprompt (it may fire before the WebAssembly runs) and prevents the mini-infobar. Settings › This browser, the connect screen, and a phone's one-time dismissible banner offer Install app, which opens the prompt; appinstalled or running standalone (display-mode: standalone, iOS's navigator.standalone) hides it. iOS and iPadOS have no prompt, so they get the steps instead: Share, then Add to Home Screen. A page that is not a secure context cannot be installed, and Settings says it needs HTTPS. The decision is pure logic in crates/web/src/install.rs.
  • Launching. The app opens at start_url, which has no token, and connects with the stored one. iOS keeps a home-screen app's storage apart from Safari's, so there the token field takes a pasted cookie web link once. The theme-color follows the page's theme, the user's override included.
  • On-screen keyboard. The page's frame and sheets take the visual viewport's height, which the keyboard shrinks, so the composer and an open sheet stay above it; the frame keeps clear of safe-area insets.
  • Background tabs.
  • A phone suspends background tabs. On visibilitychange to visible, the client checks its connection and reconnects through the shared client's resync.
  • Lost events are recovered by cursor, as after any reconnect.
  • Remote access. Reaching a remote daemon from a phone means cookie daemon --listen on a private network or VPN, or TLS. The guide page says the token crosses the network in the clear without TLS, as the daemon's --listen help already does.

docs.title: 10. Build, CI, and packaging
docs.text:
• scripts/build-web.sh
  • runs trunk build --release for crates/web, with wasm-opt for size;
  • copies the result to crates/web_assets/bundle/, which git ignores;
  • is pinned to trunk 0.21.14, to the wasm-bindgen version in Cargo.lock, and to the Tailwind version in Trunk.toml. Trunk downloads its tools on first use, so CI caches Trunk's tool directory.
  • Bundle size. scripts/build-web.sh fails when the bundle, gzipped, is over its budget of 10,000,000 bytes; CI reports the sizes in the job summary.
  • Regular gates (cargo build/test/clippy --workspace, both toolchains) build the native side only and use the placeholder page. If the chosen Leptos release needs a Rust newer than 1.88, phase W1 raises the workspace rust-version to match. It also updates the MSRV Clippy gate in CI and AGENTS.md, so crates/web is checked like every other crate.
  • New CI jobs:
  • wasm: the wasm cargo check and clippy of section 4;
  • web: wasm clippy of the page, scripts/build-web.sh, and both headless-Firefox suites (section 12) with pinned Firefox, geckodriver, and wasm-bindgen-test-runner, keeping the scenario screenshots of a failure.
  • Release.
  • The release workflow builds the bundle before cargo-dist builds cookie, so every release binary embeds the real page.
  • cookie_agent_web_assets is published to crates.io with the bundle included through include in its Cargo.toml, so cargo install cookie_agent gets the real page too.
  • The bundle archive is attached to the GitHub release for hosting elsewhere.

docs.title: 11. Protocol and compatibility
docs.text:
• No wire change is planned. The web client speaks client protocol 1.x as it is, with client.kind = "web". The daemon never branches on that kind.
  • If parity needs a method or a field, for example a convenience the TUI does through several calls, it is a minor bump under the compatibility rules and is recorded in the implementation notes.
  • Not part of the client protocol:
  • The new HTTP routes are not part of the client protocol and carry no version.
  • The embedded page always matches its daemon.
  • Origins are unchanged. allowed_origins keeps its current rules for every browser connection, the embedded page's included.
  • No configuration changes. cookie web is a new command. Its flags follow cookie attach. --standalone is a new flag of plain cookie. Finding a local daemon reads the existing [server] keys (section 13.1).

docs.title: 12. Testing
docs.text:
• Shared state. The tests that move with it run against both its users: the TUI's rendering snapshots stay, and new web rendering tests cover each display block kind's HTML.
  • Protocol client on wasm.
  • wasm-bindgen-test in headless Firefox (scripts/test-wasm-client.sh) covers the browser transport: handshake with token, refused origin, reconnect, and replay across a gap. Chrome is not run.
  • It runs against a real cookie daemon started by the test harness with a scripted provider.
  • End-to-end. Headless-Firefox scenarios (scripts/test-web-page.sh) against real daemons and a scripted model cover connecting via #token=, runs, approvals, steering, queueing, cancelling, subagents, fork and revert, compaction, goals, background calls, attachments and media, skills, permissions, every management panel, a suspended tab's reconnect, read-only snapshots, the refused origin, and the manifest. Every view is audited at 360 and 390 px portrait and a landscape phone size for sideways scroll, clipped controls, and touch targets.
  • Server.
  • Bundle serving: paths, cache headers, the 404 rule.
  • /ws and /runtime precedence.
  • The embedded page's connection is refused without an allowed_origins entry and accepted with one. The ready line names the missing entry.
  • Connect screen. URL fill-in for root and subpath pages over http and https; connecting without a click when URL and token are known; the origin hint after a refused connection.

docs.title: 13. Plain cookie and a local daemon
docs.text:
Before this change, plain cookie always started a private daemon inside its own process, even when cookie daemon was already running on the machine. That private daemon could not open a session the other one owned: it showed the session as a read-only snapshot. Its own sessions were invisible to the web client and to every other client of the running daemon.

From this change, plain cookie follows the decisions in section 1:

  1. find a daemon running on this machine and connect to it (13.1);
  2. pick the coding runtime for its sessions (13.2);
  3. with no daemon found, run in-process exactly as today.

docs.title: 13.1 Finding the daemon
docs.text:
• The token comes first. The probe happens only when this machine's config.toml has [server] token. cookie daemon writes that key on its first start and keeps it across restarts. With no token, no daemon has run with this configuration, so plain cookie starts in-process without touching the network.
  • The probe address is ws://<[server] host>:<[server] port>/ws, the address a plain cookie daemon listens on.
  • It is not [server] url. That key may name a daemon on another machine (a laptop configured for labpc), and plain cookie must never go remote on its own. Reaching another machine stays explicit: cookie attach.
  • Plain cookie authenticates with the Authorization header and the configured token, as cookie attach does.
  • Deadlines. A refused connection falls through to in-process at once. The connect and the handshake each have a short deadline (500 ms and 2 s), so a stuck listener delays startup by seconds at most.
  • What each outcome does:
Outcome Result Nothing listens (refused, or the connect deadline passes) In-process, silently Handshake succeeds Connected to the daemon (13.2, 13.3) Something answered but the handshake failed: wrong token, another protocol major, a TLS listener, not a cookie daemon In-process, with a notice (below)

The notice appears in the TUI's status area when it starts. It names the address and the reason, and suggests cookie attach to require the daemon or --standalone to stop probing. Failing outright would lock the user out when, for example, a daemon from an older major keeps running after an upgrade. - Daemons this does not find: - one started with --port or --listen on an address the probe does not reach; - one serving TLS only.

For those the user runs cookie attach, or sets [server] host and port to match. - Token exposure. Plain cookie sends the token to whatever listens on that loopback port. cookie attach with default settings does the same today. config.toml is owner-only, and the probe only happens when a token exists.

docs.title: 13.2 Choosing the coding runtime
docs.text:
After the handshake and before the first session is created, plain cookie picks the runtime its sessions use for the current directory. The steps go in order, and the first match wins:

  1. The daemon is on this machine. If ServerHello.machine_id equals this machine's ID, the daemon's local runtime serves the directory. session.create names the directory as cwd and no runtime, as cookie attach does today. If either side has no machine ID, this counts as a match, again as cookie attach does today.
  2. A runtime of the daemon runs on this machine. Otherwise, plain cookie looks for a connected runtime that:
  3. runtimes.list places on a machine whose ids (from machines.list) include this machine's ID; and
  4. offers a capability that takes a workspace.

Sessions attach that capability at the directory. Example: the daemon runs in a container or behind a forwarded port, with cookie runtime serve --daemon running here. When several runtimes match, the lowest runtime ID wins, and /runtime shows the choice. The choice uses only reported facts (machine, takes_workspace), never a runtime's kind label. 3. Nothing on this machine. Plain cookie dials in its own runtime, client_<host>, limited to the directory and living as long as the TUI. cookie attach already does this for a daemon on another machine.

cookie attach switches to the same three steps, replacing its current machine-ID check. That way the two never pick differently.

docs.title: 13.3 Once connected
docs.text:
• Behaviour matches cookie attach.
  • The session list is filtered by the directory.
  • A dropped connection is retried with the same backoff. Plain cookie never falls back to in-process mid-session, because the sessions belong to the daemon.
  • Quitting the TUI leaves the daemon running.
  • The TUI shows where it runs. The status bar shows the daemon's address when connected, and standalone when in-process. Today the two look the same.
  • Version notice. When the daemon's engine_version differs from this binary's version, the TUI notes it once: "the daemon runs 0.5.0, this is 0.6.0; restart the daemon to upgrade". This happens after an upgrade while a service daemon keeps running. The protocol versions still decide whether the two connect.

docs.title: 13.4 Overrides
docs.text:
• cookie --standalone always runs in-process and never probes. It applies to plain cookie only. Combined with a subcommand, it is a usage error.
  • cookie attach stays explicit:
  • its target comes from --url, --token (or COOKIE_DAEMON_TOKEN), then [server] url and [server] token, and may be another machine;
  • a failure is an error, never a fallback;
  • it chooses its runtime by 13.2.
  • cookie run stays in-process and never probes. Headless runs are often scripted, and a script attaching to a long-lived daemon by surprise is riskier than a TUI doing so.
  • In-process alongside a running daemon behaves as today: a session the daemon owns opens as a read-only snapshot.

docs.title: 13.5 Testing
docs.text:
• The decision logic is a pure function. It takes the probe outcome, ServerHello, runtimes.list, machines.list, and the local machine ID, and returns one of: in-process, in-process with a notice, local, an existing runtime, or a dial-in. It is tested over every row of 13.1 and every step of 13.2.
  • Integration tests use a scratch home whose [server] port points at a test daemon:
  • plain cookie connects and creates its session through the daemon;
  • with nothing listening, it starts in-process silently;
  • with a wrong token, plain cookie starts in-process with the notice;
  • --standalone and cookie run never connect;
  • a daemon reporting another machine ID gets a dial-in runtime.

docs.title: 14. Phases
docs.text:
Each phase lands as focused commits and is pushed when its gates pass.

Phase Content L Plain cookie and a local daemon (section 13): probe of [server], runtime choice shared with cookie attach, --standalone, TUI connection indicator and notices, docs. Independent of the web client, so it can land first W0 Protocol client on wasm32 (feature gating, executor shim, browser WebSocket transport), crates/client_state extracted from the TUI with its tests, markdown representation chosen, wasm cargo check in CI W1 crates/web shell with Trunk and Tailwind (connect screen, token from fragment or paste, reconnect, theme), crates/web_assets with placeholder, server bundle routes, connect-screen URL fill-in and origin hint, cookie web, ready-line URL, scripts/build-web.sh, release plumbing W2 Core chat: sessions, transcript and every display block, composer, approvals, model and agent pickers, permission mode, usage, /events W3 Session depth: subagent tree, fork, revert, compact, goal, background, media, skills, permission overrides W4 Management: runtimes, machines, MCP, providers, configuration, memory, plugins W5 Phone polish, manifest, end-to-end suite, clients/web.md, server and CLI references, specs index status

docs.title: 15. Open questions
docs.text:
None. Every choice was settled on 2026-10-19:

  • The probe of [server] was chosen over a discovery file.
  • cookie run stays in-process.
  • A daemon run as another OS user is not detected.
  • highlight.js, a plain text area for editors, no project-site hosting, and a rising MSRV were confirmed.
  • allowed_origins keeps its current rules with no special case for the embedded page. (Reversed 2026-10-21: the allowlist is removed; see section 7.1.)

docs.title: 16. Addendum (2026-10-21): web layout v2 and session deletion
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-21). Session deletion (section 16.2) is a minor protocol addition, client protocol 1.5.0, in the daemon, the shared client state, the TUI, and the web client; the web client's layout (section 16.1) and its delete control build on it. Section 16.1 also records the decisions the web layout settled while it was built. Section 16.3 records the web-only decisions of 2026-10-21 on commands, the subagent tree, the permission mode picker, and the message menu, also implemented.

docs.title: 16.1 Web layout v2
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-21:

  • Bottom bar. The agent, the model, the permission mode, and the cost sit together in the bottom bar.
  • Title bar. Only the chat's title and a ⋮ menu of commands that act on this session.
  • Sidebar toggle. The ☰ becomes a button that shows and hides the sidebar, on desktop too.
  • Icon rail. A rail of icons on the left switches between the views:
  • Chat: sessions and the transcript;
  • Agents: agent documents and presets;
  • Settings: config.toml, providers, MCP, plugins, and client preferences, in the sections Configuration, Providers, MCP servers, Plugins, and This browser;
  • Machines and runtimes;
  • Memory.
  • Theme toggle. At the bottom of the rail.
  • Desktop chrome. Once connected, the app header is gone: the connection indicator and the theme toggle sit at the rail's foot.
  • Session panel. Keeps only the commands and settings that belong to the session.
  • Deleting a session. A trash icon appears on a session row on hover, or on a long press on touch screens. It opens a confirmation, and only the confirmation sends session.delete.

Decided while the layout was built (2026-10-21):

  • Subagent tree. The open session's subagents nest under its row in the sessions list, labelled "Subagents". The tree expands on its own while a subagent is live; /agent-panel show|hide|auto controls the expansion. Superseded on 2026-10-21 by the tree rules of section 16.3.
  • Children. Child nodes have no delete control: a subagent goes with its root (not_a_root_session).
  • Delegate rows. A delegation row in the transcript shows the child's live activity.
  • Title bar when viewing a child. A breadcrumb from the root to the child, which collapses on phones to ‹ followed by the child's title.
  • The mobile layout (approved):
  • breakpoints below 640 px (phone), 640 to 1023 px (tablet), and 1024 px and up (desktop);
  • landscape phones use the tablet layout;
  • a drawer holds the rail and the sessions;
  • the session's commands open in a bottom action sheet;
  • the bottom bar is one row, and it hides while the composer has focus;
  • the status line shows only when it has something to say;
  • lists open their items as list → detail views.

docs.title: 16.2 Session deletion
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-21:

  • Users delete sessions from the TUI and from the web client.
  • Deleting is a hard delete of the whole session tree from disk: the root session and every delegated subagent session under it, with their events, metadata, and artifacts. Nothing is kept for undo.
  • A client sends the delete only after the user confirms it.
  • The daemon refuses while any session of the tree has an active run, and while another process holds the tree's owner.lock.
  • A delete that succeeds sends the existing sessions.changed removed change to every connection.
  • TUI. In the session picker (/sessions), Ctrl+D, Delete while the list has focus, or the picker's Delete button asks to delete the highlighted session, in a confirmation over the picker; y or Enter (or Confirm) deletes and n or Esc (or Cancel) keeps it. Ctrl+A, or the picker's directory button, switches the list between this directory's sessions and every directory's, whose rows then name their directory. The picker's action row names both keys.
  • Web client. Section 16.1's trash icon and confirmation.

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
session.delete deletes one root session's tree.

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "session.delete", "params": {
    "session_id": "<root session ID>", "expected_last_seq": 42 } }
  • session_id names a root session. A delegated session is refused: its tree is deleted through its root.
  • expected_last_seq is required, at least 1. It is the root's last_event_seq from the SessionMeta the client showed the user (session.list, session.get, or a sessions.changed upserted). A root whose last event is now another one is refused, so a delete never removes a turn the user has not seen, such as one another client just added. Only the root's log is compared. A change elsewhere in the tree happens during a run, and a running tree is refused anyway.
  • Params are strict like every command: an unknown member is unknown_field.

The result names every session that was deleted, the root first:

{ "deleted": ["<root session ID>", "<subagent ID>", "…"] }

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
All are -32000 registry errors with message, hint, and detail. Three codes exist already, and three are new in 1.5.0:

data.code Fields When session_not_found session_id No such session, or it was already deleted not_a_root_session (new) session_id, root_session_id The session is a delegated subagent. The hint says to delete its root session_tree_running (new) session_id, optional running_session_id A session of the tree has an active run, a compaction, or a subagent waiting for a slot. The hint says to wait for it or cancel it session_owned_elsewhere session_id Another cookie process holds the tree's owner.lock session_changed (new) session_id, current_last_seq expected_last_seq is no longer the root's last event. The hint says to look at the session again engine_error none The tree could not be moved aside on disk. Nothing was deleted, and detail says why

session_running is not reused: its message and hint speak of starting a run, which a delete does not do.

docs.title: What the daemon does
docs.text:
1. Checks. It resolves session_id: an unknown session is session_not_found, a delegated one not_a_root_session.
  2. Ownership. A tree this daemon holds is deleted on the root's session actor, which orders the delete after every request already queued for the root. A tree it does not hold is not adopted: adoption would repair the tree and append events first. The daemon takes the tree's owner.lock for the deletion itself, which fails with session_owned_elsewhere when another process holds it. Neither path writes an event.
  3. Busy and stale checks. In a held tree it refuses with session_tree_running when:
  4. a run of any of the tree's sessions is active;
  5. a compaction holds one of them;
  6. a delegated child waits in the delegation queue;
  7. or a resident session's status is running.

A tree whose lock was free has no live run. A running status there is what a crashed process left, so it does not refuse. Then expected_last_seq is compared with the root's last event: session_changed. 4. Quiescing. The tree's background calls are stopped without a report. Its uploads in progress are dropped. Every resident log of the tree closes its append handle, so no handle stays open in the directory (Windows cannot rename a directory with an open file). 5. Commit. Under the session store's exclusive mutation lock, the root directory sessions/<workdirkey>/<root>/ is renamed in place to a tombstone, sessions/<workdirkey>/.deleted-<root>-<uuid>, and the work directory is synced. The rename is the commit point: from then on no listing, lookup, or tree load finds the tree. A rename that fails changes nothing and is engine_error. On Windows it is retried while another program briefly holds a file open. 6. Forgetting. The daemon drops what it holds for each session of the tree. In the session store: - locations; - the lazy tree-load state and queued load products; - resident projections, evicted summaries, and deferred metadata tips; - ownership (the tree's entry, which drops its lock and write authority, and each session's writable or adopting entry); - live tails; - cached read-only logs; - per-tree gates.

In the engine: - session actors, whose queued requests then fail with session_not_found; - producers and the goal and producer projections; - skill grants and pending skill invocations; - compaction state; - delegation records and queue entries; - delegation recovery claims; - pending approvals; - the tree's permission mode; - the tree's grant journal, after which the visible tree grants are rebuilt; - the tree's artifact store handle; - upload leases; - fork idempotency keys whose source or fork was deleted; - steer ordering.

Queued inputs and the goal live in the log, so they go with it. 7. Unlocking. The tree lock is released. On Unix it is inside the tombstone. On Windows it is the sidecar <root>.owner.lock beside the tree, which is then removed. 8. Telling clients. A sessions.changed removed change goes to every connection for each deleted session, the root first. 9. Removal. The tombstone is removed with everything in it. A failure is logged and leaves only the tombstone. SessionStore::open removes every .deleted-* entry of its work directory, so a daemon that crashed between the rename and the removal cleans up at its next start.

What is removed on disk is the root directory and everything in it:

  • events.jsonl and metadata;
  • owner.lock on Unix;
  • grant-invalidations.jsonl;
  • artifacts/: uploads, retained tool output, and attachments;
  • subagents/index.json;
  • subagents/<child>/ with each child's events.jsonl and metadata;
  • any temporary files.

On Windows the <root>.owner.lock sidecar goes too. The work directory's own files (cwd, layout.json, and the runtime revision index) are shared by every session and stay. A fork made earlier is not touched: it hard-linked its artifacts into its own tree.

docs.title: Subscribers
docs.text:
sessions.changed removed is the only signal. No events.subscription message is added. When a tree is deleted:

  • the daemon drops the live tails of its sessions;
  • each connection forgets its subscriptions to them, so it sends nothing further for them, and events.unsubscribe answers false;
  • a client viewing a deleted session treats removed as "this session is gone": it leaves the view and drops the session's state.

A connection that fell behind gets resync as before, and the deleted sessions are then absent from session.list.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
• Only from 1.5. A client sends session.delete only to a daemon whose handshake protocol_version has minor 5 or later. To an older daemon it shows "The daemon is too old to delete sessions." without sending anything. A -32601 it gets anyway reads the same way.
  • Shared helpers. cookie_agent_client_state provides:
  • whether the daemon's version supports deleting;
  • the call that builds the params from the SessionMeta the user confirmed;
  • the outcome the TUI and the web client show.
  • TUI. The confirmation names the session's title and says how many subagents go with it. Refusals show their registry message and hint.

docs.title: 16.3 Commands, the subagent tree, and the mode picker
docs.text:
Decided by the user, 2026-10-21 (web only; the TUI is unchanged):

  • No slash commands in the web composer. / parsing and the completion popup are gone: text that starts with / (say /compact) is sent as a message. The placeholder is "Message". Every session command is in the title bar's ⋮ menu; the commands with another place keep it (the bottom bar's agent, model, and mode pickers and approvals badge, the composer's attach and Stop, the sidebar's New session, and the rail's views).
  • The ⋮ menu lists each command by a readable name with an icon and a one-line description, never slash syntax, and each opens a sheet (a side sheet on desktop, a bottom sheet on phones) with labelled fields and a main button:
  • Compact context: an optional Focus and Compact (session.compact with the focus); while it compacts, Cancel compaction, as the composer's Stop and Escape do;
  • Goal: the goal with Pause, Resume, and Cancel as the goal bar offers them, and a New objective field with Set the goal;
  • Skills: a search and the picked skill's arguments with Run;
  • Background calls, Runtimes, Permission rules, Usage, Diagnostics, and Agent preset open their existing sheets (the background sheet says so when no call runs in the background).
  • /agent-panel is gone, with its menu entries. Only the open session's row has a subagent tree, in one of two states; a click on the open session's own row switches them (a click on another session still opens it), and the browser keeps the state per session in localStorage (cookie.tree:<session id>):
  • collapsed (the default): the running subagents at any depth, and the subagent the page shows; a running subagent's ancestors that do not run show dimmed, only to place it; with nothing running, nothing shows;
  • expanded: the whole hierarchy, finished subagents included, each foldable by its chevron.

The nodes keep their rendering (status, agent, handle, task, a click opens the child) and the child's breadcrumb stays. - Permission mode picker. The mode chip no longer cycles modes or shows a toast: like the agent and model chips, it has a chevron and opens a picker (the side sheet on desktop, a bottom sheet on phones). The picker lists every mode with its shield, its name, and a line from the permissions guide, checks the current one, and sets the one clicked (session.set_permission_mode); a footnote says deny rules and the loop guard hold in every mode. The web client names the modes as the guide does: auto-approve, auto-approve-n, auto-approve-y, ask, yolo. - The message menu. A user message's ⋯ shows only while a mouse or pen is over the message's row (the whole band at the bubble's height) or the keyboard is in it; its room is kept, so the bubble never moves. A touch screen has no ⋯: a long press on the bubble (500 ms, cancelled by moving or scrolling, without the browser's callout) opens the same menu. - The composer's padding for its in-box buttons is static CSS chosen by which buttons show, so the text clears them from the first render (it was measured after a render, and missed the attach buttons that appear once the model's media are known).

docs.title: 17. Implementation notes
docs.text: Filled in as phases land.

docs.title: Phase L (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Landed as specified, with no wire change and no configuration key.

  • Where it lives. crates/cookie_agent/src/local_daemon.rs holds the probe and the runtime choice; main.rs keeps the wiring thin. cookie attach and plain cookie with a found daemon share one function, run_daemon_tui, after their different connects.
  • Probe. The TCP connect runs on its own under the 500 ms deadline, so "nothing listens" is told apart from "answered but unusable". The WebSocket upgrade then runs over that same connection through a new Rust API, Client::connect_websocket_over in the protocol crate, and it shares the 2 s deadline with the handshake. The configuration is loaded once: the in-process daemon composes from the same load, so a broken configuration still fails before the probe, as it did before.
  • Decision as pure functions. The decision is two pure functions, one per section, rather than one:
  • Probe and its notice() cover the rows of 13.1;
  • choose_runtime covers the steps of 13.2.

runtime_for reads runtimes.list and machines.list only when the machine IDs differ. A daemon that cannot list them gets a dial-in. - Step 2 details. - Own ID excluded. Step 2 never picks the runtime ID this client dials in as (client_<host>). That runtime belongs to another TUI on this machine, which limits it to that TUI's directory, and it goes away when that TUI quits. Dialing in again under the same ID retries until that TUI leaves. - Facts only. The exclusion is by runtime ID, a reported fact, not by kind. - Several workspace capabilities. A runtime that offers more than one capability taking a workspace uses the first in runtimes.list order. - Not only coding. SessionPlacement gained a capability, so a chosen runtime's workspace capability need not be named coding. - Notices (deviation). The notices render as NOTICE rows below the transcript, not in the one-line status row: - the status row truncates the address and the suggestions at narrow widths; - the first action overwrites it.

They stay for the TUI's lifetime, like goal notices. The connection label leads the bottom bar: the daemon's address (127.0.0.1:7419, with wss:// kept), or standalone. cookie attach shows it too. - Version notice. It compares the daemon's engine_version (the server crate's version) with this binary's package version, not with cookie --version, whose git hash would always differ. cookie attach shows it too. - --standalone. - Before a subcommand, main_result refuses it with a clap usage error (exit code 2). - After a subcommand's name, clap rejects it as an unknown argument. - Tests. - Unit. The pure functions are tested over every row and step. - Against a real daemon. crates/cookie_agent/src/tests.rs runs a listening daemon, with a scratch [server] pointing at it. It covers: connect and create a session through it; no token; nothing listening; a wrong token; a listener that closes; a silent listener and the handshake deadline; and a dial-in for another machine ID, whose session attaches client_<host> at the directory. - Binary. crates/cookie_agent/tests/local_daemon.rs runs the real binary against a listener at the scratch home's [server] port that counts connections. Plain cookie dials once. Without a token, and for --standalone and cookie run, nothing dials. - Not tested end to end. - The TUI over a pty. "Plain cookie creates its session through the daemon" is covered by session.create over the probed connection, not by driving a TUI over a pty. - Step 2 against a real daemon. A test daemon reports the test process's own machine ID, so it cannot place a runtime on another machine. The pure function covers step 2.

docs.title: Phase W0a (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
The first half of W0: the protocol client on wasm32 (section 4). The client_state extraction and the markdown choice follow in W0b. There is no wire change.

  • Gating. On wasm32 the crate builds as the wire types and the Client. Gated out by target:
  • the server (session/server*);
  • paths and peer (the stdio peer and its codecs);
  • StopSignals, oauth_callback, and the test corpus;
  • RuntimeMachine::this_machine.

Tokio there is sync and macros only, in a target section of crates/protocol/Cargo.toml, as are gloo-timers, wasm-bindgen(-futures), web-sys, and the js features of uuid and jiff. No getrandom is pulled in. oven-sdk (unchanged pin) and cookie_agent_identity build for wasm32 as they are. - Executor shim. session/rt.rs provides spawn, timeout, sleep, and interval: - natively it is tokio, with the old Delay missed-tick behaviour; - on wasm, spawn_local and gloo-timers, with no Send bound.

The client's logic, limits, and tests stay one copy. - Browser transport. BrowserWebSocketTransport keeps the web_sys::WebSocket in one local task that talks to the transport over channels. - Size limit. A text message over MAX_WEBSOCKET_MESSAGE_BYTES ends the transport with an error. - Entry points. A page calls Client::connect_browser_websocket(url), then the new Client::handshake_with_token. That sends the token in ClientHello.token, serialized from wiping buffers like other secrets. - Refusals before the handshake. A socket that closes before it opens fails with the new ClientError::ConnectionRefusedBeforeHandshake { code, reason }. That covers a refused upgrade, such as an origin allowed_origins does not list, and nothing listening. - Firefox reports code 1006 and no HTTP status, so the client cannot tell an origin refusal from other refusals. - The page shows the allowed_origins hint for this whole error (section 7.2). - URLs. - The browser side checks the new validate_page_websocket_url: ws:// or wss://, with a path ending in /ws (wss://abc.efg/cookie/ws). - Native clients keep validate_websocket_url, which requires the path to be exactly /ws. - Both moved to session/daemon_url.rs. - Tests. - crates/protocol/tests/browser.rs runs in headless Firefox. It covers: - handshake with the token, and a wrong token; - an origin that is not allowed, and nothing listening; - an invalid endpoint, and a subpath endpoint; - a reconnect that keeps the identity and origin; - a reconnect that replays across a gap in which another client renamed the session. - scripts/test-wasm-client.sh runs them against two real cookie daemons in scratch homes: one allowing "*" and one allowing no origin. It passes their URLs and token in at compile time. - Built without them, each test passes without connecting. - Natively, a test covers handshake_with_token against a token-requiring serve, and another covers the URL rules. - CI. A wasm job checks the crate for wasm32 and runs clippy over it with websocket and its tests. The browser tests are not run in CI: they need Firefox, geckodriver, and wasm-bindgen-test-runner.

docs.title: Phase W0b (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
The second half of W0: the shared client state (section 5). There is no wire change, and the TUI's behaviour and tests are unchanged, except for paths that moved.

  • New crate. crates/client_state (cookie_agent_client_state) is published with the other library crates, after cookie_agent_protocol.
  • It depends on cookie_agent_protocol and plain crates only: pulldown-cmark, foldhash, jiff, serde_json, base64, and web-time. web-time gives the replay watchdog an Instant that works in a browser, where std's panics.
  • Nothing in it renders, and it builds for wasm32.
  • The TUI's state module is now a re-export of it.
  • Visibility. SessionState's bookkeeping fields became public, because the TUI's tests build it with struct-update syntax.
  • Test helpers. The few helpers the TUI's tests use sit behind a test-support feature.
  • Moved.
  • The reducer, StateStore, SessionState, the runtime snapshot chain, model display names, and their tests.
  • The markdown parse (client_state::markdown).
  • ownership: classifying a session.resume result, with "owned by another process" meaning a read-only snapshot.
  • model_draft: the 300 ms publish debounce as a generation check, and yielding to a live session_model_selected from another origin.
  • subscriptions:
    • the eight-tree recency set with its eviction;
    • SessionState::is_settled;
    • the 2 s retry wait;
    • the redial backoff, 500 ms to 10 s.
  • uploads: the model's accepted media, the chunked artifact.upload.* exchange, and its refusal messages.

No timer runs in the crate: it returns the delays, and the client sleeps them. - Stayed in the TUI. - The subscription state machine (subscribing, live, recovering, resubscribe-after-ownership). Its transitions start the TUI's RPC tasks. It shares the ownership sets with the view, and it holds the watch the session switch waits on. Moving it needs a command interface better shaped with the web client as a second user (W2). - The ownership bookkeeping. The generation map and the owned and read-only sets are read across the view. - The draft's reset intent and fallback resets. - Upload file handling. Reading the file and sniffing its content with runtime_api's validate_upload stay in the TUI, because that crate is not a plain dependency. The web client needs its own sniffing or a move of that function. - Everything section 5 lists as staying. - Markdown: measured. The release-mode transcript_perf harness ran on 150 runs: 632 items, 12,814 lines, 300 code blocks, 419 KB of reply markdown. Before and after the move it measured: - unchanged redraw: 0.60 ms (0.59 ms with descendant rows), the same as before; - streaming text delta and redraw: 1.06 ms; - first draw: 1.7 to 1.8 s, the same within noise; - resize: 92 ms.

Two further measurements: - Parsing all 419 KB of reply markdown from source takes 1.26 ms, twice an unchanged redraw. - Streaming an eight-run reply in 909 deltas costs 1.16 ms when only the open tail is re-parsed, and 33.9 ms when the whole reply is re-parsed after every delta. - Markdown: chosen. The state keeps the source plus pulldown-cmark events per top-level block, parsed incrementally, as the TUI already did. - A source-only state would make each client re-implement the incremental open-tail parse, about 30 times cheaper per streamed delta than parsing the whole reply. - It would also make each client cache its parse to keep redraws at 0.6 ms. - The ratatui styling, the syntax highlighting, and the TUI's per-block render and highlight caches stay in crates/tui/src/markdown.rs. They live in each block's RendererCache, a slot that clones of a block share, so no redraw re-renders what it did not before. - CI. The wasm job also checks cookie_agent_client_state and runs clippy over it.

docs.title: Phase W1 (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Landed as specified, with no wire change and no configuration change.

  • Leptos and MSRV. Leptos 0.8.22 is the current stable release; 0.9 is a release candidate. It declares rust-version = 1.88, and its dependencies build on 1.88, so the workspace MSRV is unchanged.
  • crates/web (cookie_agent_web, not published) is the client-side rendered Leptos page.
  • It contains:
    • the connect screen (URL fill, #token= handling, paste box, "Forget this daemon", automatic connect, the origin hint after a refusal before the handshake);
    • the connected state, showing the daemon's address and versions;
    • redial with client_state's backoff under the tab's identity, kept in sessionStorage;
    • a check on visibilitychange;
    • the theme toggle.
  • It compiles natively, where only the browser connect is a stub. Native tests cover connect (URL fill, fragment, auto-connect, hint) and theme.
  • Styling.
  • Trunk's rel="tailwind-css" asset runs Tailwind 4.3.3, pinned in Trunk.toml with wasm-bindgen 0.2.126 (Cargo.lock's) and wasm-opt version_131.
  • style/main.css defines the landing palette as @theme colour tokens, @sources src, and makes dark: follow a dark class set from the system setting or the stored override.
  • JetBrains Mono (regular and bold, with its OFL licence) is bundled through Trunk's copy-dir.
  • Build. scripts/build-web.sh checks the pinned trunk (0.21.14) and wasm-bindgen versions, then builds with a new web cargo profile (opt-level = "z", fat LTO, panic = "abort") and wasm-opt -Oz.
  • It copies the result to crates/web_assets/bundle/ and prints sizes.
  • wasm-opt needs the feature flags current Rust emits (bulk memory and others), passed in index.html.
  • W1's bundle is 3.24 MB, 1.24 MB gzipped. Most of it is the 3.0 MB wasm, mainly the protocol crate's types.
  • The daemon serves it uncompressed. Precompressed serving and a size budget are left for W2, which section 10 allows.
  • crates/web_assets embeds the bundle through a build script that writes a table of path, content type, immutability, ETag, and bytes.
  • It falls back to a placeholder index.html.
  • It is published with the bundle through include. Cargo counts the git-ignored bundle as uncommitted, so the release publishes this one crate with --allow-dirty.
  • Server. A fallback route serves the page, with /ws and /runtime explicit and so taking precedence. Anything else, or a method other than GET or HEAD, is a 404.
  • Caching (deviation). Spec 7.1 assumed every bundle file has a hashed name, but Trunk does not hash files copied with copy-dir (here, the fonts). So a file is sent immutable only when its name carries Trunk's hash, and no-cache with an ETag otherwise, like index.html.
  • Headers. Every file carries nosniff.
  • No origin special case. The page's own /ws connection follows allowed_origins.
  • Ready line. The machine-readable daemon-ready line is unchanged, because its format is pinned for supervisors. The page's address and the empty-allowed_origins warning follow it as human log lines.
  • cookie web. It prints <page>#token=<token>, resolving the daemon like cookie attach. --open runs xdg-open, open, or start. cookie_agent_server::page_url derives the page from the client URL, for this command and the ready lines.
  • CI and release.
  • A web CI job:
    • installs trunk through install-action;
    • caches ~/.cache/trunk;
    • runs wasm32 clippy on cookie_agent_web;
    • runs scripts/build-web.sh, with the sizes in the job summary.
  • The release workflow:
    • builds the bundle once (build-web);
    • hands it to every dist build job and to publish-crates;
    • attaches cookie-agent-web.tar.gz to the release.
  • AGENTS.md lists the wasm clippy gate and the build script.
  • Tests.
  • Server:
    • every page path, its content type, cache rule, and ETag revalidation;
    • 404s for other paths and methods;
    • /ws and /runtime precedence;
    • the page's origin refused without an allowed_origins entry and accepted with one.
  • CLI: cookie web derivation and the ready-line page lines.
  • Browser: scripts/test-web-page.sh runs two real daemons, one allowing the page's origin and one allowing none, and drives headless Firefox through geckodriver. It passes:
    • the page connects by itself from the cookie web link, shows the connected state, removes the fragment, and stores the token;
    • against the refusing daemon, it quotes its exact origin as the entry to add.
  • Not in CI. The browser test is not a CI job yet, because it needs Firefox and geckodriver; W5's end-to-end suite adds them.

docs.title: Phase W2 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Core chat landed as specified, with no wire change.

  • Moved into cookie_agent_client_state.
  • The subscription state machine (subscriptions::Subscriptions). It covers subscribing, live, and recovering, a resubscribe once ownership arrives, the recent-tree release, and recovery after a failure.
    • Its methods return the events.subscribe requests to send (a Subscribe with its attempt), and the client reports each outcome back (finish, note_replay_end, release, recovery_failed). The client owns the clock and the RPCs.
    • The TUI drives it from ui/app/subscriptions.rs. The watch its session switch waits on stays in the TUI, keyed by session.
    • The TUI's tests are unchanged except that app.next_subscription_attempt reads app.subscriptions.last_attempt().
  • session_actions, also switched over in the TUI:
    • installing an approval.list into the store;
    • the permission-mode cycle and its labels;
    • toggling and finishing the complete content of a cut block (toggle_full_content, finish_full_content, FullContentState::of_read, block_full).
  • Ownership bookkeeping stayed in each client (deviation). The generation map and the owned and read-only sets stayed, because the TUI's tests read and write those HashSets and HashMaps directly. The web client keeps the same small bookkeeping over the shared ownership::classify_session.
  • The page (crates/web/src/{workspace,views}.rs):
  • Sessions: a list with a directory filter fed by the sessions' cwd_identity (all directories by default) and live sessions.changed.
  • New session: a draft whose first message creates the session. It attaches global and local's coding at the named directory, or takes the daemon's defaults, and applies the draft's mode.
  • Ownership: read-only snapshots for sessions another process owns.
  • The shared reducer, fed by every delivery, with voided input restored to the composer.
  • Composer:
    • Enter, Alt+Enter, Shift+Enter, Ctrl+J, Escape, and Up, mapped by the pure keys::composer_action;
    • Send, with a long press or the ▾ menu to queue;
    • the queue strip with recall;
    • run.cancel;
    • one session.submit_input per message.
  • Approvals: answered at their revision and fingerprint, refreshed on approvals_changed.
  • Pickers: agent, model and variant, and preset, from the runtime.snapshot.get / runtime.changed chain. The draft is published after 300 ms and yields to another client's pick.
  • Status bar: the permission mode and its cycle, the cost (from session.usage, debounced 250 ms as in the TUI), the /usage panel with the session and its tree, and the context size.
  • /events: the level filter, kept in localStorage.
  • Commands: the TUI's names and aliases for W2's commands (/new, /sessions with /resume, /load, /continue, /agent, /model, /preset, /usage, /cancel, /events), plus two with no TUI command of the same name: /approvals (the TUI docks approvals over the composer) and /mode (the TUI cycles the mode from its bottom bar). The ☰ menu lists them all.
  • Transcript HTML (crates/web/src/render/): pure functions, tested natively.
  • Markdown comes from MarkdownBlock events. Raw HTML becomes text; links are kept only for http, https, mailto, and relative URLs, and open in a new tab without an opener; images become links.
  • Display blocks: every kind has its own renderer, and none branches on a tool name.
    • Diffs number lines from the hunks' starts.
    • Terminal SGR becomes spans: classes for the 16 standard colours in both palettes, inline styles for 256-colour and RGB.
    • Media blocks are read with artifact.read into Blob URLs.
    • A block of a kind this build does not know renders nothing, as in the TUI. The daemon already turns a newer kind into its text fallback for an older client.
  • Interaction. Interactive parts carry data-action attributes, which one click handler dispatches.
